{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:25:44.979650+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddcf7310e3245480c68231e2fa545837ff28963d0737266a432f2f99dd5fca32","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 38 (Boundary identity in dimension two) of arXiv:2605.11451, '2605.11451'] Let $\rho\ge0$ and $u(s)=(1-s^p)^\alpha$. Let
\[
 \theta(\varphi)=ae_1+be_2,
 \qquad
 a=\sqrt\sigma\cos\varphi,
 \qquad
 b=\sqrt\sigma\sin\varphi,
\]
with $a>0$ and $0\le b\le a$. Put $B=b/a$ and $\ell=\rho/a$. If
\[
 F_\rho(\varphi)=\int_{B_p^2}(\rho^2-\langle\theta(\varphi),x\rangle^2)_+\,\dd x,
\]
then
\begin{align}
 -F_\rho'(\varphi)
 &=2a^2\alpha\int_0^{1/2}
 \big((1-t)^{2\alpha-1}-t^{2\alpha-1}\big) \notag\\
 &\qquad\times
 \big[Q_\ell(t^\alpha,(1-t)^\alpha)-Q_\ell((1-t)^\alpha,t^\alpha)\big] \dd t.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:09.065822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd0b46475877dc9486644e9b067179e200769ed65364bf4c41a494cfa208634","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 (Properties of the limit process) of arXiv:2606.27117, 'Occupation-Time Fluctuations of an Age-Dependent Branching System Driven by Poisson Immigr'] $\,$  
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item The limit process $\X$ is self-similar with self-similarity index
$\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}$, that is, for every $a>0$,
\[
\{\X(at),\ t\ge0\}
\stackrel{d}{=}
\left\{a^{\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}}\X(t),\ t\ge0\right\}.
\]
   
   
\item For every $0\le s<t$, we have $C(s,t)>0$. In particular, the covariance functional of $\X$ is strictly positive.
    
       
\item For every $0\le s\le t$,
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\left(4-2^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}\right) s^{\gamma}(t-s)^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}
\le
\EE\big(\X(t)-\X(s)\big)^2
\le
\frac{2}{\gamma} (t-s)^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\X$ is not a semimartingale.
    
    
\item $\X$ has Hölder-continuous sample paths of any order less than
$\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}$; that is, for every
\(
\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}\right)
\)
and every $L>0$, there exists a random variable $K_{\varepsilon,L}\ge0$ such that, almost surely,
\[
|\X(t)-\X(s)|
\le
K_{\varepsilon,L}
|t-s|^{(3-d/\alpha)/2-\varepsilon},
\qquad s,t\in[0,L].
\]

\item $\X$ is not Markovian.

\item $\X$ exhibits long-range dependence  in the sense that, for
$0\le r<v\le s<t$,
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}
T^{d/\alpha}
\EE\big[(\X(t+T)-\X(s+T))(\X(v)-\X(r))\big]
=
\frac{2-d/\alpha}{\gamma(1+\gamma)}
(t-s)\big(v^{1+\gamma}-r^{1+\gamma}\big).
\]
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.649094+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd4e20bfd3dd49b8d37a8d98a3fb70fd6d7867fa0b97356656ac3de70c53df1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] Put $(\sR/p)_{\red}:=(R/\sqrt{pR},N)$
 and let $\DA_R^{\str}$ be the category of strict Dieudonn\'e algebras over $R$ from \cite{BLM}.
There is a functor
\[
\mathcal W\uomega^*_{-/\sR}\colon
\mathrm{lPoly}_{(\sR/p)_{\red}}
\longrightarrow
\DA_R^{\str}
\]
characterized as follows. For
$\sP_0=(P_0,L_P)\in\mathrm{lPoly}_{(\sR/p)_{\red}}$, let $\sP$ be its
standard $p$-complete polynomial $F$-lift over $\sR$, and put
\[
\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)
:=
\WSat\bigl(\widehat{\uomega}^*_{\sP/\sR}\bigr)
\in(\DAlogSs)^{\str}.
\]
Then $\mathcal W\uomega^*_{\sP_0/\sR}$ is the underlying strict
Dieudonn\'e algebra of $\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)$.

Let
\[
q_{\sP}\colon
\widehat{\uomega}^*_{\sP/\sR}
\longrightarrow
\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)
\]
be the  unit map, and let
\[
e_{\sP_0}\colon
\sP_0
\longrightarrow
\left(
 (\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)^0/p)_{\red},L_P
\right)
\]
be its reduction on degree zero. For a morphism
$u\colon\sP_0\to\sQ_0$, the morphism
$\mathbf W_{\sR}(u):\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)\to \mathbf W_{\sR}(\sQ_0) $ 
is the unique strict logarithmic Dieudonn\'e
algebra morphism satisfying
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf W_{\sR}(u)^0/p)_{\red}\circ e_{\sP_0}
=
e_{\sQ_0}\circ u.
\end{equation}
Precomposing with reduction gives, in particular, a functor on
$\mathrm{lPoly}_{\sR/p}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:16:46.109724+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd565cec187823e1608701db2d957bf33d8b750310c249b529e4602192ea2dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop IGgoup of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $\omega\in\Omega_0$. There exists a process $\bigl\{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}:\theta\in\Theta^\omega,(x,s)\in\IG\theta,{\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}\bigr\}$ of bi-infinite space-time paths such that the following hold for all $\theta\in\Theta^\omega$ and $(x,s)\in\IG\theta$.
    \begin{enumerate} [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt 
    \item For each ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is a continuous space-time path.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)\le \Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(t)\in\IG\theta$.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, if $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)<\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$, then $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)$ is right-isolated and $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$ is left-isolated. Conversely, if $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$, then this point is neither left- nor right-isolated.
    \item $(x,s)\in\{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s),\,\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s)\}$.
Moreover, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s)=(x,s)$ if and only if $(x,s)$ is not left-isolated, and
$\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s)=(x,s)$ if and only if $(x,s)$ is not right-isolated. 
    \item For any $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(r)}^{\theta-}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}$ and $\Psi_{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(r)}^{\theta+}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}$.
    \item For any $(x',s')\in\IG\theta$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, either $\Psi_{(x',s')}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}$ or $\Psi_{(x',s')}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}\cap\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}=\varnothing$.
    \item For any $s'\in\mathbb{R}$, 
    \begin{align}
    \begin{split}
    &\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\prec\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\preceq\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\quad\text{and}\\
    &\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\preceq\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\prec\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}.
    \end{split}
    \end{align}
    \item For any $s'\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Upsilon\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\preceq\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}\preceq\Upsilon\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}$.
    \item For any ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$,
$\displaystyle\lim_{|t|\to\infty}t^{-1}\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(t)=(\theta,1)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Standard Borel covariate; strictly positive measurable score almost surely, finite mean score.","Fixed retention fraction strictly between zero and one.","Conditional unbiasedness and the mean positive-weight retention budget; no claim about estimator asymptotics."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:15.363712+00:00","domain":"Statistical data selection and inverse-probability weighting","id":"claim_ddd5fc36f48265162995ac3142dd2378fa412c120b9b084e148942e78dec54b7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon optimal unbiased selection, strictly positive-score specialization. Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). There is a unique c>0 such that E pi_star(X)=gamma. The minimum is E[Z(X)/pi_star(X)]=E[max(Z(X),sqrt(Z(X))/c)]<infinity. Every minimizer has this same retention probability almost surely and has constant weight 1/pi_star(X) on its retained observations, conditional on X. Uniform random retention has objective E Z/gamma; the optimal objective is strictly smaller unless Z is almost surely constant. This is the convex allocation problem in Proposition4.2 and AppendixB of Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon, with the strict-positive-score restriction stated explicitly to avoid zero-score conventions. It optimizes an unbiased influence objective; it does not establish the asymptotics of a pruned max-margin estimator.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160007+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd6491be1c5db5cdc2f2ad6faed5d6d4413eeba2fa8fac7c0c78e51208bdedf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 1 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix parameters $\alpha, L, r,s, \iota, \epsilon$. As above, let $\omega$ denote a random variable, and let $\bG, \bXi$ be $M\times N$ matrices with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries, with rows $\barbg^1,\ldots,\barbg^M$ and $\bmeta^1,\ldots,\bmeta^M$ respectively, such that $\bXi$ is independent of $(\bG,\omega)$. Let $\bar{\bx} = \bar{\bx}(\bG)$ and $\hat{\by} = \hat{\by}(\bG, \bXi)$ be $L$-Lipschitz, $\R^N$-valued functions such that 
\begin{align*}
    &\E \|\bar{\bx}\|^2 = \E \|\hat{\by}\|^2 = N\,, \\ 
    &\E(\hat{\by}\,|\,\bG) = \bzero\,\,\text{almost surely}\,.
\end{align*} As in \eqref{e:fp-partition}, let $ \hat{\cB} = \hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)$ be a random partition of $[M]$ and $[N]$ into $r$ and $s$ parts respectively, with proportions $\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega)$ as in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}. Assume these proportions satisfy condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda}, so that $r,s$ must satisfy condition~\eqref{e:r-s-bd}. Then, for all sufficiently large $N$,  we have
    \beq
        
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \lambda_j(\bG,\omega) \,
        \Cost(\bbb_j,\uuu_j,\vvv_j)
        \le \frac1\alpha
         \bigg(
            \sum_{j=1}^s
            \mu_j(\bG,\omega)
            (\www_j)^{1/2}
        \bigg)^2
        + \epsilon
    \eeq
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$, where $c$ is a positive constant depending on the parameters $\alpha, L, \iota, \epsilon$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.937433+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd922941e90c58e06a587832eddc29dd3678487294f57026a46387111a974fa","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $\eta>0$, $n,k,d\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge k$, and $d\ge2$. There exists a
constant $C(\eta,k,d,n)>0$, depending only on $\eta,k,d,n$, such that, for
every absolutely continuous log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and
every
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in\mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
such that
\[
\sigma_{f_j}^2:=\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f_j)>0
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \eta,
\]
the following two estimates hold.

First, for every $\psi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ satisfying $0\le\psi\le1$,
one has
\[
\bigl(\sigma_{f_1}^2\cdot\ldots\cdot\sigma_{f_k}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\int_{\mathbb R^n}\psi(f)\,d\mu
\le
C(\eta,k,d,n)
\|\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^k)}^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}.
\]
Second, for every unit vector $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, every $t>0$, and every
$\varphi\in C_b^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ satisfying
\[
\|\varphi\|_\infty\le t,
\quad
\|\partial_\theta\varphi\|_\infty\le 1,
\]
one has
\[
\bigl(\sigma_{f_1}^2\cdot\ldots\cdot\sigma_{f_k}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\biggl|
\int_{\mathbb R^n}(\partial_\theta\varphi)(f)\,d\mu
\biggr|
\le
C(\eta,k,d,n)t^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}
\biggl(\sum_{j=1}^k\sigma_{f_j}^2\biggr)^{\frac{k-1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:41:03.331299+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddda1c85f8b521e76297234044f9796d3b659c10424a089f94048f0e35f9a262","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2411.09075, 'Weak Poincar{\'e} Inequalities, Simulated Annealing, and Sampling from Spherical Spin Glas'] We say $\pi$ satisfies a \emph{weak \Poincare inequality} if for some error functional $\Error: \R_{>0}^{\Omega} \to \R_{\ge 0}$ and $\CPoi > 0$,

    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.746107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de12232140b00c54f654a321a766291084b9267f14677bea219692b0e6f96eed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P","Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha","Finite second moment of xi_0","Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k","Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:05:57.431397+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; Markov jump linear systems","id":"claim_de1b5940314d04a7ddcbc45caa566cc8e834b108f83b393e8aa92596fbff4e17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Fix real d-by-d matrices A_i, real d-vectors b_i and a constant alpha. Set H_i=I+alpha A_i and let xi_(k+1)=H_(z_k)xi_k+alpha b_(z_k). Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. For stacked q_k and v_k=(vec(Q_k^1),...,vec(Q_k^N)), columnwise vectorization gives q_(k+1)=H11 q_k+alpha(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_d)b and v_(k+1)=H22 v_k+H21 q_k+alpha^2(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_(d^2))b2, where b stacks b_i, b2 stacks b_i tensor b_i, H11_(j,i)=p_ij H_i, H22_(j,i)=p_ij(H_i tensor H_i), and H21_(j,i)=alpha p_ij[b_i tensor H_i+H_i tensor b_i]. In particular H22=(P^T tensor I_(d^2))diag_i(H_i tensor H_i); the update factor uses the departure state i. The raw second moment is sum_i Q_k^i and E||xi_k||^2=sum_i trace(Q_k^i); these Q_k^i are not centered conditional covariances. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:07.876882+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de2e9fcb830b0dce242036c59270968aa9a4dc9ee9dcd48146d2b1374a1a3efd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_regular of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Given a convex chain $\mathcal{C}$, let $f_\mathcal{C}\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be the maximal convex function starting at $f_\mathcal{C}(0)=0$ and satisfying $f_\mathcal{C}(x)=y$ for every $(x,y)\in\mathcal{C}$.
That is, $f_\mathcal{C}$ is piecewise linear with corners at the elements of $\mathcal{C}$, and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$ unless $(1,y)\in\mathcal{C}$ for some $y\in[0,1)$.

Given $\rho\in(0,\frac12)$, we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-regular} if $f_\mathcal{C}(1-\rho)\geqslant\rho$ and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$.
Otherwise we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-irregular}. 
Note that if $\mathcal{C}$ is $\rho$-regular, then it is $\rho'$-regular for every $\rho'\in(0,\rho]$.
\hfill\ensuremath{\square}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356404+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de6ed04e0e0829407fc76e9f9053d5e379c62e487fac745c92001f9f22aa70f4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $\cA_N$ is a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm.
	Then there exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ depending on only $\alpha$ and $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
			 \le C(\alpha)
			\,\,\text{and}\,\,
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
	Furthermore, for any $k\ge 1$, there exists $C(\alpha,k)$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,
	\beq
		\max\bigg\{
			\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op})^k]}
				{N^{k/2}}, 
			\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^k]}{N^{k/2}}
		\bigg\} \le C(\alpha,k)\,.
	\eeq
\begin{proof}
	By Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}, there exists $C(\alpha)$ such that 
	\beq
		
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
		 \le C(\alpha)
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Since the mapping $(\bG,\bg^\aux) \mapsto \|\bx\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian.
	Combined with the equality $\E[\|\bx\|^2] = N$ from Definition~\ref{d:Lip}, this readily implies
	\[
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bx\|}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 \le 2\bigg) 
		 \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
which gives \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail}.
	By Jensen's inequality,
	\[
		\frac{\E\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}}
		\le 
		\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^2]^{1/2}}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 = 1
		 \,.
	\]
Since $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian, for any $u\ge1$ we have
	\[\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg)
		\le \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\| - \E\|\bx\|]}{N^{1/2}} \ge u - 1
		\bigg) 
		\le \exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}
		\bigg)\,.\]
Integrating this bound gives
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le 2^k + \int_{2^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt
		= 2^k + \int_2^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du \\
		&\le 2^k + \int_2^\infty \exp\bigg(-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du 
		\le 2^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	Since the mapping $\bG \mapsto \|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-subgaussian.
	Then \eqref{e:confinement.wishart.restated} implies that $\E[\|\bG\|_{\op}] \le C(\alpha) N^{1/2}$. Then, by a similar calculation as above, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt \\
		&= (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1} \,du \\
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty
		\exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-C(\alpha))^2 N}{2}
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du
		\le (2C(\alpha))^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	This proves \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.808832+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de6f56791f4a4f41f56742afdc1449f7df32121e5f736fa0f4eca1ba9641b4d2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Lem:prin of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] {BFMS25}}]

T_t) is the law at time t of a classical (resp. free) strictly alpha-stable process and the initial law mu has a finite moment of order 2 + alpha, then mu * S_t (resp. mu boxplus T_t) is unimodal for all large t. \]
Then \(\Phi_{P,r,\Sigma}\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(\R^r\) and

 i^{-r}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.495274+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec1f14d27a1db30a6d8dabe2fe80c84dc4cfadfc7e265da9ef866b4244aced3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let
\[
\mathcal R(u):=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|u|^2\,dx},
\qquad
\mathcal A:=
\{u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}:M(u)\geq0\}.
\]
Suppose that \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) is a local minimizer of
\(\mathcal R\) on \(\mathcal A\). Then there exist
\(\mu_0,\mu_1\geq0\), with \(\mu_0+\mu_1>0\), such that
\begin{equation}
	\mu_0D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu_1DM(\bar u),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	\mu_1M(\bar u)=0.
\end{equation}
If \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), then \(\mu_0>0\), and consequently there exists
\(\mu\geq0\) such that
\begin{equation}
	D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu\,DM(\bar u),
	\qquad
	\mu M(\bar u)=0.
	
\end{equation}
Thus, under the constraint qualification \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), the
Fritz John conditions \cite{John} reduce to the usual Kuhn--Tucker
conditions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\eqdef(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},\tilde\sigma_1,\dots,\tilde\sigma_{p({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})})\,.
\end{equs}
Fix ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and
suppose that for every $i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we are given tuples of times $(t_{i},s^{\tau_i})\in(-\infty,1]\times\R^{\mathfrak{s}(\tau_i)}$.
We then write
\begin{equs}
    t_{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef (t_{\tau_1},\dots,t_{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}})  \in (-\infty,1]^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,\;\text{and}\;s^{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef(s^{\tau_1},\dots,s^{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}}) \in \R^{\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,
\end{equs}
where $\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{$\mathfrak{s}$}(\tau_i)$ is the \textit{size} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$. We also write $\mathfrak{l}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})+\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. 

Finally, we define the \textit{scaling} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by
\begin{equs}    |{\boldsymbol{\tau}}|\eqdef\big(p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})-1\big)+\sum_{i=1}^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}|\tau_i|\,,
\end{equs}
the \textit{order} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by $\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef \sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}(\tau_i) $, and set $r({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}r_i$ and $u({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}u_i$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.642694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dedb47cb49ca03e3d809abd5685ffdbcbde13bd9575f46646317a0119f60760b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 13 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(Z\) be a subordinator with Laplace exponent \(\psi\), and let \(\mu_Z\) be the random measure on \([0,\infty)\) induced by \(Z\), namely
\[
\mu_Z((a,b]) := Z_b-Z_a
\quad (0\le a<b<\infty).
\]
Let \(A\subset [0,\infty)\) be a Borel set with \(\lambda(A)<\infty\), where \(\lambda\) denotes the Lebesgue measure.
Then
\begin{align}
  E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0). 
\end{align}
In particular,
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{\lambda(A)},
\]
and if \(A,B \subset [0,\infty)\) are disjoint, \(\mu_{Z}(A)\) and \(\mu_{Z}(B)\) are independent.
More generally, if \(A\) is a random Borel set independent of \(Z\), then
\[
E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}\mid A]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0),
\]
and hence, if \(\lambda(A)=a\) almost surely for some \(a\ge0\), then
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{a}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.451258+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_deed56290d8f535b90be8e27ba5e8551c242b22c8242d4b59a606c5f064f2e55","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 14 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] Let $\cB_p$ be the orthonormal basis of the direct sum $H^p = H^{\oplus p}$ induced by the orthonormal basis $\cB$ of $H$, $k \in \N_0$, $R > 0$, and $Q \in \Tr^1(\cB_p)$.
Write
\[
\norm{Q}_{j,c,R} \coloneqq \sup_{(\cA,\tau) \in \mathbb{W}}\ \sup_{n\geq 0}\ \sup_{j_0+\dots+j_n=j} \norm{\Big(\widetilde{\partial}^{(j_n)}\circ\cdots\circ \widetilde{\partial}^{(j_1)}\circ \partial^{(j_0)}Q\Big)^{\cA}}_{\cA,c,R},
\]
where we view $\Big(\widetilde{\partial}^{(j_n)}\circ\cdots\circ \widetilde{\partial}^{(j_1)}\circ \partial^{(j_0)}Q\Big)^{\cA}$ as a function from $\cA_{c,\sa}^{\cB,p\times (j+1)}$ to $\cA$ where each of the $j+1$ tensorand is evaluated in different variables.
We then set
\[
\norm{Q}_{\cC^k,R} \coloneqq \sup_{0\leq j\leq k} \norm{Q}_{j,c,R}.
\]
Define $\cC^k_p(\cB)$ to be the Fr\'echet-space completion of $\Tr^1(\cB_p)$ with respect to the family $\big\{\norm{\cdot}_{\cC^k,R} : R > 0\big\}$ of seminorms and $\cC^{\infty}_p(\cB)$ to be the Fr\'echet-space completion of $\Tr^1(\cB_p)$ with respect to the family $\big\{\norm{\cdot}_{\cC^k,R} : R > 0, \, k \in \N\big\}$ of seminorms. And finally, we set $\cC^k(\cB)$ the union of every $\cC^k_p(\cB)$.","status":"unverified"}

\[
\bH=\diag(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots),

0\leq\rho<1,
\qquad
\sigma>0.

\[
\Delta_{\nesterov}(x)
:=
2B(1-\rho^2)
+
\left[4B\rho^2+(B-1)\rho-(B+1)\right]x

(B+1)\rho(1+2\rho)x^2.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198334+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df26d27bad5c5d1eeef1c6602c0d167196e97df45a91ccf2597a76b1fb895a00","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 125 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $J\equiv J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then the coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:cts.coeffs} satisfy the estimates 
	\[
	\max\left\{
	\begin{array}{c}
	|\tbbb(t,y)^2
		-\Tbbb(t,y)^2|,\\
	|\tvvv(t,y)-\Tvvv(t,y)|,\\
	|\tuuu(t,y)^2-\Tuuu(t,y)^2|
	\end{array}
	\right\}
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \lambda
	\]
for all $(t,y)\in( [q_*,1]  \setminus J)\times\R$. 

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} gives
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\tB(t,y)&=\tB^N(t,y)+o_N(1)\,,\\
	\Tbbb(t,y)&=\Tbbb^N(t,y)+o_N(1)
	\end{aligned}\]
for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$. Recall that $(p^N)'(t)$ converges to $p'(t)$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, for \emph{every} $t$, we can find $s\in[t-\tep,t+\tep]$ such that $(p^N)'(s)$ converges to $p'(s)$. If $t\notin J$, then $t\notin J^N$ for sufficiently large $N$ by Lemma~\ref{l:bad.times.JN.J}, so $p'(s)$ differs from $p'(t)$ by at most $\lambda/2$, while $(p^N)'(s)$ differs from $(p^N)'(t)$ by at most $\lambda$. Therefore, for $t\in[q_*,1]\setminus J$, we have
	\[
	\Big|\tbbb(t,y)-\tbbb^N(t,y)\Big|
	=\bigg|\frac{\tB(t,y)}{p'(t)^{1/2}}
	-\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2}}\bigg|
	\le o_N(1)
	+ \bigg( \frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda\,,
	\]
using the bounds on $\tB^N$ and $\tB$ implied by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}.
Additionally, since $t\notin J^N$,
Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} bounds the discrepancy between $\tbbb^N(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb^N(t,y)$.
Sending $N\to\infty$ gives the claimed bound on the discrepancy between $\tbbb(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb(t,y)$. The other bounds follow by similar arguments:
	\begin{align*}
	\Big|\tvvv(t,y)-\tvvv^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|
	\frac{\tV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	-\frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}\bigg|\,,\\
	\Big|\tuuu(t,y)-\tuuu^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\tU(t,y)}{[ p(t)
		\cdot t p'(t)]^{1/2}}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df2ec02ab8113e2c74344a7c95930cb4ecc1735b76c9be1b5407fe24fca67876","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 234 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exist $C(\alpha) > 0$ and $C(\alpha,L,K) > 0$, such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	If $\cA_N$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm and $\cA_{N[K]}$ is as in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, then 
	\begin{align}
		
		\max\{ 
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		,\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2
		\}
		 &\le C(\alpha)\,, \\
		
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4 &\le C(\alpha,L,K)\,.
	\end{align}
	Furthermore, for $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2 \le C(\alpha)
			\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof $c > 0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha,L$ which may change line by line. Recall that we abbreviate $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
	We prove \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} first. Recalling the definition of $\fm$ from Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, note that
\beq
		\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		=\frac{\|\fm\|^2}{M} 
		= \frac{1}{M} \bigg\|\frac{\bG \bx}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\|^2
		\le \frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2}{MN} \,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the above is
	\[
	\le \frac{C(\alpha)^2 N \cdot 4N}{MN} 
		= \frac{4C(\alpha)^2}{\alpha}\,.
	\]
	This proves \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.
	Next, note that
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		= \E \|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		= 
		\frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M} 
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.step1}}{\le} 
		\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2]}{MN} \,.
	\]
By H\"older's inequality and the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{\E [(\|\bG\|_{\op})^4]^{1/2} \E[\|\bx\|^4]^{1/2}}{MN} 
		\le \frac{C(\alpha,4)N^2}{MN} 
		= \frac{C(\alpha,4)}{\alpha}\,,
	\]
	for $C(\alpha,4)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}.
This proves the first part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$. For the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}, we split into cases depending on whether $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$. Recall that the truncated algorithm $\cA_{N[K]}$ resamples the rows indexed by $S_K(\cA_N)$. If $a\notin S_K(\cA_N)$, then $\tilde{\fm}_a$ is equidistributed as $\fm_a$, so they have the same second moment. If $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$, then 
	\[\tilde{\fm}_a
		= \frac{(\bg^a, \tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
where $\bg^a$ is independent of $\tilde{\bx}$, as $\cA_{N[K]}$ does not use the input $\bg^a$.
	Thus, the distribution of $\tilde{\fm}_a$ conditional on $\tilde{\bx}$ is a (one-dimensional) centered gaussian random variable with standard deviation $\|\tilde{\bx}\| / N^{1/2}$. It follows in this case that
	\[
	\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^2]
	= \frac{\E[\|\tilde{\bx}\|^2]}{N}=1\,.
	\]
Altogether this gives
	\[
	\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|^2
	=\frac{ \E[\|\tilde{\fm}\|^2]}{M}
	\le
	\frac{ \E[\|\fm\|^2 + M]}{M}
	\le C(\alpha)+1\,.
	\]
This proves the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.

Finally we turn to the proof of  \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}. Recalling the notations of Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, let
	\[
	\tilde{\fm}_a
	\equiv

		\Big)

	\]
where we recall that $\tilde{\bx}\equiv \cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))$. 
We then aim to bound
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4
		= \E \Big[\|\mu_\bG(\cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))\|_{L^4}^4\Big]
		= \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M 
		\E\Big[
		(\tilde{\fm}_a)^4\Big]\,.
	\]
To this end, we will show that there exists $C(\alpha,L,K)$ such that
	\beq
		\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^4] \le C(\alpha,L,K)
	\eeq
	for all $a\in [M]$, which implies \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.897970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df3e6ebb290d7b0f2ea7bfc5e4c3bc16082f28eb79826863386b3b49d7f365fc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.00449, 'First-order phase transitions in the hard-core model'] \label[definition]{def:orders}
    Suppose that $G$ is an infinite graph such that a phase transition occurs at $\lambda^*>0$. 
    For $\lambda>0$ and a vertex $u$ of $G$, let $D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ be defined as 
    \[ D_{G,u}(\lambda) = \sup_{\mu,\nu}\left| \mu(u) - \nu(u) \right|, \]
    where the supremum is over all pairs of hard-core measures $\mu,\nu$ on $G$ at fugacity $\lambda$.
    Suppose also that for each vertex $u$, the one-sided limit from above $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*) = \lim_{\lambda\downarrow \lambda^*} D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ exists.
    
    If there exists a vertex $u\in V(G)$ such that $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)>0$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{first-order} phase transition.
    If, on the other hand, $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)=0$ for all $u\in V(G)$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{second-order} phase transition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["0 < p < 1 fixed as n -> infinity (for p depending on n with np -> lambda the limit is Poisson instead)","k ranges over integers with (k - np)/sqrt(npq) bounded, or o(n^{1/6}), for the local form"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626235+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_df6a466ce933ab4f9b4f32b64d7076ef5a00cf02548046ad963d1ae983e2702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let S_n be binomial with parameters n and p, 0 < p < 1, q = 1 - p, and write k = np + x sqrt(npq). LOCAL FORM: uniformly for x in any bounded interval (indeed for |x| = o(n^{1/6})), P(S_n = k) = (2 pi n p q)^{-1/2} exp(-x^2 / 2) (1 + o(1)) as n -> infinity. INTEGRAL FORM: for fixed a < b, P(a <= (S_n - np) / sqrt(npq) <= b) -> Phi(b) - Phi(a), the standard normal probability of [a, b]; equivalently (S_n - np)/sqrt(npq) converges in distribution to N(0,1). {"assumptions":["t>0.","The classical Ibragimov characterization for nondegenerate absolutely continuous laws."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df81d86c41a2e859c5a707fc5ae34d83a64ca8c89b34f2c04e48ecc49cc1f09a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved special case of Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. Call lambda freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal probability measure nu. For every t>0 the centered Cauchy distribution C_t with density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] is not freely strongly unimodal: some unimodal nu makes nu boxplus C_t nonunimodal. The proof combines the Cauchy convolution identity with Ibragimov's characterization of classical strong unimodality by log-concavity of the density; the Cauchy density is not log-concave. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","a one-parameter family of unitaries or an exponential e^{itT} is being used","the continuity and self-adjointness hypotheses are the ones at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772569+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum dynamics","id":"claim_df9328ea820c9b58103e280388d82cc43f63148f9a76b0b2e1fdd63f459b8d1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). There is no unitary group whose generator extends S, so exponentiating a symmetric operator to 'e^{itS}' is not legitimate: only self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness followed by taking the closure) licenses the unitary group. Audit rule: in quantum dynamics arguments, check that the Hamiltonian has been shown self-adjoint on a stated domain before using e^{itH}, unitarity, conservation of norm, or invariance of D(H).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732600+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_dfb0e656c58d4f14dd665a85b8ce62d25a662a2455b987541fa0436ab64565e1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:23:25.633918+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dfd4549abb5dcd3f26ed7d9297622e210cd2cd15f47c3a71adaad260cef6016e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Result1 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m>1$ and let $c_1,c_2,c_3,\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$. Then
\[
  f_1(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\bigl(c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+x^{q+2}\bigr)
\]
is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ if and only if one of the following
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\gamma=0$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)\neq0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)=\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)=0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)\neq\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$, $m$ is odd, and, with
        $A:={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_3\gamma^3+\gamma^{q+2})$,
        \[
          A\neq0,\qquad
          {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma^2)+(c_3\gamma+\gamma^{q})^{q+1}=0,\qquad
          A\bigl(1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)\bigr)+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2^2\gamma^4)=0 .
        \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.738823+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dfeae846fc728b813d8462c1bf3d183847b4171b9188dcd17a1e88853ae6fbfd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Geometric interpolation of two equivalent Gaussian measures on Hilbert space}]
		
		Let $\mu_i = \Ncal(m_i, C_i) \in \Gauss(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$, $i=0,1$, where
		$C_i = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_i)C_{*}^{1/2}$, $S_i \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{<I}$. Let the corresponding 
		Radon-Nikodym densities with respect to $\mu_{*}$ be denoted by $p_i = \frac{d\mu_i}{d\mu_{*}}$. Then
		for $\alpha \in [0,1]$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) = \frac{d\mu_{\alpha}}{d\mu_{*}},
			
			
		\end{align}
		where $\mu_{\alpha} = \Ncal(m_{\alpha}, C_{\alpha}) \in \Gauss(\Hcal,\mu_{*})$, $C_{\alpha} = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})C_{*}^{1/2}$, with
		\begin{align}
			S_{\alpha} &= I - [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1} \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{< I},
			
			\\
			C_{\alpha} &= C_{*}^{1/2} [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1}C_{*}^{1/2},
			
			\\
			m_{\alpha} &= m_{*} + C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})[(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*}) 
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad + \alpha(I-S_1)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})].
			
		\end{align}
	The normalizing factor is given by
	\begin{align}
		&Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)
		\nonumber
		= 
		\int_{\Hcal}p_0^{1-\alpha}(x)p_1^{\alpha}(x) d\mu_{*}(x)
		\\
		&=\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}]^{-1/2}
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||(I-S_0)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times 
		\exp\left[-\frac{\alpha}{2}||(I-S_1)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right).
		
	\end{align}
		Here $I + A = (I-S_1)^{-1/2}(I-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} > 0$, with $A =(I-S_1)^{-1/2}(S_1-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} \in \Sym(\Hcal)\cap \HS(\Hcal).$
		In particular, for $S_0, S_1 \in \SymTr(\Hcal)_{< I}$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) &	=[\det(I-S_{\alpha})]^{-1/2}
			\nonumber
			\\
			& \quad \times \exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra \right\}
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp(\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra)
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right].
			
		\end{align}
Let $P_N = \sum_{k=1}^Ne_k \otimes e_k$, $N \in \Nbb$, be the orthogonal projection onto the $N$-dimensional subspace of $\Hcal$ spanned
by $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^N$, where $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ are the orthonormal eigenvectors of $C_{*}$.
In the expression in Eq.\eqref{equation:geometric-interpolation-Gaussian-S-Tr},
\begin{align}
	&\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty} \la C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\\
	&
	\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra 
	\nonumber
	\\
	&\doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty} \la C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{*})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra,
\end{align}
with the limits being in the 

$\Lcal^2(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$ sense. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.375619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dff9bffa0ab891c73511e0184790ef06096f22a114fc8353137b035d6e8368dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] There exists a stochastic process 
\begin{align}
    \bigl(B^{h{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\, h \in \mathcal{H},\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)
\end{align}
on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\{B^{h-}= B^{h+}\}=1.
\]
When $B^{h-}(\omega) = B^{h+}(\omega)$, call the common cocycle $B^h(\omega)$.
\item \textup{(}Forward measurable Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h\in \mathcal{H}, B^h \in \mathcal K_c^+$.
\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$, $\mathbb{E}[B^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in \mathcal{H}$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\mathbb{P}$ almost every $\omega$
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1)  
\]
and
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2).
\]
\item \textup{(}Left-/right-continuity\textup{)} For $\mathbb{P}$-almost all $\omega$, all $h\in \mathcal{H}$, and all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \nearrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y) \,\text{ and }\, B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \searrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y).
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this process is unique in the sense that any two processes satisfying the above conditions are equal almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.593474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e01d5d09db42bfc35e775f7244f04d49e8975ab9c0242e8d9c0df1121448b943","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02743, 'Sharp mean-field estimates for diffusive log/Riesz gases in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime'] \\begingroup We study fixed-temperature logarithmic and Riesz gases after subtracting the leading mean-field contribution relative to a prescribed background law. For repulsive interactions in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime, we prove $N$-uniform bounds and quantitative convergence of the resulting modulated partition function to a normalization expressed by the Carleman--Fredholm determinant of the centered interaction operator. We show that the Hilbert--Schmidt threshold is sharp and obtain explicit lower bounds on the rate of divergence at and above it; these rates are expected to be nonoptimal. The proof combines positive-definite truncations and a low/high-frequency decomposition with exponential inequalities and Gaussian-chaos asymptotics for canonical degree-two $U$-statistics. As consequences, we establish entropic commutator estimates with the sharp $O(N^{-1})$ additive scale in the modulated-free-energy method, a static joint linear-statistics central limit theorem, and a dynamical central limit theorem for joint linear statistics at finitely many times. This extends the logarithmic partition-function estimates of the first two authors to the full Riesz Hilbert--Schmidt range and identifies the limiting determinant normalization. For the attractive logarithmic interaction at sufficiently small inverse temperature, we also prove analogous results. \\endgroup","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.976050+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e0228a8876c77951bd23cfc70305cbadfb799fd70fa98dfc56f36d6b1b3550f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 48 (Fock energy and free-capacity balance) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Assume in this theorem that \(M\) is continuous and that \(V_T\leq K\)
almost surely for a deterministic \(K<\infty\).  Let \(Z^\lambda\) and
\(Z^{\lambda,N}=P_{\leq N}Z^\lambda\) be the exterior lifts above, and put
\[
 T_t^N=Z_t^{\lambda,N}\otimes Z_t^{\lambda,N},
 \qquad T_t=Z_t^\lambda\otimes Z_t^\lambda.
\]
The finite-level bracket is \eqref{cc:eq-exterior-Fock-bracket}, and its
trace-class limit is the equality of positive
\(\mathcal S_1(\mathcal F_{\wedge}(H))\)-valued measures
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm d\langle Z^\lambda\rangle_t
 =\lambda^2\mathcal B_{\mathrm dR_t}(T_t).
 
\end{equation}
More explicitly, write
\(
 \mathrm dR_t=r_t\,\mathrm dV_t
\), where \(r_t\succeq0\) and
\(\operatorname{Tr}r_t=1\) for \(\mathrm dV\)-almost every \(t\), and set
\[
 Y_t=\|Z_t^\lambda\|^2,
 \qquad
 L_t=2\int_0^t
      \langle Z_s^\lambda,\mathrm dZ_s^\lambda\rangle.
\]
Then \(L\) is a real continuous local martingale and
\begin{align}
 \mathrm dY_t
 &=\mathrm dL_t
   +\lambda^2\operatorname{Cap}^{\mathrm{free}}_{r_t}(T_t)
      \,\mathrm dV_t \notag\\
 &=\mathrm dL_t
   +\lambda^2\left(
      Y_t-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm d\Gamma(r_t)T_t)
     \right)\mathrm dV_t,
 \\
 \mathrm d[L]_t
 &\leq4\lambda^2Y_t
   \operatorname{Cap}^{\mathrm{free}}_{r_t}(T_t)
   \,\mathrm dV_t.
 
\end{align}
Thus the predictable growth of Fock energy is exactly the free capacity;
the occupied part is removed, rather than estimated away.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.056837+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e02df6e7008de2572a83edb0462c226bcad4b7a0dff7276dbd117a9e18dd763b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:first-order-interval-correspondence of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Suppose that Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) holds.  For every $\alpha\geq0$,
every regular weight $w$ of order $\alpha$, every interval $I=(r_0,r_1)$,
every integer $m\geq1$, and
\begin{equation*}
 F\in L_w^2(I;\mathbb R^m),\qquad \eta\in L^2(\mu_{r_1};\mathbb R^m),
\end{equation*}
there is a unique first-order occupation-energy solution in the sense of
Definition~(def:first-order-occupation-solution of the paper), denoted by
$\mathcal U_I^w(F,\eta)$.  In the following BSDE, $D_xu$ is the $m\times d$
Jacobian and
\begin{equation*}
 \mathsf Z u:=(D_xu)\sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}.
\end{equation*}
For $m=1$, its single row is identified with the column vector
$\sigma D_xu$ in (equation eq:reference-operators of the paper).  For every
$s\in(r_0,r_1)$, the composition of $u$ has a continuous version on
$[s,r_1]$ and
\begin{equation}
 u(t,X_t)=\eta(X_{r_1})+\int_t^{r_1}F(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d r
 -\int_t^{r_1}\mathsf Z u(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d W_r.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, for $\kappa\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 +\left\lVert \mathsf Z u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 \leq e^{\operatorname{osc}_{\alpha,I}(w)}\left(
  \kappa^{-1}\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
  +w_\kappa(r_1)\norm\eta_{L^2(\mu_{r_1})}^2\right).
 
\end{equation}
The construction is independent of the weight: if the same data belong to
the spaces associated with two regular weights $w_1,w_2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U_I^{w_1}(F,\eta)=\mathcal U_I^{w_2}(F,\eta)
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(I\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^m).
 
\end{equation}
Thus the superscript may be omitted and the solution written as
$\mathcal U_I(F,\eta)$; the full-interval notation is $\mathcal U(F,\eta)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:06:39.320429+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e0591a8f177295dd9b78ddf50bd06a308d4e4040b19920696ab99bffde067828","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:local_solutions_NSE of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Suppose that (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli1 of the paper) and (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli4 of the paper) are satisfied.
Let $Q=I\times B$ be a parabolic cylinder with center $(t_0,x_0)$ and radius $\varrho>0$, i.e., 
$$
Q_{\varrho}(t_0,x_0)=(t_0-\varrho^2,t_0)\times B_{\varrho}(x_0).
$$ 
We say that $(v,\pi,(\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n)$ is a local solution to (equation eq:turbulent_stokes_caccioppoli of the paper) if the following are satisfied.
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm(1)}]
\item The processes 
$$
v:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d), \quad \pi:I \times \Omega\to L^2(B) \ \ \text{ and }\ \  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;\ell^2), 
$$
are progressively measurable, and a.s.,
\begin{align*}
v&\in C(\overline{I};L^2(B;{\mathbb R}^d))\cap L^2(I;H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d)) \\
\pi&\in L^2(Q),\quad \text{ and }\quad  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n \in L^2(I;H^1(B;\ell^2)).
\end{align*}

\item The following conditions hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item a.s.\ for all $t\in I$, and all $\phi\in C^\infty_{{\rm c}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)$:
\begin{align*}
\int_{B} v(t)\cdot \phi
&=
\int_{B} v(t_0-\varrho^2)\cdot \phi\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t  \int_{B} \Big[ 
\pi\,\nabla \cdot \phi+ \Big(-F -\nu \nabla v+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{n} (\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n)\Big):\nabla \phi\Big]\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t \Big(\int_{B} \big[(-\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_n + (\zeta_n\cdot \nabla) v) +G_n\big]\cdot \phi \Big)_{n} \, \mathrm{d} \mathcal{W}_{\ell^2},
\end{align*}
\item a.e.\ on $I\times \Omega$, 
in $\mathscr{D}'(B)$,
\begin{align*}
\nabla \cdot v&=0,\\
\Delta \pi
&= \nabla^2 :F - \frac{1}{2} \nabla \cdot \sum_{n}\nabla \cdot(\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n )  ,\\
\Delta \widetilde{\pi}_n
&= \nabla \cdot [(\zeta_{n}\cdot \nabla)v]+\nabla \cdot G_n.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.060628+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e05b91a1c5270332be7572b9980f8499073e2f5c7e468d516e6039c7f73ed5ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [Type characterisation lemma]}

Consider a Galton--Watson tree with the offspring law $(p_k)_{k\in\N_0}$ satisfying $p_1 =p\in (0,1)$ and $p_2= 1 -p$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[\rm{(a)}] 
The root can only be either positive or neutral. It is neutral if and only if it is a branching point and its two children are branching-linear points.
\item[\rm{(b)}] 
A linear point is negative if and only if it is the child of the root and is not the parent of a branching point. It is positive if and only if it is the parent of a branching point and is not the child of the root.
\item[\rm{(c)}] 
A branching-linear point is neutral if and only if its parent is the root and its child is a linear point, otherwise, it is positive.
\item[\rm{(d)}] 
A branching point that is not the root is either negative or neutral. It is neutral if and only if its parent and both of its children are also non-root branching points.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,d) is a compact metric space","T: X -> X is a homeomorphism","T is expansive with expansive constant c > 0 for the metric d","alpha is a finite Borel partition with diam(A) < c for every A in alpha","for the cover statement, U is a finite open cover with mesh(U) < c","for the entropy consequence, mu is a T-invariant Borel probability measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814532+00:00","domain":"topological and ergodic dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_e0991e6f5703dfafed9b8ef66c327d54b46c44f7e1c7b2d0847a9c270a85228d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and let T: X -> X be a homeomorphism which is EXPANSIVE with expansive constant c > 0, meaning: for every pair of distinct points x, y in X there exists an integer n with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c. Let alpha = {A_1, ..., A_k} be a finite Borel partition of X whose mesh is below the expansive constant, i.e. diam(A_i) < c for every i. CONCLUSION: alpha is a two-sided generator. Precisely, the smallest sigma-algebra containing T^{-n}(A_i) for all n in Z and all i is the full Borel sigma-algebra of X. Consequently, for EVERY T-invariant Borel probability measure mu, alpha is a generator mod mu, and the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem gives h_mu(T) = h_mu(T, alpha) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(alpha v T^{-1}alpha v ... v T^{-(n-1)}alpha): the measure-theoretic entropy is already computed by that one fixed finite partition, with no refinement over scales. TOPOLOGICAL COUNTERPART, same hypotheses: if U is a finite OPEN cover of X with mesh(U) < c, then h_top(T) = h_top(T, U); in particular an expansive homeomorphism of a compact metric space has finite topological entropy, and the entropy is reached at one fixed finite scale. SHARP EDGES. (a) Expansiveness is indispensable, not a convenience: for the identity map on [0,1] (which is not expansive) every finite partition alpha satisfies alpha v T^{-n}alpha = alpha for all n, so the generated sigma-algebra is the finite algebra generated by alpha and never the Borel sigma-algebra, however small the mesh. More generally, for a non-expansive system no bound on the mesh forces the generator property. (b) The constant c depends on the metric even though expansiveness itself does not: on a compact metric space expansiveness is independent of the choice of compatible metric, but 'mesh below c' must be read in the SAME metric for which c is an expansive constant. (c) The conclusion is about the TWO-SIDED sigma-algebra, using T^{-n} for all n in Z. For a one-sided generator (only n >= 0), which is what is needed for one-sided entropy statements and for non-invertible maps, one needs POSITIVE expansiveness (some n >= 0 with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c); a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive, so that strengthening is not available here. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.671932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e09bdeb89af170e687f698b66b53450bff40ae034a1df56a10e06ed6422f2823","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 35 (Finite-cover descent) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let
\[
 \pi_{\mathrm{fin}}:M_{\mathrm{fin}}\longrightarrow M
\]
be a connected, \(d\)-sheeted finite regular cover of closed connected
manifolds, with deck group \(\Gamma\).  Let \(g(t)\), \(t\geq T\), be a
\(C^0\)-continuous family of Riemannian metrics on \(M\), let
\(g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)=\pi_{\mathrm{fin}}^*g(t)\), and let \(a(t)>0\) be
continuous.  Put
\[
 \widehat g(t)=a(t)g(t),\qquad
 \widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)=a(t)g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t).
\]
Then the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
At every time,
\[
 \diam(M,\widehat g(t))
 \leq \diam(M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))
 \leq 2d\,\diam(M,\widehat g(t)).
\]
Consequently, any \(O(1)\), \(o(1)\), or two-sided positive diameter bound
for either normalized family transfers to the other, with constants depending
only on \(d\).

\item
If
\[
 (M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))\longrightarrow\pt
\]
in the Gromov--Hausdorff sense, then
\((M,\widehat g(t))\to\pt\).

\item
Suppose that
\[
 (M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))\longrightarrow C_L
\]
for a metric circle of length \(L>0\).  Then
\((M,\widehat g(t))\) has a full Gromov--Hausdorff limit.  It is either a
metric circle of length \(L/m\) or a closed interval of length \(L/(2m)\),
for some positive integer \(m\) dividing \(|\Gamma|\).  The limit is a circle
if every limiting action of \(\Gamma\) on \(C_L\) is orientation preserving;
it is a closed interval if a limiting action contains an
orientation-reversing isometry.

\item
The manifolds \(M_{\mathrm{fin}}\) and \(M\) have the same universal cover,
and the lifts of \(g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)\) and \(g(t)\) to it agree.  Hence every
pointed Cheeger--Hamilton limit of one lifted family is the corresponding
limit of the other.

\item
Suppose, for an integer \(m\geq0\), that
\(\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)\) converges in a fixed-coordinate
\(C^m\)-norm to a Riemannian metric \(g_{\mathrm{fin},\infty}\).  Then the
limit is \(\Gamma\)-invariant, descends to a metric \(g_\infty\) on \(M\),
and \(\widehat g(t)\to g_\infty\) in \(C^m\).  A uniform exponential rate
on the cover descends with the same exponent.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:38:36.830346+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e0a65af24f67596daca271b5090e101206d886a00bd633a311924e7a3983a8a7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:master of arXiv:2606.28869, '\bfseries A General Theory of Paths:\\ \large Signatures, Jump Lifts, and Expected Signatu'] The constructions in the paper assemble into the following six-layer representation theorem, each layer being valid under the hypotheses stated in the cited results.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.25em]
\item \textbf{Algebraic path layer.} Bounded-variation signatures satisfy Chen multiplicativity and the shuffle identity; group-like signatures have Lie logarithms, and reduced bounded-variation paths are characterized by their signatures modulo tree-like equivalence.
\item \textbf{Jump and stream layer.} Finite-variation c\`adl\`ag{} paths admit forward It\^o{} and Marcus lifts. The forward lift fails shuffle by the jump bracket, while the Marcus correction restores geometricity. For pure-jump paths, the forward lift is the iterated-sums signature and the Marcus lift is Hoffman's exponential image.
\item \textbf{Geometricity-defect layer.} The two canonical failures of shuffle multiplicativity are second order: quadratic covariation for non-geometric conventions and coordinate covariance for expected signatures. Consequently, an expected signature is group-like only in the deterministic reduced-path case.
\item \textbf{Probabilistic and geometric layer.} Truncated signature kernels yield MMDs equal to Euclidean distances between truncated expected signatures, while the truncations of geometric signatures form a central tower of free nilpotent groups whose forgotten layers have Witt dimensions.
\item \textbf{Self-exciting layer.} Affine processes have finite linear closures for truncated expected signatures after state-weight augmentation. Scalar exponential Hawkes clocks admit the explicit systems (equation eq:hawkes-matrix of the paper) and (equation eq:A2 of the paper), local parameter recovery through (equation eq:ident-reconstruct of the paper), and a directional cross-area detecting two-channel excitation asymmetry to first order.
\item \textbf{Boundary and continuation layer.} Raw expected signatures have intrinsic heavy-tail moment thresholds, normalized expected signatures provide bounded characteristic replacements under the hypotheses of [chevyrev2022], reversal acts by the tensor antipode, and signature large deviations follow by contraction from rough-path large deviations.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356673+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e10d86a0e5ae172fc845f728151fa8a6f3e5bef5b0cd722074bd9020ffc74a17","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 235 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ such that for all $\fq\in [1,2)$ and any sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$, the following holds.
	For all sufficiently large $N$,
	\[
		\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu(\cA_N), \mu(\cA_{N[K]})\Big)
		\le \frac{C(\alpha)}{K^{2/\fq-1}}\,.
	\]
\begin{proof}
	Consider $N$ large enough that the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} holds: this gives
	\[
	C(\alpha)
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} }{\ge}
	\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
	= \frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M}
	\ge \frac{\|\E\fm\|^2}{M}
	\ge \frac{|S_K(\cA_N)| K^2}{M}\,.
	\]	
We can thus couple $x\sim \mu(\cA_N)$ and $y\sim \mu(\cA_{N[K]})$ such that 
$\P(x\neq y) \le C(\alpha) / K^2$. It follows from  the first assertion of  Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} that 
	\[
		\E[|x-y|^2]
		\le 2\E[x^2+y^2]
		= 2(\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2 + \|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}}{\le} 4C(\alpha)\,.\]
Applying H\"older's inequality then gives
	\begin{align*}
		&\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu(\cA_N), \mu(\cA_{N[K]})\Big)^\fq
		\le \E[|x-y|^\fq]
		\le \P(x\neq y)^{1-\fq/2} \E[|x-y|^2]^{\fq/2}
	\\
	&\qquad
		\le \bigg(\frac{C(\alpha)}{K^2}\bigg)^{1-\fq/2} (4C(\alpha))^{\fq/2}
		= \frac{2^\fq C(\alpha)}{K^{2-q}}
		\le \bigg(\frac{2\max\{1,C(\alpha)\}}{K^{2/\fq-1}}\bigg)^\fq\,.
	\end{align*}
	The result follows by renaming $2\max\{1,C(\alpha)\}$ to $C(\alpha)$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the optimism theorem for weighted least squares; weights normalised to sum to one","regime (2) beyond the Loewner bounds uses row exchangeability given the weights as a first-order approximation of the two moment matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T11:47:28.060880+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment","id":"claim_e133d7fdae691c4a0638ff9a8fb3a814a36acd27f937ccf5fa74ff1dd0aeeb11","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the setting of the optimism theorem for weighted least squares, normalise the weights to sum_i s_i = 1. (1) Uniform weights and homoscedastic errors give the Mallows-Efron optimism 2 sigma^2 m / n. (2) Concentrated weights with homoscedastic errors: the Loewner bounds s_min X'SX <= X'S^2 X <= s_max X'SX give 2 sigma^2 m s_min <= optimism <= 2 sigma^2 m s_max, and when the rows are exchangeable given the weights (E[x x'] = G for every row) the two moment matrices are (sum s_i) G and (sum s_i^2) G to first order, so the optimism is 2 sigma^2 m sum_i s_i^2 = 2 sigma^2 m / n_eff with Kish's n_eff = (sum s)^2 / sum s^2; relative to the noise level sigma^2 of the loss the gap is 2 m / n_eff, and a concentrated weighting behaves as a small sample. (3) Variance-stabilising weights s_i = c / sigma_i^2 (Aitken's weights) give S^2 Sigma = c S, the trace collapses to c m, the optimism is 2 c m whatever the concentration of the weights, and relative to the noise level c n of the loss it is 2 m / n again: under Aitken weights a small Kish n_eff is not a small sample but the balanced sample of the stabilised problem. Which regime a weighted fit is in is therefore an empirical question about how the error variance scales with the weights; an additive error floor sigma_i^2 = a + b/s_i mixes the two, the summand becoming s_i (a s_i + b), and the concentration re-enters through the floor on the heavily weighted rows.","status":"unverified"}

\begin{itemize}

\item "steps up" corresponding to $(\sigma_j, \sigma_{j+1}) = (0,1)$

\item "steps down" corresponding to $(\sigma_j, \sigma_{j+1}) = (1,0)$.

\end{itemize}

There is a natural identification $\bs{\sg}_{N-1} \mapsto \big(\sigma_1, X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \big)$
where $X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \subset \intn{1}{N-2}$ is the set of level changes.  That is, $\sigma_1$ is the first element in the sequence and

$$X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \,  = \, \big\{ j \in \intn{1}{N-2} \, : \,  \sigma_j \neq \sigma_{j+1} \big\} \, .$$

Note that one has the partitioning $X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \, = \,  X_\downarrow(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \cup X_{\uparrow}(\bs{\sg}_{N-1})$ where
$X_\downarrow(\bs{\sg}_{N-1})$ is the set of down steps and $X_{\uparrow}(\bs{\sg}_{N-1})$ is the set of up steps of $\bs{\sg}_{N-1}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:19:56.700051+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e158a26529489086a6fc99ab090f248350a3c5755295954738ed28b09bc2fbdf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Def 31 (Local good approximations) of arXiv:2608.30990, 'Convergence of symmetries: nilpotency, dimension, and perfectness'] Let $G_i$ be a sequence of locally compact Hausdorff local groups and $G$ a locally compact Hausdorff local group. We say a sequence of functions $\phi _ i : G_i \to G$ consists of \emph{local good approximations} if there are open, pre-compact, symmetric, multiplicative sets $A_i \subset G_i$, $A \subset G$ such that:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\Roman*${}_{\text{loc}}$]
        \item (Almost surjectivity) For all $U \subset A $ open nonempty, one has $\phi_i (A_i) \cap U \neq \emptyset$ for $i$ large enough.
        \item (No expansion) For all $V \subset G$ open with $\overline{A} \subset V$, one has $\phi_i (A_i) \subset V$ for $i$ large enough.
        \item (Almost homomorphism) For each identity neighborhood $U \subset G$, there is $i_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that if $i \geq i_0 $ and   $g, h \in A_i ^8 $, then $ [ \phi_i (gh)^{-1} \phi _i (g) \phi_i (h) ]  \in U $. 
        \item (No compression) For each compact $K\subset A$, there is $i_0 \in \mathbb{N}$  such that if $i \geq i_0$, and $g \in A_i^8$ satisfies  $\phi_i (g) \in K $,  then $g \in A_i$. 
        \item (Almost continuity) For each identity neighborhood $U \subset G$, there is a sequence of identity neighborhoods $U_i \subset G_i$ with $\phi_i (U_i) \subset U $ for $i$ large enough. 
    \end{enumerate}
    If properties (I${}_{\text{loc}}$--V${}_{\text{loc}}$) hold, we call the sets $A_i$ and $ A$ \emph{regular neighborhoods} with respect to the approximations $\phi_i$. 

    \emph{Small subgroups} and the \emph{NSS property} in the context of local good approximations are defined in exactly the same way as they were defined for good approximations (see Definition \ref{def:ss2}).","status":"unverified"}
