{"assumptions":["Conclusion is constancy on the closure of U x [0,t_0] only","U must be connected","The maximum must be attained at a point with x_0 in U and t_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106923+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_e5db45cf444dc11d943ed80dd9009a1a1904ce853e38b9031ae8a4e06c9b3559","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a solution of the heat equation attains its maximum over $\\overline{U_T}$ at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)\\in U_T$, the conclusion is that $u$ is constant on $\\overline U\\times[0,t_0]$ -- the past of $t_0$ -- and nothing at all is claimed for $t>t_0$. Heat is not time-reversible, and the mean value property over heat balls only looks backwards. Counterexample: on $U=(0,\\pi)$, $T=2$, let $h(t)=1$ for $t\\le1$ and $h(t)=1-e^{-1/(t-1)}$ for $t>1$ (smooth, $h\\le1$, $h<1$ for $t>1$), and let $u$ be the solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with $u(\\cdot,0)\\equiv1$ and $u(0,t)=u(\\pi,t)=h(t)$. On $[0,1]$, $u\\equiv1$ by uniqueness; the weak maximum principle gives $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=1$, attained at the interior point $(\\pi/2,1)\\in U_T$; but for $t>1$, $u$ is not constant (its boundary values are $<1$ while, by continuity, $u$ stays near $1$ in the middle). So constancy holds exactly up to $t_0=1$ and fails afterwards. A second load-bearing hypothesis is connectedness of $U$: for $U=(0,1)\\cup(2,3)$ the solution equal to $1$ on the first component and to $e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\phi_1$ on the second attains its maximum at an interior point of the first component and is not constant on $U$. Finally, the interior maximum must be attained in $U_T$, i.e. at a point with $x_0\\in U$: a maximum on the lateral boundary says nothing about constancy (that is the Hopf lemma's domain, which asserts instead that the outward normal derivative is strictly positive there).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The counterexample uses H(p) = p^2 (smooth, uniformly convex) and zero data, so no exotic Hamiltonian is needed","'Solution a.e.' means Lipschitz plus the equation at points of differentiability","Uniqueness is restored by the viscosity property or, equivalently for convex superlinear H, by the semiconcavity bound of the Hopf-Lax solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418105+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_e6002f2b1fb67f105d5effe237759fa92f79220ba532358144c459114f6ad305","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in any uniqueness statement for u_t + H(Du) = 0 the solution must be a VISCOSITY solution (equivalently, for convex superlinear H, a Lipschitz a.e. solution satisfying the one-sided semiconcavity estimate). Satisfying the equation at almost every point plus the initial condition is far too weak. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = p^2, initial datum g ≡ 0. Both u ≡ 0 and v(x,t) := min(0, |x| - t) are Lipschitz on R × [0,∞), vanish at t = 0, and satisfy v_t + v_x^2 = 0 at every point of differentiability: for |x| < t one has v = |x| - t, v_t = -1, v_x = ±1; for |x| > t one has v ≡ 0. Only u ≡ 0 is the viscosity solution (it is also what the Hopf-Lax formula gives, since L(q) = q^2/4 and min_y ( |x-y|^2/(4t) ) = 0). Why v fails: at a point (0,t) with t > 0, v has a local minimum in x with a convex kink, so φ ≡ v(0,t) + c(t'-t) touches from below with φ_x = 0, φ_t = -1, and the supersolution inequality φ_t + φ_x^2 ≥ 0 reads -1 ≥ 0. Equivalently v violates semiconcavity: v(z,t) - 2v(0,t) + v(-z,t) = 2|z|, which is not O(|z|^2). Auditor's check: whenever a proof concludes 'u is the solution' from 'u is Lipschitz and solves the PDE a.e.', the argument is incomplete unless viscosity, semiconcavity, or a variational (Hopf-Lax) representation is verified.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:32:11.153410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6142a3f45c20d3df0e2acadb0566dc2b27b8c92aa0a7d38cb5b5103947e66ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:RBG of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] Let $R_1 < R_2$ be two integer numbers,
set  $H = R_2 - R_1$. 
Let $\eta : \mathbb{Z}^d \to  \mathbb{N}$
be the initial particle configuration
with support in $\partial B_{R_1}$
and number of particles $N_1 = \sum_{z \in 
\partial B_{R_1}} \eta(z)$. 
Let further $Z_1, \ldots Z_{N_1}$ be i.i.d.\  random variables with distribution 
 supported in   $ \{1, \ldots,  H\} $  given by
\begin{equation}
P( Z_i = h) = \frac{ h^{d-1} }{\sum_{r =1 }^H  r^{d-1}},
\end{equation}
The $\{ Z_i\}$ represent the sequence of heights at which the BRWs will probe the space for settlement. 

The RBG consists of a discrete time
Markov chain  $(A_t)_{t \in \mathbb{N}}$
and a sequence of random variables 
$(  \tilde G_t,  \tilde R_t)_{  t \in \mathbb{N}_0  }$,
 defined as follows. 
We set $A_0 =  \emptyset$ 
and label the particles in $\eta$ with integers from $1$ to $N_1$ in some arbitrary order. 
At each step $t \in \{1, \ldots, N_1\}$, 
we start, from the $t$-th particle of $\eta$, an independent BRW
stopped on $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$ 
and let $\xi_t$ be the configuration of pioneers  on $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$.
We define the aggregate of the step $t$ as 
the union of the aggregate of the step $t-1$ and 
the support of the  pioneers configuration,  namely 
$$
A_t := A_{t-1} \cup \{ z \in \partial  B_{ R_1 + Z_t  } \, \, : \,   \xi_t(z) > 0     \}.
$$
After that we proceed as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)]
For each particle reaching $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$ within 
$A_{t-1}$ we start an independent critical branching random walk stopped on
$\partial B_{ R_2  }$  and call $\tilde{G}_t$ the total number of pioneers 
on $\partial B_{ R_2  }$, which we dub \textit{green particles}.
\item[(b)]  
For each vertex 
 $ x \in \partial  B_{ R_1 + Z_t  } \setminus A_{t-1}$
 with $\xi_t(x)>0$,
 we let exactly one of the $\xi_t(x)$ particles at $x$ settle
 and  start 
 $(\xi_t(x) - 1) \1_{ \{ \xi_t(x)>0 \}  }$
  independent critical branching random walks
 stopped on $ B_{ R_2  }$ from $x$, 
 namely one critical Branching Random Walk from each particle which has not settled at $x$. 
 We call $\tilde{R}_t$ 
 be the total number of pioneers on $\partial B_{ R_2  }$,
 which we dub \textit{red particles}.
\end{enumerate}
We then move to the step $t+1$ and iterate the procedure
up to reaching $t = N_1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496248+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6248aa0074ed65c0cb416759fb98cfbee64e1b86f405d7a62cdf77ef9f92b0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (First-break localization and tails) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level defined by
\[
        \Prob(K_d=k)=\pi_{d,k}\quad(1\le k\le d-1),
        \qquad
        \Prob(K_d=d)=\rho_d,
\]
where
\[
        \rho_d:=\prod_{r=1}^{d-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
\]
is the probability that no one-sided tie-break occurs before simultaneous completion.  Thus the value $K_d=d$ records this exceptional terminal event.  Then
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
In particular,
\[
        K_d\to\infty,
        \qquad
        \frac{K_d}{d}\to0
\]
in probability.  More precisely, for $k=o(d)$,
\[
        \prod_{r=1}^{k-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
        =\exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{d}+O\left(\frac{k^4}{d^3}\right)\right),
\]
and there are absolute constants $C,c>0$ such that, for every $R\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge R\sqrt{d\log d}}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C d^{-cR^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
More generally, for every $M\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge M\sqrt d}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C e^{-cM^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $R$ large enough the tail in
\eqref{eq:first-break-tail} is $o(d^{-1})$.","status":"unverified"}

(1).    For $H\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, sample the walk  $W(t)$ in $\tilde{\mathcal{W}}(\cdot,H,L;N)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149207+00:00","domain":"functional analysis for elliptic PDE","id":"claim_e668a967db6b2df1576259501b51767438bb0d124e237c2d8edd4b1aa48d5602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: there is beta > 0 with B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2 for every u in the Hilbert space H. Strict positivity (B[u,u] > 0 for u nonzero) is not enough, and neither is injectivity of the associated operator. Counterexample: H = l^2, B(u,v) = sum_k u_k v_k / k. This form is bounded (|B(u,v)| <= ||u|| ||v||), symmetric and strictly positive, but B(e_k, e_k) = 1/k tends to 0, so it is not coercive. The bounded functional F(v) = sum_k v_k / k is represented by the sequence (1/k) in l^2, yet B(u, .) = F forces u_k = 1 for all k, which is not in l^2: the equation has no solution. PDE instances of the same failure: (i) on H^1_0(Omega) the form B[u,v] = integral (grad u . grad v - lambda_1 u v) satisfies B[u,u] >= 0 with equality exactly on the first eigenfunction, and the Dirichlet problem for -Laplacian - lambda_1 is not solvable for general right-hand sides (the Fredholm orthogonality condition appears); (ii) on H^1(Omega) the Neumann form integral grad u . grad v annihilates constants, and integral f = 0 is necessary for solvability; (iii) on an unbounded Omega the Poincare inequality may fail, so integral (grad u . grad v) is not coercive for the full H^1 norm. Two further points a careful reader should keep straight: coercivity is sufficient but not necessary (for lambda strictly between two Dirichlet eigenvalues the form of -Laplacian - lambda is indefinite, yet the problem is uniquely solvable by the Fredholm alternative), and Lax-Milgram does not require B to be symmetric - symmetry only turns the solution into the minimizer of a quadratic energy (Riesz representation / Dirichlet principle).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6789d4681558e1453083424208786d0dc56c6880309cc2396d52ceae8d18ee8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 189 (error between $Q$ and $\tilde{Q}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as given by \eqref{e:qv.covar} and \eqref{e:tQ.notIs}. Then
	\[\Big|
	\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(1)\bigg\{
	\eta^2
	+
	\sum_{\rho\in\{\sigma,\tau\}}
	\bigg[
	\eta\bigg(
	\min\Big\{
	\Delta Q^\rho(q_d),
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^\rho(q_d)\Big\}
	\bigg)^{1/2}
	+ \Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg]
	\bigg\}\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$.
The same bound holds with $Q^\frozen$, $\tilde{Q}^\frozen$, $E^\frozen$
in place of $Q$, $\tilde{Q}$, $E$.

\begin{proof} Recall that $\vZ\equiv \vY-\vD$, so we can rewrite \eqref{e:qv.covar} as
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	= \bE \bigg[
		\Big( \Delta Y^\sigma(q_d)
			-\Delta D^\sigma(q_d)
			\Big)
		\Big(
		\Delta Y^\tau(q_d)
		-\Delta D^\tau(q_d)
		\Big)
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\,.
	\]
For simplicity of exposition, let us consider the case $\sigma=\tau=\RomI$.
Similarly to the argument for
Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep},
let $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$ denote the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} then tells us that $\Delta Y^\RomI(q_d)$ is within $2\eta$ of $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$, where
$a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from
$B$. Thus define $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ to be the process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^\RomI(q_d)
	\Big)^2
\,.
	\eeq
 It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	=\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	O(\eta)
	+\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2\,,\]
which allows us to bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg|
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta) 
	\bigg[\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^2\bigg]^{1/2}\\
	&\qquad\le
	O(1)\bigg\{ \eta^2+\eta 
		\Big( \Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}\bigg\}\,.
	
	\end{align}
This shows that increments of
$Q^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ are close. We can further bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	=\bigg| \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2
	- \frac{1}{|B|}\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^2\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	- 2
	\Big( \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)
	\bigg|\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	-2\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\bigg|\\
	&\qquad\le O(1)  
	\bigg\{
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2
	+ \eta\Big|\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| + \eta^2\bigg\}
	\le O(1)
	\max\bigg\{\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,\eta^2\bigg\}
	
	\,,\end{align}
having used the definition of $\bar{D}$ from \eqref{e:barD}, together with Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep}. Combining the bounds gives
	\[
	\Big|
	\Delta E^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le  O(1)
	\bigg\{ \eta^2 
	+\eta\Big( \Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Next note that \eqref{e:barQ.to.tildeQ} implies
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta \bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\,.\]
Meanwhile \eqref{e:Q.to.barQ} implies that either 
$\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$, in which case
$\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$ also,
or $\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)$ is much larger than $\eta^2$, in which case it is of the same order as
 $\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)$. It follows that
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.103264+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_e68f193186254c789712f4d9509a62ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle (i.e., a cylinder), but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle (product of two line segments) without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle (an even number of twists or an odd number of twists). The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group $H^{1}(S^{1},\\{+1,-1\\})$ which can be computed as isomorphic to the group $\\{+1,-1\\}$ where $+1$ corresponds to an even number of twists, and $-1$ to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.285897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e69ce9a9193dcd224bc7a66db7e2a67e23fd8a7e452dc938eec983f2b0dee69b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma KacRice of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[0,1]$ with a $2$-atom prefix
		$\{0,q\}$ for some $q\in(0,1)$, and let $\varepsilon\in(0,q/2)$.
		Let $\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)$ be the number of critical points $\mathbf{m}$ of
		$F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}$ such that
		\[
		\mathbf{m}\in \mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\frac1N F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\in(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon).
		\]
		For $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$, write $q_\mathbf{m}:=\frac1N\|\mathbf{m}\|^2$.
		
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item \textup{(Mixed case.)}
			Assume that for every $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ with
			$q_\mathbf{m}\in(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$, the Gaussian vector
			\[
			\bigl(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\bigr)
			\]
			is non-degenerate.  In particular, this holds for a genuine mixed
			$p$-spin Hamiltonian, i.e.\ when
			\[
			\xi(t)=\sum_{p\ge 2}\beta_p^2 t^p
			\]
			has at least two non-zero coefficients.
			Then
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=N\int_{[-1,1]^N}\int_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\,
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf'
				\right]
				\\
				\times
				\varphi_{(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))}(0,Nf')\,
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}\,\mathrm{d} f'.
			\end{multline}
			
			\item \textup{(Pure case.)}
			Assume that $\xi(t)=\beta_p^2 t^p$ is pure $p$-spin for some $p\ge2$.
			Recalling the notation~(equation eq:def-Rex-KR of the paper),
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=
				\int_{[-1,1]^N}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0
				\right]
				\varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				\\
				\times
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathbf{1}_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\!\left(\frac1N\mathcal R^{\rm ex}_\zeta(\mathbf{m})\right)
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}.
			\end{multline}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R^d)","the Plancherel transform is the L^2 extension of the L^1 transform"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264524+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_e6a7de372efdb69b5dda51fbcd54ebeef72e1430e1bd848aa9b086939563f833","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing distinction: for $f\\in L^1$ the transform is an honest absolutely convergent integral, bounded, continuous, defined at every $\\xi$; for $f\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$ it is defined only as the $L^2$-limit $\\hat f=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\widehat{f\\mathbf 1_{\\{|x|\\le R\\}}}$ (the unique continuous extension from the dense subspace $L^1\\cap L^2$), hence is an equivalence class defined only almost everywhere. Example: $f(x)=\\sin(\\pi x)/(\\pi x)\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$, whose Plancherel transform is $\\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ a.e.; the truncated integrals converge to $1$ for $|\\xi|<1/2$, to $0$ for $|\\xi|>1/2$ and to $1/2$ at $\\xi=\\pm1/2$, but no value at $\\pm1/2$ is meaningful for the $L^2$ transform. Consequences an auditor should check: (i) claims like '$\\hat f(\\xi_0)=0$' or '$\\hat f$ is continuous' are meaningless for $L^2$ data without naming a representative (the usual legitimate versions are 'a.e.' statements or support statements up to null sets); (ii) $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ is unavailable; (iii) that $\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\int_{-R}^Rf(x)e^{-2\\pi ix\\xi}dx$ exists for a.e. $\\xi$ when $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ is a deep result (the Fourier-integral form of Carleson's theorem), not a corollary of Plancherel, which only gives $L^2$ convergence and hence a.e. convergence along some subsequence of radii. On $L^1\\cap L^2$ the two definitions agree a.e., which is what makes the extension consistent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T12:08:18+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_e6ae446cd6fd7036517cf71cccaaa1cb4fa2b1cf94cd433f14ec3cf8acbcb1e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. Then the probability that all of them lie in a single open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin, equivalently the probability that the origin is not in their convex hull, equals $2^{-N+1}\\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\\binom{N-1}{k}$. In particular this probability is $1$ whenever $N \\le d$. Note that symmetry alone does not suffice: general position is needed, since for instance two points i.i.d. uniform on $\\{\\pm e_1\\} \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$ are symmetric (their joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin) but not in general position, and they lie in a common open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin with probability $1/2$ (exactly when the two points coincide; $e_1$ and $-e_1$ lie in no such halfspace, and the origin is in their convex hull), whereas the formula gives $2^{-1}\\left(\\binom{1}{0}+\\binom{1}{1}\\right)=1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.568178+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6ccd3bfb0bebac58eb198b65ce853be21569a59e5c13f54c485fca3321989c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Let $\psi$ denote a Lemari\'e-Meyer  wavelet  and $\varphi$ the associated scaling function. The hyperbolic wavelet basis is defined as the system $$\{\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2} :  \, (j_1, j_2) \in (\mathbb{N}\cup \{-1\})^2, \, (k_1, k_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\}$$
where
\begin{itemize}
\item if $j_1,j_2\geq 0$,
$$
\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1=-1$ and $j_2\geq 0$
$$
\psi_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1\ge 0$ and $j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{j_1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;,
$$
\item if $j_1=j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;.
$$
\end{itemize}
For any $f\in\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$, one then defines its hyperbolic wavelet coefficients by
\begin{eqnarray*}
c_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_1+j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1,j_2\geq 0\;,\\

c_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=-1\mbox{ and }j_2\geq 0\;,\\
c_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}&=&<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=j_2=-1\;.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.433035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6e52dfefc826fecfc9e941613dba88a029b6b84c724b1b3fc1e41c47966fad7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:ito-expansion-Lp of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Let \(p>2\), and recall that 
\[
    L_p(t)
    :=
    \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
    \phi_{a,p}(Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j),
    \qquad
    \phi_{a,p}(y,z)
    :=
    a|y|^p+|z|^p+\frac m\gamma |y|^{p-2}\langle y,z\rangle \,,
\] and $\Delta_\alpha(t):=m_X(\mu_{X_t^J})-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)$. Hence, $ X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)=Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)\,,$
and
\[
    \mathrm d\hat Z_t^j
    =
    (-K_Z\hat Z_t^j-K_YY_t^j)\mathrm d t+\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}},
\]
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}
    :=
    \frac{\sigma}{m}
    \left[
        \left(1-\frac1J\right)
        S(Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^j
        -
        \frac1J\sum_{k\ne j}
        S(Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^k
    \right].
\end{equation}
The stochastic differential of \(L_p(t)\) is
\begin{align}
    \mathrm d L_p(t)
    &=
    \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
    \Bigg\{
    \left[
        \left(\frac{ap}{\gamma}-\frac m\gamma K_Y\right)|Y_t^j|^p
        -
        pK_Z|\hat Z_t^j|^p
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \left(
            ap-\frac m\gamma K_Z+\frac{m(p-1)}{\gamma^2}
        \right)
        |Y_t^j|^{p-2}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle
        -
        pK_Y|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}\langle \hat Z_t^j,Y_t^j\rangle
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}|\hat Z_t^j|^2
        +
        \frac{m(p-2)}{\gamma}
        |Y_t^j|^{p-4}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle^2
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)\,\mathrm d t
    +
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    \Bigg\},
    
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    :=
    p|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle \hat Z_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle
    +
    \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle Y_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle .
\end{equation}
We denote $ M_{p,t}:=\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J M_{p,t}^j$ as the local martingale part of \(L_p(t)\). The noise trace satisfies
\begin{align}
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)
    &=
    \frac12
    \operatorname{Tr}
    \left(
        \nabla^2(|\hat Z_t^j|^p)\,
        \mathrm d\langle M^{j,\mathrm{center}}\rangle_t
    \right)
    \notag\\
    &=
        \frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2}\left(1-\frac1J\right)^2 |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right] \notag \\
        &\quad
        +\frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2J^2}\sum_{k\ne j}|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right]\\
        & \leqslant
    \frac{p\sigma^2\chi_S}{2m^2}
    |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left(
        |Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
        +
        \frac1J\sum_{k=1}^J |Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
    \right).
    
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.652433+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6ed5087bc835c0e0267def06b8ca3039bf74ae3cab9c6d23231d02ed4127901","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 30 of arXiv:2608.29972, '\bf Cram\'er transform, half-space depth and threshold phenomena for convex bodies'] \rm 
Let $(\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of probability measures $\mu_n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $(T_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ a sequence of positive numbers. 
We say that $(\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ exhibits a sharp threshold around $(T_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ if for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, there exists some $n_0=n_0(\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $n \geq n_0$
$$\varrho_1(\mu_n,\delta_n)\geq(1-\varepsilon)T_n \qquad\hbox{ and }\qquad \varrho_2(\mu_n,\delta_n)\leq(1+\varepsilon)T_n,$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6f9e9d7ec2498c7cb28bfb52e107a4ef3ff20917a8c2f635ef00dcfe2ad1c75","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Conjecture conj:barcode_kernel_intro of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Around any macroscopic point $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ in the waterfall region $\mathcal{W}$, the
	random configuration of square lozenges
	on a horizontal slice
	converges to a
	determinantal \textbf{barcode process} on $\mathbb{Z}$ with the symmetric correlation kernel
	$\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)$.\footnote{In particular, 
	we conjecture that the limit (equation eq:K_barcode_intro of the paper) exists for all integers $s\ge t$.}
	The barcode process depends only on the parameters $q$ and $\kappa$,
	but not on the geometry of the hexagon or the macroscopic location $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$
	inside $\mathcal{W}$, as long as the waterfall phase is present, i.e., $\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$.
	
	The limiting kernel is $2\times 2$ block Toeplitz, that is,
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)& \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t+1)\\
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t+1)
		\end{pmatrix}

			\begin{pmatrix}
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{00}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{01}(s-t)\\
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{10}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{11}(s-t)

			\qquad s,t\in 2\mathbb{Z},

	in $q$ and $\kappa$ is given in (fig:density_rho_even_3d of the paper)).
	Consequently, the barcode process has global density $1/2$

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.323476+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7231056bed6a6a0348702a18d5f03ae9b094b240dfc94e28d6c9f5fd349886f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma fiberwise-kappa-compactly-gen of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}}\in\textup{Pr}^S_T$ and let $\kappa$ be $(S,T)$-regular such that each ${\mathcal{C}}(A)$ is $\kappa$-compactly generated and each restriction preserves $\kappa$-compact objects. 
    Denote by ${\mathcal{C}}^{\kappa}\subset {\mathcal{C}}$ the full $T$-subcategory given in degree $A\in T$ by the $\kappa$-compact objects. 
    Then ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ has $\kappa$-small $S$-colimits, and for any ${\mathcal{D}}\in\CAT_T^\textup{$S$-cc}$, restriction along the inclusion defines an equivalence
    \[
        \ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$\kappa$-small $S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}}^\kappa,{\mathcal{D}}). 
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        It follows directly from the assumptions that restriction along ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ defines an equivalence $\ul{\textup{Fun}}_T^\text{fib $\kappa$-filt cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{\textup{Fun}}_T({\mathcal{C}}^\kappa,{\mathcal{D}})$. Moreover, ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ has fiberwise $\kappa$-small colimits, and applying [HTT]*{Example~5.3.6.8} pointwise, we see that a functor ${\mathcal{C}}\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$ preserves fiberwise colimits if and only if its restriction to ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ preserves fiberwise $\kappa$-small colimits. 

        As each of the left adjoints $s_!\colon{\mathcal{C}}(A)\to{\mathcal{C}}(B)$ preserves $\kappa$-compact objects (its right adjoint admits another right adjoint, so it is in particular $\kappa$-accessible), we see that each $s^*\colon{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(B)\to{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(A)$ for $s\colon A\to B$ in $S$ admits a left adjoint. We claim that also $s_!'\colon{\mathcal{C}}(X)\to{\mathcal{C}}(C)$ for $s'$ as in $((diag:pb-regular-card of the paper))$ restricts to ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(X)\to{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(C)$ (beware that the left-hand side is a priori different from ${\mathcal{C}}(X)^\kappa$); with this established the Beck--Chevalley condition for ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ will follow from the one for ${\mathcal{C}}$, i.e.~${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ will have $\kappa$-small $S$-colimits.

        To prove the claim, write $X\simeq\mathop{\textup{colim}}_iX_i$ as a $\kappa$-small colimit of representables in $\PSh(S)$, so that $s^*$ agrees up to equivalence with $(s_i^*)_{i\in I}\colon{\mathcal{C}}(C)\to\lim_{I^{\textup{op}}}{\mathcal{C}}(X_\bullet)$ for some cocone $(s_i)_{i\in I}$. By [descent-lim]*{Theorem~B}, this then admits a left adjoint given on objects by sending an object $(y_i)_{i\in I}\in\lim_{I^{\textup{op}}}{\mathcal{C}}(X_\bullet)$ to the colimit of a certain diagram $i\mapsto s_{i!}(y_i)$. If each $y_i$ is $\kappa$-compact, then so is each $s_{i!}(y_i)$ by the above, whence so is their colimit as $I$ is $\kappa$-small. This completes the proof of the claim, and hence of ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$ having $\kappa$-small $S$-colimits.

        It only remains to show that a functor $F\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$ for $S$-cocomplete ${\mathcal{D}}$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition with respect to the maps $s\colon A\to B$ in $S$ if and only if this holds for the composite $Fi\colon{\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\to\ul{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{A}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}},{\mathcal{D}})$. This follows at once by observing that the collection of $X\in{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ such that $s_!FX\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;} Fs_!X$ is closed under ($\kappa$-filtered) colimits and contains ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa(A)$, as ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition by construction of the left adjoints for ${\mathcal{C}}^\kappa$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.294863+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e728a09a852f93852d34e3f95dbbcc26f263235526c6e2a1e3cac7d63bce212c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:resampling_target of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Let $\Gamma$ be a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} in $D$.  Let $W\subseteq D$ open and $r > 0$. Suppose that we are given the following random variables.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M^*<\infty$.
\item  A set $\{(\ell_i^1,\ell^2_i)\}_{i=1,\ldots,M^*}$ of pairs of arcs in $\Gamma$ with $\ell_i^1,\ell^2_i \subseteq W$ and such that none of them overlap with each other.
\item A set of $M^*$ points $\underline{y}$ such that
\begin{itemize}
 \item $y_i\in  \ell_i^1\cap \ell^2_i$ and $B(y_i,4r)\subset W$ for $i=1,\ldots,M^*$,
 \item the endpoints of $\ell^1_i, \ell^2_i$ lie outside $B(y_i,4r)$,
 \item $B(y_i,4r)\cap B(y_j,4r)=\varnothing$ and $(\ell_i^1 \cup \ell_i^2) \cap B(y_j,4r) = \varnothing$ for all $i\neq j$.
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
We denote these target pivotals by $\mathfrak F_{W,r} = \{(\ell^1_i,\ell^2_i,y_i)\}_{i=1,\ldots,M^*}$.

If $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ is a resampling of $\Gamma$, then we say that $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ is $\mathfrak F_{W,r}$-successful if the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item The loops and strands of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ are identical when restricted to the set $D \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{M^*} B(y_i,4r)$.
 \item Let $\tau_i^j$ (resp.\ $\overline{\tau}_i^j$) be the first (resp.\ last) time that $\ell_i^j$ is in $\overline{B}(y_i,4 r)$, for $i=1,\ldots,M^*$, $j=1,2$. Then in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ the connections between the four strands $\ell_i^1|_{[0,\tau_i^1]}$, $\ell_i^1|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^1,1]}$, $\ell_i^2|_{[0,\tau_i^2]}$, $\ell_i^2|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^2,1]}$ (assuming that they are parameterized on $[0,1]$) are flipped, i.e.\ the strand $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},1}_i$ (resp.\ $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},2}_i$) in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ starting with $\ell_i^1|_{[0,\tau_i^1]}$ (resp.\ finishing with $\ell_i^1|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^1,1]}$) is linked to $\ell_i^2|_{[0,\tau_i^2]}$ or $\ell_i^2|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^2,1]}$. Moreover, it holds again that $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},1}_i \cap \ell^{{\mathrm{res}},2}_i \cap B(y_i,r) \neq \varnothing$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

If \(\ell\cdot\1\ne0\), then there exist random vectors \(X^+,X^-\in\R^n\) such that \(\left(X_i^+\right)_{i\in T}\stackrel{d}=\left(X_i^-\right)_{i\in T}\) for every \(T\subseteq\left[n\right]\) with \(\lvert T\rvert=k\), but

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.052688+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e75c9c0700f7694ee2e217f11d87d183919719f1ca741d6c5aa882a6c8caeeb4","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:schur of arXiv:2608.30888, 'Three-term asymptotics for discrete\\ Hardy--Rellich constants in high dimension'] Let $H$ be a semibounded self-adjoint operator with closed form $\mathfrak h$,
and let $P$ be a finite-rank orthogonal projection such that
$P\mathcal H\subset\operatorname{Dom}(H)$.  Put $Q=I-P$, assume that $P$ preserves
the form domain, and let $H_Q$ be the self-adjoint operator represented by the
restriction of $\mathfrak h$ to $Q\mathcal Q(H)$.  Let $z\in\mathbb R$.  If
$H_Q-z\geq\eta Q$ for some $\eta>0$, then
\[
 \mathcal F_P(H-z)
 =P(H-z)P-PHQ(H_Q-z)^{-1}QHP
\]
is self-adjoint on the finite-dimensional space $P\mathcal H$; here $PHQ$ denotes
the bounded adjoint of $QHP$.  Moreover,
\[
 z\in\sigma(H)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 0\in\sigma\bigl(\mathcal F_P(H-z)\bigr).
\]
The dimensions of the corresponding kernels agree.  If $b_Q$ is a lower form
bound for $H_Q$, then the spectral projection of $H$ on $(-\infty,b_Q)$ has
dimension at most $\operatorname{rank}P$.  Its range is a finite sum of
eigenspaces, and every eigenvalue in this interval is detected by the Schur
complement.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.595219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77108d69273ab028a1744f0813b99f2291b438ccad572ffcfaf6dc41b2d0df7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:diffusion+jumpHKE of arXiv:2412.05030, 'Characterization of Subordinate Symmetric Markov Processes'] (Diffusion+jump type heat kernel estimates [CKW2020])
  

  For a regular Dirichlet form $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ of the diffusion+jump type, 
  we say HK$_{-}$($\phi_c,\phi_j$) holds if there exists heat kernel $p(t,x,y)$ of $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$
  and 
  there exist a properly exceptional set $\mathcal{N}$ and 
  constants $c_1 ,c_2,c_3,c_4 > 0$ such that
  for all $t > 0$ and $x,y \in M \backslash \mathcal{N}$
  \begin{equation}
    \begin{split}
        &c_1\left(\frac{1}{V(x,\phi^{-1}(t))} 1_{\{\phi(c_2 r) \le t\}} + \frac{t}{V(x,r)\phi_j(r)} 1_{\{\phi(c_2 r) > t\}}\right)\\
    &\le p(t,x,y)\\
    &\le c_3\left(\frac{1}{V(x,\phi^{-1}(t))} \wedge (p^{(c)}(c_4t,x,y) + p^{(j)}(t,x,y))\right).
    \end{split}
    
  \end{equation}
Here $p^{(c)}(t,x,y)$ defined in ((eq:diffusionHKE of the paper)) appears as the sub-Gaussian heat kernel and 
  $p^{(j)}(t,x,y)$ defined in ((eq:JumpHK of the paper)) appears as the stable-like heat kernel.
See Example (ex:diffusion+jump of the paper) for concrete examples of processes that enjoy ((eq:diffusion+jumpHKE of the paper)).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H real separable Hilbert, W isonormal Gaussian on H","the L^2 space is with respect to the sigma-algebra GENERATED BY W","f_n symmetric, and then unique"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77fa0481be857539e984e1e66a556b4287a9c335209411aaef62032c500226b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real separable Hilbert space and let W = { W(h) : h in H } be an ISONORMAL Gaussian process, that is a centred Gaussian family with E[ W(h) W(g) ] = <h, g>_H. For n >= 0 let the n-th WIENER CHAOS H_n be the closed linear span in L^2 of { He_n( W(h) ) : h in H, ||h||_H = 1 }, with H_0 the constants. Then the H_n are mutually ORTHOGONAL and L^2( Omega, sigma(W), P ) is their orthogonal direct sum. Equivalently, every square-integrable functional F of the Gaussian process has a unique expansion F = E[F] + sum_{n >= 1} I_n(f_n) with f_n a symmetric element of the n-fold symmetric tensor power of H, where I_n is the multiple Wiener-Ito integral, and the Ito isometry gives E[F^2] = E[F]^2 + sum_{n >= 1} n! ||f_n||^2. For H = L^2([0,T]) and W Brownian motion, I_n(f_n) is the n-fold iterated Ito integral of f_n and the expansion is the classical chaos expansion. The sigma-algebra must be the one GENERATED BY W: the decomposition describes L^2 of that sigma-algebra and says nothing about functionals involving independent randomness. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.197113+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7a383e6e8a4882c83dceb16fa43d908c014c42efb8a516fc5d67ed46e77a32d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Distribution of the Stoppage Point.}

For $a\in \R$, let us note the $h_a(\mathrm{R})$ highest point in $\mathrm{R}$ above $a$:
\[h_{\mathrm{R}}(a):= \sup \{b: (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}\}.\]
In the last definition we can for instance adapt the convention that the supremum of an empty set is minus infinity.

Let $\landsc$ be a given random landscape.\\
Then, for $(x, y) \in \Half$ the stoppage point $X_{stop}(x, y)$ of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ has its CDF given by the following reformulation of events:
\[\{X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t\} =  \mathrm{below}([x, t],h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)})\cap \{t\leq\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}\} .\]

When $\landsc$ is a Poisson Building Process of intensity $\lambda$ and height distribution $\mathcal{L}$, Lemma \ref{dessous_diago} yields the following:
\[\p (X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t) = \exp \left(\int_{x}^{t} -\lambda \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\mathds{1}_{t \leq \max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} .\]
In other words, $X_{stop}(x, y)$ has its law equal to
\[g\times\Leb_{|[x,\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}]}+ \ \exp \left(-\lambda\bigintsss_{\hspace{-10pt}x}^{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} \hspace{-90pt} \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\delta_{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}},\]
where 
\[g: u\mapsto \lambda \mathcal{L}([h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(u), +\infty[)\exp\left(-\lambda \int_{x}^{u}\mathcal{L}(h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), +\infty[ \rm{d}a\right).\]

Moreover, conditioned on the stoppage point, the stoppage height is distributed according to $\mathcal{L}$ conditioned on being greater that $h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(X_{stop}(x, y))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499132+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e7b91c575adbfa0bce4ab714ce4186dd09394e0d520b2b9976c347c96e5089d7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and each is routinely dropped. (1) The cycle must be null-homologous in the domain where f is holomorphic (apart from the listed singularities). On the annulus U = {1 < |z| < 3} the function f(z) = 1/z is holomorphic with no singularity in U at all, yet the integral over the circle |z| = 2 equals 2πi, not 0: the circle winds once around 0, a point outside U. 'No singularities inside the contour' is not the hypothesis; 'winding number zero about every point off the domain' is. (2) Winding numbers multiply the residues. For the curve γ(t) = e^{2it}, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π (the unit circle traversed twice), the integral of 1/z is 4πi = 2πi times n(γ,0) Res, with n(γ,0) = 2. A figure-eight curve can even give cancellation, with winding numbers +1 and -1 about two poles. (3) The singularities must be isolated and f single-valued. f(z) = 1/sin(1/z) has poles at z = 1/(kπ) accumulating at 0, so 0 is not an isolated singularity, no residue is defined there, and the circle |z| = 1/2 encloses infinitely many poles: the residue theorem does not apply as stated (one must exhaust or use a different region). Similarly log z and sqrt(z) are not single-valued holomorphic functions on any punctured disk about 0, so they carry no residue at 0; a branch cut and a keyhole contour are required. Two further habits worth checking: a residue of 0 does not mean the singularity is removable (1/z^2 has residue 0), and when the contour is closed 'in the upper half-plane' the estimate showing the added arc's contribution tends to 0 (Jordan's lemma or an explicit bound) is part of the proof, not a formality.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378680+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e7c278a5c929afee616c48ad2dda5bb811314d807cba3f15b58d3461e5e114d4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A (deterministic, one-tape) Turing machine consists of: a finite set of states Q with a designated start state and designated halting states (for decision problems, an accept state and a reject state); a finite tape alphabet Gamma containing a blank symbol and an input alphabet Sigma not containing the blank; and a transition function delta mapping (non-halting state, tape symbol) pairs to (state, tape symbol, direction) triples with direction left or right. The machine operates on an infinite tape of cells each holding one symbol of Gamma, with a single head; initially the tape holds the input string from Sigma* followed by blanks, and the head is at the leftmost input cell. A configuration records the state, tape contents, and head position; each step applies delta to the current state and scanned symbol, rewriting the cell, changing state, and moving the head one cell. The machine halts upon entering a halting state; it may also run forever. It computes a partial function from strings to strings (output read off the tape at halting); it decides a language L if it halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings in L, and it recognizes (accepts) L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, possibly failing to halt off L. The Church-Turing thesis asserts that Turing machines capture exactly the effectively computable functions; the model is robust under adding tapes, two-way infinite tape, larger alphabets, or nondeterminism (for computability).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.724229+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7dbdb86447c0d12fc22cde62cf660427fd1de06c7b12fca11f62814e740f179","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:iml of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] We say a modal logic $L$ is \emph{intuitionistic} if the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item $\textbf{Int} = L \cap \mathscr{L}_p$.
    \item $L$ is axiomatized over $\textbf{Int}$ by a set of schematic axioms and rules.
    \item $L + \varphi \lor \neg \varphi$ is a classical modal logic extending $\textbf{K}$ (or $\textbf{K}_\Box$ or $\textbf{K}_\Diamond$, if the language of $L$ is $\mathscr{L}_\Box$ or $\mathscr{L}_\Diamond$, respectively).
    \item $L$ enjoys DP.
    \item If the language of $L$ is $\mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$, then $\textsf{Dual}_\Box \notin L$ and $\textsf{Dual}_\Diamond \notin L$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We note that our (2) is a stronger requirement than Simpson's (2), as we also require $L$ to be closed under uniform substitution and every additional rule in it.
  We also list some nice-to-have properties for $L$:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $L$ should be finitely axiomatized if $L + \varphi \lor \neg \varphi$ is finitely axiomatized.
    
    \item $L$ should be complete and sound with respect to some class of Kripke-like frames, which will be introduced in later sections.
    \item If $L$ is meant to be the intuitionistic equivalent of $\textbf{K}$, then for any $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$, it should be that $\varphi \in L$ iff $\forall x\,\mathrm{ST}_x(\varphi)$ is valid in every intuitionistic first-order structure for $\mathscr{L}_{\text{ST}}$.
    \item $L$ should have a cut-admissible sequent calculus if $L + \varphi \lor \neg \varphi$ has.
    \item It should be able to embed $L + \varphi \lor \neg \varphi$ into $L$ by a Glivenko/G\"odel--Gentzen-style translation.
    \item $L$ should enjoy Craig, Lyndon, and uniform interpolation properties if $L + \varphi \lor \neg \varphi$ does, respectively.
  \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022562+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7f41a590668f96e971e280a5fd9dbfb77e47dd230eac59b266459a3f53e42ea","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Computational Distance]
Fix two distributions $\mu, \nu$ on a state space indexed by a size parameter $n$, and fix a degree parameter $d > 0$. We define
\be 
d_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mu,\nu) = d_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mu,\nu;n,d) \equiv  \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}_{n,d}} | \mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f]|,
\ee 

where $\mathcal{F}_{n,d}$ is the collection of real polynomials in the ambient coordinates of degree at most $d$ satisfying
\be 
\max(\Var_{\mu}(f),\Var_{\nu}(f)) = 1.
\ee","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a real-valued sequence, or for the approximate version a sequence with a controlled, typically o(n) or summable, subadditivity defect","the subadditive inequality a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n holding for all, or eventually all, pairs m, n","boundedness of a_n/n from below, or explicit acceptance that the limit may be -infinity, for the limit to be meaningful in context","for statistical-mechanics applications: correct identification of the quantity, such as a log partition function, as subadditive under the relevant combination operation, such as concatenation or union of volumes"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e80a55c79ea7ae42ed54422481e1478f6dc6886bfc54622384ee814fe9cfdb74","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). If a real sequence (a_n)_{n>=1} is subadditive, meaning a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m,n>=1, then lim_{n->infinity} a_n/n exists, possibly equal to -infinity, and equals inf_n a_n/n. This elementary but powerful lemma converts a one-directional combinatorial inequality into existence of a limit, and is the deterministic backbone behind results such as convergence of the free energy per site in statistical mechanics or the growth rate of a combinatorial quantity, for instance existence of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks, or existence of free energy limits in the Ising or Potts models under volume-doubling or concatenation subadditivity. An approximate or almost-subadditive version, a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n + e(m,n) with a controlled error term, such as e(m,n)=o(m+n) or a summable correction, still yields convergence of a_n/n to an infimum-type limit under mild additional conditions, a form often needed when exact subadditivity fails because of boundary effects. It does not give any rate of convergence, only existence of the limit, and it does not apply to sequences that are only superadditive or that fail monotonicity entirely without the appropriate sign flip; Kingman's theorem is the random, ergodic-theoretic generalization for stationary sequences and is not itself implied by Fekete's lemma. Typical failure: Verifying subadditivity only for a convenient special subsequence, such as powers of 2 or specific volume shapes like cubes, and then applying Fekete's lemma as though the inequality had been established for all m, n; the lemma genuinely requires the inequality for all pairs, or at least a cofinal family closed under addition, and skipping intermediate cases silently assumes exactly the regularity, such as shape-independence of the volume limit in statistical mechanics, that itself needs a separate van Hove or Fisher-type argument. Canonical reference: Fekete, 1923, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM, Chapter 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.498624+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e81aae0473c7fafb255ac8990b980331175a03e8cb21895d97485ccf7955480b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"On a bounded domain, sup over the domain of |f| equals sup over the boundary. On an unbounded domain this is false without a growth restriction, and the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle is exactly the repair: the conclusion |f| ≤ M inside holds only under a subcritical growth bound, and the critical rate is attained by explicit functions. Load-bearing hypothesis and its failures: (1) Strip of width π, S = {|Im z| < π/2}. The function f(z) = exp(exp(z)) is entire, satisfies |f| = exp(e^x cos y), so |f| = 1 on both boundary lines Im z = ±π/2, yet |f(x)| = exp(e^x) → ∞ along the real axis. Its growth is exp(exp(|Re z|)), i.e. exactly the critical rate α = 1, so the hypothesis 'α < 1' cannot be relaxed to 'α ≤ 1'. (2) Sector of opening π/2, S = {|arg z| < π/4}. The function f(z) = exp(z^2) has |f| = 1 on both boundary rays (there z^2 is purely imaginary) and |f(x)| = exp(x^2) → ∞ on the axis of the sector; its growth exp(|z|^2) matches the critical exponent β = α = 2, so again the strict inequality β < α is needed. (3) Three-lines theorem without boundedness on the closed strip: f(z) = exp(-i exp(iπ z)) is entire, |f(x + iy)| = exp(e^{-πy} sin(πx)), so |f| = 1 on both lines Re z = 0 and Re z = 1, while on the middle line Re z = 1/2 it equals exp(e^{-πy}), which is unbounded as y → -∞. Hence M(0) = M(1) = 1 but M(1/2) = ∞: log-convexity of M fails without the boundedness hypothesis. Practical rule when auditing: whenever a bound 'on the boundary' is promoted to a bound 'inside' on a strip, sector, half-plane or any unbounded region, find the explicit growth estimate in the argument and check that its exponent is strictly below the critical one for that region's opening angle.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.961928+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e81b00e985624fee19cb943e6d0c07e04ef5f3956bbd7589fad8d3b9043a5842","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] Let $(p:\mathcal P\to N,\omega)$ be a Cartan geometry of type

{"assumptions":["a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS","for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]","for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances (then increment domination is equivalent to E[X_sX_t]>=E[Y_sY_t]); no correlation-sign condition replaces them","measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e8207cb5ab491259a97da1f7e7a1894939cc36b16bef511c7e7ace855947706c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and with the equal marginal variances the same condition, equivalently E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s,t, also gives the tail comparison P(sup X > u) <= P(sup Y > u) for every u; no condition on the sign of the correlations is needed, and none can replace the equal variances. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_e82eac33ac8c92bb29c9b15bfd94cbfbd85cf0c046e3d5255a98565d37d2934a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens at every $x$ whose orbit meets the set where $A$ is singular, hence almost everywhere when $T$ is ergodic and $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

# Opposite-head balanced two-cycles: exact family and full linear stability

Claim T328-W698-016, v1. Target 1. PROOF, UNAUDITED.
This is a family classification, not a classification of all balanced cycles or a global GD theorem. No novelty claim is made.

## Exact family

Let b,kappa>0. There is a unique T in (1/2,1) with

    cosh(T)^2 = 2 cosh(T/4)^2.

Put a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2,
d=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa),
g=(1+exp(-VH))^(-1), eta=2V/(gH).
For logistic loss log(1+exp(-v*h(kq))) and h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
simultaneous Euclidean GD has the exact two-cycle

    (V,w,-w) -> (-V,w/2,-w/2) -> (V,w,-w).

Both states have margin -VH and loss log(1+exp(VH))>log 2.
Since 0<a<b this is a legitimate separable two-token link. Repeating the same signed link permits any number of examples and either raw label, but this theorem makes no claim about distinct links.

Indeed, h(-w^2)=-H, h(-w^2/4)=H, and h'(-w^2/4)=2d.
The head increments are -2V and 2V. Writing delta=eta*v*g*h',
the factor multipliers are delta_0=1/2 and delta_1=-1; on k=-q the
k multipliers are 1-delta, namely 1/2 and 2. All cycle identities follow.

## Full spectrum

Set tau=(1-g)VH, R=2T(tanh T+tanh(T/4)),
D0=1/2+2T*tanh T, D1=2-T*tanh(T/4).
On balanced coordinates (v,k), the two Jacobians are

    Jj = [[1-2tau, B], [B/2, Dj-R*tau]],
    B=-w(1+tau)/V,  B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2.

The full two-step Jacobian has spectrum {0, eigenvalues(J1*J0)}.
The zero multiplier is the normal coordinate k+q. The larger balanced
multiplier is >25/12 throughout the family, so these cycles are never attracting.
Here and below a multiplier is an eigenvalue of the two-step derivative,
not a one-step derivative between the two different points.

Let S=D0+D1, P=D0*D1 and define

    Q(tau) = q0 + q1*tau + q2*tau^2,
    q0 = 2R(2R-S-2),
    q1 = 20R^2-8R-4P+4,
    q2 = 4(P-1)+10RS+24R^2-4R.

There is a unique positive root tau_c of Q. The other balanced multiplier
lambda_minus is positive and is <1, =1, or >1 exactly when tau is <tau_c,
=tau_c, or >tau_c, respectively. Thus the full linear spectrum consists of
one contracting zero multiplier, an always expanding positive multiplier,
and a positive multiplier with this exact threshold. At equality no nonlinear
classification along the unit eigendirection is asserted. Both strict regimes
are realized as b/sqrt(kappa) varies. The cycle always has an unstable direction.

## Root and elementary bounds

The function cosh T/cosh(T/4) has positive logarithmic derivative
tanh T-(1/4)tanh(T/4) for T>0. At T=1/2 its value is <sqrt 2:
cosh(1/2)<=8/7, since (2n)!>=2^n bounds the cosh series geometrically.
At T=1 its value is >sqrt 2, because cosh 1>37/24 and
cosh(1/4)<=32/31, and (1147/768)^2>2.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove uniqueness.

For the cosh series at 1, the terms beginning at 1/24 have consecutive
ratios at most 1/30. Consequently

    cosh 1 <= 3/2 + (1/24)/(1-1/30) = 179/116 < 31/20 < 8/5.

Also 7/3<e<3 (the lower bound follows from 1+1+1/2; the upper follows
from 1/n!<=1/2^(n-1) for n>=2, strictly for n>=3). Hence
tanh(1/2)>2/5 and tanh 1<4/5.

Write A=tanh T, B0=tanh(T/4). The root equation gives

    A^2=(1+B0^2)/2,
    R = 2T*sech(T)^2/(A-B0) = 2T(A+B0).

Since A-B0 is the integral of sech(u)^2 from T/4 to T,

    (8/3)*sech(T)^2 < R < 8/3.

In particular R>3200/2883>11/10, and also R>25/24. Further,

    9/10 < D0 < 21/10,    1 < D1 < 2.

For y=VH>0, tau=y/(1+exp y) satisfies 0<tau<1/3: the Taylor lower bound
exp y>1+y+y^2/2 implies 1+exp y>3y since (y-2)^2/2>=0.
Thus alpha=1-2tau>1/3. Both diagonal terms of the balanced Jacobians
are positive, since

    D0-R*tau > 9/10-8/9 = 1/90,
    D1-R*tau > 2-T*tanh(T/4)-8/9 > 1/9.

Put C=B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2>25/12. The monodromy trace is

    tr(J1 J0)=alpha^2+2C+(D0-R*tau)(D1-R*tau)>25/6.

Its two off-diagonal entries are B*(alpha+D0-R*tau) and
(B/2)*(alpha+D1-R*tau), both negative. Its eigenvalues are distinct and
real, since their discriminant is the squared diagonal difference plus
four times a strictly positive off-diagonal product. The larger eigenvalue
is therefore greater than half the trace, hence >25/12.

Moreover

    det Jj = (1-2tau)*Dj - R*(2+5tau) < Dj-2R < 0.

For j=0 use Dj<21/10<2R, and for j=1 use Dj<2<2R. Thus
det(J1 J0)>0 and, its trace being positive, both balanced multipliers are
positive. Direct expansion gives

    det(J1 J0-I) = Q(tau).

Since lambda_plus>1, the sign of Q is exactly the sign of lambda_minus-1.
Finally q0<0: using R=2T(A+B0),

    2R-S-2 = 2T*A+5T*B0-9/2
             < 8/5+5/4-9/2 < 0.

Also q1>13/5, since P<21/5 and the function 20R^2-8R is increasing for
R>11/10, with value 77/5 at 11/10. The coefficient q2>0 follows from
P>0, S>0 and 24R^2-4R>4. These signs give the unique positive root and
all the asserted eigenvalue comparisons.

## Both strict regimes occur

For completeness we verify tau_c<1/4 without floating point. The same
geometric tail bound gives, at x=9/10,

    cosh x <= 1+x^2/2 + (x^4/24)/(1-x^2/30).

The square of this rational upper bound is strictly less than
2*(1+(x/4)^2/2)^2. Thus T>9/10. The exponential Taylor bounds
exp(9/5)>17/3 and exp(9/20)>3/2 imply A>7/10 and B0>1/5, so
R>81/50>8/5. These finite rational comparisons are reproduced in
scripts/verify_opposite_cycle_exact.py.

At tau=1/4, expansion yields

    8Q(1/4)=84R^2-11RS-50R-6P+6.

Using S<41/10, P<21/5, R>8/5, and monotonicity of
84R^2-(951/10)R on R>=8/5, the right side exceeds

    84*(8/5)^2-(951/10)*(8/5)-6*(21/5)+6 = 1092/25 > 0.

Hence 0<tau_c<1/4. The quantity y=VH is a positive constant times
b/sqrt(kappa), so it ranges over all positive numbers. Since tau(y)->0
as y->0 or y->infinity, while tau(1)=1/(1+e)>1/4, both strict regimes
occur. This is a full linear stability classification for this family,
including the unit-multiplier threshold, not a proof about other cycles.

## Differentiation and ambient-coordinate check

At a balanced point (v,k,-k), let s=-k^2, h=h(s), d=h'(s), e2=h''(s),
g=(1+exp(vh))^(-1), delta=eta*v*g*d. The balanced Jacobian is

    J11 = 1-eta*g*(1-g)*h^2,
    J12 = -2*eta*k*g*d*(1-(1-g)*v*h),
    J21 = J12/2,
    J22 = 1-delta+2*k^2*eta*v*(g*e2-g*(1-g)*v*d^2).

Substitution gives the displayed J0,J1. In full coordinates U=k+q obeys
U_+=(1+delta)U. Along U=0 its derivative has no dependence on the
balanced perturbations, since the term U*d(delta) vanishes. Its two-step
multiplier is (1+1/2)*(1-1)=0. The derivative is block triangular with
balanced block J1 J0, so this accounts for its complete three-dimensional
spectrum even without assuming an imbalance invariant for GD.

The independent ambient numerical check differentiates the loss as
Lvv=g(1-g)h^2, Lvs=g(1-g)vhd-gd,
Lss=g(1-g)v^2d^2-gv*e2, Ls=-gvd, and uses

    Hessian L = [[Lvv, q Lvs, k Lvs],
                 [q Lvs, q^2 Lss, kq Lss+Ls],
                 [k Lvs, kq Lss+Ls, k^2 Lss]].

This numerical comparison is evidence only. The proof above uses exact
real identities and explicit rational inequalities, with every series tail
bounded geometrically or used as a nonnegative Taylor remainder.

## Scope and unresolved obstruction

The normal multiplier alone would falsely suggest attraction: the balanced
block always has an expanding eigenvalue. This family therefore supplies
no positive-volume attracting third fate. The remaining route is to classify
asymmetric opposite-head cycles (unequal head magnitudes), factor-sign-flip

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176978+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e87893e03c3956901ebb73d020004cb8882eac031dff045929b18cde73468c35","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 73 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any function $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $p(q_0)=0$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}), there exists sufficiently large $L$
 (depending on $p,\epsilon$) and $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ satisfying $1/L \le \tilde{p}(q_0) \le \epsilon$ and $\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1}) 
 such that $\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1 \le \epsilon$. 
If $p$ is furthermore concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.3}), then the same conclusion holds with $\tilde p$ also concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}). 
\begin{proof}
Since $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is absolutely continuous, we have $p' \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$. Since $p(q_0) = 0$ and $p(1) = 1$, we have $\|p'\|_1 = 1$. 

Throughout this proof, we use the term ``step function'' to refer to a function on $[q_0,1]$ that is piecewise constant with finitely many discontinuities. Since step functions are dense in $L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, there exists a step function $g_1 : [q_0,1] \to [0,+\infty)$ such that
	\[\|p' - g_1\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6\,.\]
For sufficiently large $L$, there exists a smooth function $g_2 : [q_0,1] \to [0,L]$ with $\|g_2\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L/10$, such that $\|g_1 - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6$, which implies
	\[\|p' - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 3\,.\]
Since $\|p'\|_1 = 1$, we have $\|g_2\|_1 \le 1 + \epsilon/3$. 
We then define
	\[\tilde p(t) = 1 
		- \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
		\int_t^1 g_2(s)\,ds\,,\]
and we note that $\tilde{p}$ is smooth and nondecreasing with
$\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$. For $\epsilon < 1$, we can bound
	\[
    \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    = \bigg\|p' - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) g_2\bigg\|_1
    \le \|p' - g_2\|_1 + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \|g_2\|_1
    \le \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg) \frac{\epsilon}{2}
    \le \epsilon\,.
\]
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows that
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) \le p(q_0) + \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    =\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
     \le \epsilon\,.
\]
For sufficiently large $L$, we also have
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) = 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) \|g_2\|_1 
    \ge 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
    	\bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg)
	\ge \frac{\epsilon}{6} 
    \ge \frac{1}{L}\,.
\]
Thus $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, as desired.
If $p$ is concave, then $p'$ is nonincreasing, and we can further arrange for the approximations $g_1$ and $g_2$ to be nonincreasing: in this case the resulting $\tilde{p}$ is concave, and so it satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(Omega_1, mu) and (Omega_2, nu) are sigma-finite measure spaces","L^2(mu) and L^2(nu) are separable","k is in L^2(nu ⊗ mu) in part (a); T is Hilbert-Schmidt in part (b)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572679+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, integral operators","id":"claim_e88f4cb77b3cc3163a131050495e2a27716c9e4fb987bc783cad197ba892ce26","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega_1, mu) and (Omega_2, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces such that L^2(mu) and L^2(nu) are separable. (a) If k is in L^2(nu ⊗ mu), then for nu-almost every y the function x -> k(y,x) f(x) is mu-integrable for each f in L^2(mu), and (T_k f)(y) = integral of k(y,x) f(x) dmu(x) defines a Hilbert-Schmidt operator T_k: L^2(mu) -> L^2(nu) with ||T_k||_2 = ||k||_{L^2(nu ⊗ mu)}; in particular T_k is bounded and compact, with ||T_k|| <= ||k||_{L^2}. (b) Conversely, every Hilbert-Schmidt operator T: L^2(mu) -> L^2(nu) is of the form T_k for a kernel k in L^2(nu ⊗ mu) that is unique up to a null set. Thus k -> T_k is an isometric isomorphism of L^2(nu ⊗ mu) onto the Hilbert-Schmidt class S_2(L^2(mu), L^2(nu)). (c) The adjoint of T_k is the integral operator with kernel (x,y) -> conjugate of k(y,x). Note that an L^2 kernel is defined only almost everywhere, so its values on the diagonal (a null set when the diagonal is null) carry no information.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T02:56:00.871551+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2511.18562, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_e8977109a5f44050854db38b288ba238","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Example 1 (summarizing Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 of Li and Li, 2024) of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] For sufficiently large $d$, consider training a two-layer neural network of the form $\\displaystyle F(X)$ $\\displaystyle=\\big(F_{1}(X),F_{2}(X),\\ldots,F_{k}(X)\\big),$ $\\displaystyle F_{i}(X):$ $\\displaystyle=\\sum_{r\\in[m]}\\sum_{p\\in[P]}\\widetilde{\\mathrm{ReLU}}\\!\\big(\\langle w_{i,r},x_{p}\\rangle\\big),$ where $X=(x_{p})_{p\\in[P]}\\in(\\mathbb{R}^{d})^{P}$, $w_{i,r}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are trainable weights, and $m=\\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ denotes the network width. Suppose the model is initialized randomly and trained for $T=\\Theta(\\mathrm{poly}(d)/\\eta)$ iterations on a sampled training dataset $\\mathcal{Z}$ using a learning rate $\\eta$. Under these conditions, the following properties hold with high probability: 1. Standard Training: The model at T iteration $F^{(T)}$ converges to a non-robust global minimum. Let $F_{i}^{T}$ be the $F_{i}(X)$ at T-th iteration. Adversarial Training: The model $F^{(T)}$ converges to a robust global minimum. Consequently, for perturbations $\\|\\Delta\\|_{\\infty}\\leq\\epsilon$, the robust test accuracy is high: $\\displaystyle\\mathbb{P}_{(X,y)\\sim\\mathcal{D}}\\Big[\\exists\\Delta\\in(\\mathbb{R}^{d})^{P},\\ \\|\\Delta\\|_{\\infty}\\leq\\epsilon\\ \\text{s.t.}\\$ $\\displaystyle\\arg\\max_{i\\in[k]}F^{(T)}_{i}(X+\\Delta)\\neq y\\Big]$ $\\displaystyle=o(1).$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.480013+00:00","domain":"commutative algebra and algebraic number theory","id":"claim_e89bd28c5484e7e479a76fd3746c437dac0762bede0ee46e5d42cae90e3d1519","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"An integral domain R (not a field) is a Dedekind domain if it is Noetherian, integrally closed in its field of fractions, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal (Krull dimension 1). Equivalent characterisations: every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals; every nonzero ideal is invertible (the fractional ideals form a group under multiplication); the localisation at every nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring and R is Noetherian; R is Noetherian, integrally closed, of dimension 1. Examples: every principal ideal domain (Z, k[x]); the ring of integers O_K of any algebraic number field K; the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension of its fraction field (which is how O_K is proved Dedekind); the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve over a field. Non-examples: Z[sqrt(-3)] (not integrally closed; its normalisation Z[(1 + sqrt(-3))/2] is Dedekind), k[x, y] (dimension 2). Facts: a Dedekind domain is a unique factorisation domain if and only if it is a principal ideal domain, if and only if its ideal class group (fractional ideals modulo principal ones) is trivial; for O_K the class group is finite (Minkowski) and its order is the class number; every ideal in a Dedekind domain is generated by at most two elements, and every fractional ideal is projective of rank 1; a nonzero prime p of Z factors in O_K as p O_K = P_1^{e_1} ... P_g^{e_g} with sum e_i f_i = [K : Q], f_i the residue degrees, and p ramifies (some e_i > 1) exactly when p divides the discriminant of K. Dedekind domains are exactly the one-dimensional regular Noetherian domains, so 'Dedekind' is 'smooth curve' in arithmetic.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.319832+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e89ff28c01a4f11fd7a249da36523ae526b230dec0177d0895e280ea1524aa16","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma le:aux-W-l-1 of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Let the graph $G$ be finite and $l\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$. 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
    Given $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$, the random vector $\beta^{(l)\neq}$ has the
  conditional distribution $\nu_{\Lambda_l}^{W^{(l)\neq}}$. 
  \item 
    Assuming $l\ge 1$, take an arbitrary edge $\bar e=e_{j,l-1}\in E_{l-1}$ with
      $e\in E$ and $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $v=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)}\in \Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      its midpoint.
      It splits $\bar e$ into the two edges $e'=e_{2j-1,l}$ and $e''=e_{2j,l}$ in $E_l$. 
      Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
   W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}=\frac{W_{e'}^{(l)}W_{e''}^{(l)}}{2\beta_v^{(l)\neq}}.
 \end{align}
\item 
  Assume $l\ge 2$, which implies that $\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0\neq\emptyset$. 
  Take an arbitrary vertex
      $\bar v=v_{e,2^{-(l-1)}j}\in\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0$ with $e\in E$ and
      $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}-1$. In particular, $\bar v$ belongs also to
      $\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $e^1=e_{2j,l}\in E_l$ and $e^2=e_{2j+1,l}\in E_l$ the
      two edges adjacent to $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Call
      $v^1=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)},v^2=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j+1)}\in\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      the two neighboring vertices
      of $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
        2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l-1)\neq}=2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l)\neq}-\frac{(W_{e^1}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^1}^{(l)\neq}}
      -\frac{(W_{e^2}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^2}^{(l)\neq}}.
    \end{align}
  \item
     Assume $l\ge 1$ again.
