{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:04:55.814822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f211d8d5a884c11a94d5b23a1548d9dddc603bcb6167e91690ca0ebdb92424ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop p:efron-stein-classical of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Let $X_0,X_1,\dots,X_n, Y$ be random vectors (possibly with different and/or infinite lengths) on the same probability space, such that $X_0,\dots,X_n$ are conditionally independent given $Y$.
    Write $\mathbf{X} \coloneqq  (X_0,\dots,X_n)$.
    Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = (\widetilde{X}_0,\dots,\widetilde{X}_n)$ be a conditionally independent copy of $\mathbf{X}$ given $Y$.
    Write
    \begin{align*}
        \widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)} \coloneqq  (X_0,\dots,X_{k-1},\widetilde{X}_k, X_{k+1},\dots,X_n).
    \end{align*}
    Note that we have the equality of unconditional joint laws
    \begin{align*}
        (\mathbf{X},Y)\overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}},Y) \overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(0)}, Y)\overset{d}{=} \cdots \overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(n)},Y).
    \end{align*}
    

    Let $Z=Z(\mathbf{X},Y)$ be a square-integrable function of $(\mathbf{X},Y)$.
    Then
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}[\Var(Z \mid Y)]
        = \frac12
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left(
                Z(\mathbf{X},Y)
                - Z(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}},Y)
            \right)^2
        \right]
        &\leqslant
        \frac12
        \sum_{k=0}^n 
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left(
                Z(\mathbf{X},Y)
                - Z(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)},Y)
            \right)^2
        \right].
    \end{align*}
    In fact, the above holds almost surely with $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,|\,Y]$ in place of $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.836982+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f212a955617f67401fa3ee364172c3cf3f3dcf3634c453a30fb36e4f9d32ab1e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2607.20646, 'The Independence-Preserving Property and Planar Web Geometry'] Let $(\mu_X,\mu_Y,\mu_U,\mu_V)$ be probability measures on $(0, \infty)$ having positive continuous density.
Then $\HIp|_{(0,\infty)^2}$ preserves their independence if and only if there exist $p,q,r\in\R$ with $\max\{p, 0\} < \min\{q, r\}$ such that
\begin{alignat*}{3}
    \mu_X(\dd x)
        &\propto (1 + \alpha x)^{p}\Big(\frac{1}{1+x}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{\alpha x}{1+\alpha x}\Big)^r\frac{\dd x}{x} &
        &\propto x^{r-1}(1+x)^{-q}(1+\alpha x)^{p-r}\,\dd x,\\
    \mu_Y(\dd y)
        &\propto (1 + \beta y)^{p}\Big(\frac{\beta y}{1+\beta y}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{1}{1+y}\Big)^r\frac{\dd y}{y} &
        &\propto y^{q-1}(1+y)^{-r}(1+\beta y)^{p-q}\,\dd y,\\
    \mu_U(\dd u)
        &\propto (1 + \alpha u)^{p}\Big(\frac{\alpha u}{1+\alpha u}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{1}{1+u}\Big)^r\frac{\dd u}{u} &
        &\propto u^{q-1}(1+u)^{-r}(1+\alpha u)^{p-q}\,\dd u,\\
    \mu_V(\dd v)
        &\propto (1 + \beta v)^{p}\Big(\frac{1}{1+v}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{\beta v}{1+\beta v}\Big)^r\frac{\dd v}{v} &
        &\propto v^{r-1}(1+v)^{-q}(1+\beta v)^{p-r}\,\dd v.
\end{alignat*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:03:35.764879+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f21945168965d91d3814c75ca2e8370abe9f7795ba4ae1acefba822be9fb5225","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:commutator-transfer of arXiv:2608.22910, 'A Commutator Framework for Selective Spectral Alignment in Deep Neural Networks'] Fix \(t\geq0\) and \(\ell\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\), and set
\[
C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}:=[\mathcal S_\ell,\mathrm{NFM}_\ell],
\qquad
C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}:=[Q_\ell,P_\ell].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}
=W_\ell^\top C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}W_\ell
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}\|_F
\leq
\|W_\ell\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F.
\end{equation}
If \(W_\ell\) has full row rank, and \(\sigma_{\min}(W_\ell)\) denotes
its smallest singular value, then
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\min}(W_\ell)^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F
\leq
\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}\|_F
\leq
\sigma_{\max}(W_\ell)^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F,
\end{equation}
and hence \(C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}=0\) if and only if
\(C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}=0\).","status":"unverified"}

We define the chronological loop-erasure of $\lambda$, denoted by $\text{LE} (\lambda)$, in the following manner. First, set
$$ t_0 \coloneqq \max\{t \ge 0 \, : \, \lambda(t) = \lambda(0)\}.$$
For each $i \geq 1$, define
$$ t_i \coloneqq \max\{t \ge 0 \, : \, \lambda(t) = \lambda(t_{i-1}+1)\}. $$
Let 
$$n = \min\{i \, : \, t_i = m\}.$$
    Then, the chronological loop-erasure of $\lambda$ is given by
    $$\text{LE} (\lambda) \coloneqq [\lambda(t_0), \lambda(t_1), \ldots, \lambda(t_n)].$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.375742+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f228afb5fec46a77ed7a68dc1f47d716ae8d82f9cf50f0d93b7eb9f226275609","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $S_1\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}$
    \begin{proof}
        We may compute $S_1$ explicitly. We have, via a combinatorial identity,
        \[S_1=\frac{n-2m-3}{2^{n-2m-4}}\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}-m-2}\]
        By a special case of Stirling's estimate, we have
        \[\binom{n}{n/2}\sim 2^n(\pi n/2)^{-1/2}\] 
        This gives
        \[S_1\sim \frac{(n-2m-3)(2^{n-2m-4})}{(2^{n-2m-4})\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}=\frac{(n-2m-3)}{\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-2m-3}{\sqrt{n-2m-4}}\right)\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-2}{\sqrt{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-3}}\right)\]
        \[\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}\]
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined nonnegative counting or indicator-sum random variable X = sum_i X_i","a computable or boundable first moment E[X]","a computable or boundable second moment E[X^2], in particular control of the pairwise correlations E[X_i X_j]","the correlation sum not growing asymptotically faster than (E[X])^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.982598+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f22c0577c492845332c3c1bfdcfe54194e3ac9704f0f1fdb3d81ba1f6e0e27d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a nonnegative random variable X, typically a count of some combinatorial structure written as X = sum_i X_i for indicator random variables X_i, the Paley-Zygmund inequality gives P(X > 0) >= (E[X])^2 / E[X^2]. Expanding E[X^2] = E[X] + sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j], the method succeeds in proving P(X>0) is bounded away from 0 exactly when the pair-correlation sum sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j] is of the same order as (E[X])^2, that is, when correlations between the indicators do not overwhelm the square of the mean. This is the standard route to existence results, such as an infinite cluster, a long crossing, or a large clique, once a first-moment computation has already established that E[X] is large or diverging, complementing the first-moment method, which by Markov's inequality only ever gives upper bounds on P(X>0). The method does not give any rate of convergence beyond the crude Paley-Zygmund ratio, gives no lower bound at all if the correlation structure is not controlled, and can produce a vacuous (near-0) bound whenever the variance is dominated by rare, strongly correlated configurations even though the mean itself is large. Typical failure: Computing a large or diverging first moment E[X] and declaring existence of the structure without bounding E[X^2]; if the indicators X_i are strongly positively correlated (a common situation for overlapping structures), the pair-correlation term can dominate (E[X])^2, making the Paley-Zygmund bound vacuous even as E[X] -> infinity, which is exactly the situation where a large first moment gives a false sense of near-certain existence. Canonical reference: Paley and Zygmund, 1932, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society; Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition, Wiley.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.225060+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f23020d8445bd253c00a0b60b7f7daea1deb6edc5666d5be40a7ebe62b0a92be","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (Replica Wick polynomial) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] For
\[

one has the polynomial identity

 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)

where

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.021850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f23551d1d6ce286a848c4a114798a230aaed7866f5fe5c8fbdd9a751ae99fd49","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 37 (Convergence, stated with a reference measure; Theorem \ref{thm:posdens}) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\XX$ be a set, $\XXA$ a $\sigma$-algebra on $\XX$, and $\lambda$ a
$\sigma$-finite measure on $(\XX,\XXA)$. Let
\[
  p : \XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty)
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \tau : \XX\times\XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty), \quad (x,y) \longmapsto \tau(y \mid x),
\]
be measurable, respectively $\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable, and define the probability
measure $\pi$ and the Markov kernel $T$ by
\[
  \pi(A) := \int_{A} p \dd\lambda,
  \qquad
  T(A \mid x) := \int_{A} \tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y)
  \qquad (A \in \XXA,\ x \in \XX),
\]
where $\int_{\XX} p \dd\lambda = 1$ and $\int_{\XX}\tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) = 1$
for every $x \in \XX$. Write $\Xp := \{ y \in \XX : p(y) > 0 \} \in \XXA$ and assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item \emph{(invariance)} $\displaystyle\int_{\XX} \tau(y \mid x)\,p(x)\,\lambda(\dd x) = p(y)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $y \in \XX$;
  \item \emph{(the support is not left)} for every $x \in \XX$: $\ \tau(y \mid x) = 0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $y \in \XX\setminus\Xp$;
  \item \emph{(positivity)} $\tau(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y) \in \Xp \times \Xp$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty} \tv{T^{n}\circ\mu - \pi} = 0 \qquad\text{for every } \mu \in \Prob .
\]
Theorem \ref{thm:posdens} of the introduction is the special case in which $p > 0$
everywhere, so that $\Xp = \XX$ and hypothesis (ii) is vacuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.868818+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f25330ccb17a2bdea4a968591cbb16cfbff2a560539b000697aab4eb9d53e94c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 4 of arXiv:2608.29148, '2608.29148'] A $\Theta$-metric $g$ on $(\ol X, [\Theta])$ is called an {\it asymptotically complex hyperbolic (ACH) metric} with CR infinity $(M, H, J)$ if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  For any boundary defining function $r$, we have 
\[
\Bigl|\dfrac{dr}{r}\Bigr|^2_g=\dfrac{1}{4}\quad \textrm{on}\ M,
\]
or, equivalently, $|\nu|^2_g=4$. 
\item[(ii)] For any $p\in M$, the map
\[
L_p\longrightarrow {}^\Theta T_p \ol X, \quad Z\longmapsto [\nu_p, Z]
\]
gives the identity map on $L_p$.
\item[(iii)] For any contact form $\th$ on $M$, we have 
\[
\lambda_\th^*(g|_{L})=2h_{\a\ol\b}\th^\a\cdot\th^{\ol\b},
\]
where the right-hand side denotes the Levi form on $H$ associated with $\th$.
\end{enumerate}
We call $(\ol X, [\Theta], g)$ an {\it ACH manifold}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:47:12.026502+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f25c31164f52aee7d95a5487832ff8ba214c01e8a796f43bdd2590ffb2003181","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:doubling-metric-dim of arXiv:2512.06984, 'Infinite Dimensional Multifractal Analysis of the Wiener measure'] Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space.
		
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (A)] (Doubling $\Rightarrow$ finite metric dimension)
Assume that there exists an integer $N\ge 1$ such that for every $x\in X$ and $R>0$, the ball $B(x,R)$ can be covered by at most $N$ balls of radius $R/2$.
Then $(X,d)$ is $(C,s)$-homogeneous in the sense of Assouad, with
\[s=\log_2 N, \qquad C=N,\]
hence $\Dim(X,d)<\infty$.
			
\item[\rm (B)] (Finite metric dimension $\Rightarrow$ doubling)
Assume that $(X,d)$ is $(C,s)$-homogeneous: for all $0<a<b$ and all $Y\subset Z\subset X$ with $\mathrm{diam\, }(Z)\le b$ and $Y$ $a$-separated, one has $\#Y\le C(b/a)^s$.
Then $(X,d)$ is doubling: every ball $B(x,R)$ can be covered by at most
\[N_0:=C\,2^{s}\]
balls of radius $R/2$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:14:57.697915+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f28cced144ddd8d12a6fff5a14ac4b95f1bf1902889b9a579971a1efe1c90cdb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma area Lemma of arXiv:2605.29095, 'Asymptotics of the number of components of random polynomial lemniscates'] [Area Theorem] [Ahlfors], [crane-polynomialpreimage] 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let \( f \) be a univalent (injective holomorphic) function on a domain \( D \subseteq \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \subset D \) be a measurable set. Then the area of the image \( f(K) \) is given by:
\[
\text{Area}\big(f(K)\big) = \int_K |f'(z)|^2 \, dA(z),
\]
where \( dA(z) = dx \, dy \) denotes the Euclidean area element in \( \mathbb{C} \).
\item Let \( p \) be a polynomial of degree \( n \) over \( \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \) be any measurable subset of the complex plane. Let \( n(z, p, K) \) be the number of preimages of \( z \) under \( p \) that lie in \( K \) counted with multiplicity. Then,
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{C}} n(z, p, K)\, dA(z) = \int_K |p'(z)|^2\, dA(z).
\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.629651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2985b380df672ca006dd72171da5601738e771bd695b2c1682f7e5387b705ab","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma L:basis-for-comparison of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $y_1 \le y_2 \in \mathbb{Z}, t \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $[x,1]_{\textsf{L}}\le [y_1,t]_{\textsf{L}}$ and $[x,1]_{\textsf{L}}\le [y_2,t]_{\textsf{L}}$, and take $f:\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. {"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite fourth moments","M/n -> c > 0, m/n -> r in (0,1)","the two parts of the split are disjoint (independence of V_1 and S_2 is what carries the argument)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.563112+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation","id":"claim_f2a2a51ee2fc2c34c5acc49ed5282836e853f6346ca1c35a46bb72807e699342","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X$ be $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with covariance $\\Sigma$. Split the rows into two independent parts of sizes $m$ and $n - m$ with sample covariances $S_1 = V_1\\Lambda_1 V_1^T$ and $S_2$. The nonparametric eigenvalue-regularised covariance estimator is $\\hat\\Sigma = V_1 \\operatorname{diag}(V_1^T S_2 V_1)\\, V_1^T$, averaged over $K$ random splits. Then: (i) $\\mathbb{E}[V_1^T S_2 V_1 \\mid V_1] = V_1^T \\Sigma V_1$, so each diagonal entry $v_i^T S_2 v_i$ is an unbiased estimate of the population variance in the direction $v_i$ - the Ledoit-Peche oracle $d_i^* = v_i^T\\Sigma v_i$ evaluated on independent data; (ii) as $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $M/n \\to c > 0$ and $m/n \\to r \\in (0,1)$, $\\hat\\Sigma$ is asymptotically optimal in Frobenius loss among estimators of the form $V_1 D V_1^T$ with $D$ diagonal (Lam 2016, Theorem 1); (iii) $\\hat\\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite and carries no bandwidth, floor or shrinkage constant beyond the split fraction (Lam recommends choosing $m$ by minimising $\\|\\hat\\Sigma_m - S\\|_F$ over a grid; $m = n/2$ is the usual default). A population direction of genuinely small variance keeps a small estimate (its held-out variance is small too); a direction whose small sample variance was a finite-sample cancellation receives the variance it actually has out of sample.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:25:12.199767+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2a304b908b4ba5300ffa78b81f8ff1e1288a1b237313bc7dba785c638cda538","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 59 of arXiv:2510.22783, 'Universality of Cutoff for Riffle Shuffling'] The string $s\in [k]_0^{K}$ is \textbf{collision-likely} (we write $s\in \CL$) if $s$ satisfies the following properties.

			\item For all $(i,l)\in T$, we have \[
            s \mbox{ contains } \beta_l^{(i)}\log(N) \mbox{ of } l\mbox{-digits in } \{\alpha_{\tot}+\lfloor2\rho\log N\rfloor+1\leq t\leq K: \bn^{(t)}/N\in D_i\}.
            \]
		\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E and C symmetric p x p; the estimator class is restricted to the eigenvectors of E"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943255+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f2c72c8f5c4a1fb5da7d3fb5c8cdf44405907d5be714dd864209131af7efd314","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E$ be a symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix with eigen-decomposition $E = \\sum_k \\lambda_k u_k u_k^T$ (for instance a sample covariance) and let $C$ be any symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix (the population covariance). Among all estimators of the form $\\Xi = \\sum_k \\xi_k u_k u_k^T$ - the same eigenvectors as $E$, free eigenvalues - the Frobenius loss $\\|\\Xi - C\\|_F^2$ is minimized by the oracle choice $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, the projection of the population matrix onto the $k$-th sample eigenvector, with minimal loss $\\|C\\|_F^2 - \\sum_k (u_k^T C u_k)^2$. In particular the oracle eigenvalues are convex combinations of the population eigenvalues (they lie between the smallest and largest population eigenvalue) and their sum equals $\\operatorname{tr} C$: a rotationally invariant estimator that is optimal in Frobenius loss never moves the trace and always shrinks the spread of the sample spectrum toward the population spread.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.756992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2c8ae5ef5ac85c776bfa5f4ce43dd5aa65d1dc2314cc459488cebd658f030a8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 11 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Let $\alpha$ be a quadratic irrational, let $ax^2+bx+c$ be its minimal polynomial with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\mathrm{gcd}(a,b,c)=1$ and $a>0$, and let $Q(x,y)=ax^2+bxy+cy^2$ be the corresponding binary quadratic form. For any constant $\theta>1$ and any integer $M \ge 1$, we have
\[ \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta}} = c(\alpha, \theta) \log M +O(1) \]
with an implied constant depending only on $\alpha$ and $\theta$. The constant $c(\alpha, \theta)$ is given by
\[ c(\alpha, \theta) = \frac{D^{\theta/2}}{\log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{n \in \mathbb{Z} \\ n \neq 0}} \frac{R_Q(n)}{|n|^{\theta}}, \]
where $D=b^2-4ac>0$ is the discriminant, $R_Q(n)$ is the number of primary representations of $n$, and $\varepsilon=(t_0+u_0\sqrt{D})/2$ with the smallest positive solution $(t_0,u_0)$ of Pell's equation $t^2-Du^2=4$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249409+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2d6391f59833740293808b811f91c84a58e6e86c5a2835f4556e601d7e426f5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:VEB-escape of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] There exists a real number $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds. Suppose that $\overline{p}$ has finitely many bins which are strongly exposed. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with
birth rate~$2 \lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set~$\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
Let $j_0\geq 5$ be a sufficiently large positive integer such that all strongly-exposed bins are in $[j_0-1]$.
Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$ be the event that, for every step $t' \in [T^{\overline{p},j_0}]$, $n^{X^B} \ge 2$. 
We will condition on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$.
Let
$\tau_0 =  T^{\overline{p},j_0}$. 
Let

with $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be   the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper) and let $\ensuremath{\Psi^{\mathrm{BB}}(\Psi_0)}$  (Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-state-space of the paper)) be the  $\Psi_0$-closure (Definition~(def:hls-closed of the paper)) of~$\mathrm{hls}$.

Lemma~(lem:backoff-bounding-valid of the paper).

Conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$,
the VEB-coupling (Definition~(equation def:VEB-couple of the paper)   couples $X$ with a volume process $V$ from $\Psi_0$ with  transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ and with a sequence $E_1, E_2,\ldots $ of escape processes with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$. 
The coupling uses $b_i^{E_0}(\tau_0+1)$ as a synonym for $\mathbf{e}_i^X(\tau_0+1)$.

With probability at least~$2/3$,

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]

$\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)}  = \textup{advancing}$
and the $S\in \mathcal{S}^{\Psi(t)}$,

\item for all $t> \tau_0$ such that 
$\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)} \notin \{\textup{failure},\textup{advancing}\}$ and all $k \in [j^{\Psi(t-1)}-1]$ such that $W_k \ge (j^{\Psi(t-1)})^\chi$, $p_kb_k^{E_{g^{\Psi(t-1)}}}(t) \le \lambda/80$. Moreover, there is at least one such $k\in [j-1]$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.674209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2ed3477afc3d07457bef4a154dbb7751193b6e2f0e726f426a90c07f78cebfd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 3 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional Finsler metric measure manifold. Assume that $\mathbf{S}\geq -\vartheta$ for some $\vartheta \geq 0$.
Then for $p>\frac{n}{2}$ and $K>0$, we have the following inequalities.
\ben
\item[{\rm (1)}] If $0< r\leq R\leq \frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{K}}$, then
\beq
& &\left[\frac{A(R)}{e^{\vartheta R} \sin^{n-1}(\sqrt{K} R)}\right]^{\frac{1}{2p-1}} -\left[\frac{A(r)}{e^{\vartheta r} \sin^{n-1}(\sqrt{K} r)}\right]^{\frac{1}{2p-1}} \nonumber\\
&&  \leq \left(\frac{n-1}{(2p-1)(2p-n)}\right)^{\frac{p-1}{2 p-1}}\left(\left\|{\rm Ric}_{\infty}^{K}\right\|_{p, R, \vartheta}(x_{0})\right)^{\frac{p}{2p-1}} \int_{r}^{R}\left(\frac{1}{\sin (\sqrt{K} s)}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2p-1}} ds.

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a martingale with respect to (F_n)","for the optional stopping consequence: tau an almost surely finite stopping time and the martingale uniformly integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3381e7ccdd3a3ab4f50fa4aa3f0083f4b6eac81113da66a80d044e9f35491f6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n)_{n >= 0} be a martingale for a filtration (F_n) and let F_infinity be the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the F_n. The following are equivalent: (i) the family {X_n} is uniformly integrable; (ii) X_n converges almost surely AND in L^1 to some X_infinity; (iii) there exists Y in L^1 with X_n = E[Y | F_n] almost surely for every n, that is the martingale is CLOSED. When these hold one may take Y = X_infinity, and X_infinity = E[Y | F_infinity]. Consequences: for a UI martingale, E[X_infinity] = E[X_0], and the optional stopping identity E[X_tau] = E[X_0] holds for EVERY almost surely finite stopping time tau, with no boundedness assumption on tau or on the martingale - this is a genuinely stronger conclusion than the standard three sufficient conditions (bounded tau, bounded martingale, or E[tau] finite with bounded increments). An L^1-bounded martingale need not be UI, and then only the almost sure half of (ii) survives. For p > 1, an L^p-bounded martingale is automatically UI by de la Vallee Poussin and converges in L^p as well; p = 1 is the exceptional case. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorems 13.3 and 14.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each f_n Riemann integrable on the compact interval [a,b]","uniform bound |f_n| <= M","pointwise convergence to f, AND f Riemann integrable - an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752811+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f36289c5312e1ca03cfca5ba87601f4ac8063f5554a56039a9f33e45b9a5702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be Riemann integrable, uniformly bounded (|f_n| <= M for all n), and suppose f_n -> f pointwise on [a,b] where f is ALSO Riemann integrable. Then integral_a^b f_n -> integral_a^b f. The Riemann integrability of the limit must be ASSUMED and does not follow: enumerate the rationals of [0,1] as q_1, q_2, ... and let f_n be the indicator of {q_1, ..., q_n}. Each f_n is Riemann integrable with integral 0, the family is bounded by 1, and f_n increases pointwise to the indicator of the rationals, which is not Riemann integrable. This is the essential defect that the Lebesgue integral repairs: the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem needs only measurability of the limit, which is automatic for a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Historically Arzela proved this in 1885 by a direct and rather delicate covering argument, before the Lebesgue theory existed. [Arzela (1885); see e.g. Luxemburg, 'Arzela's dominated convergence theorem for the Riemann integral', Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971)]","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}
\item An element $x$ in $E$ is invertible if and only if the quadratic representation $\mathrm P(x)$ is invertible. If $x$ in $E$ is invertible then $\mathrm P(x)^{-1}=\mathrm P(x^{-1})$.
\item If $x$ is invertible then $\mathrm P(x)(x^{-1})=x$.
\item If $x,y\in E$ then $\mathrm P(\mathrm P(y)(x))=\mathrm P(y)\mathrm P(x)\mathrm P(y)$.
\item If $x,y\in E$ are invertible then $(\mathrm P(x)(y))^{-1}=\mathrm P(x^{-1})(y^{-1})$.
\item The differential of $x\in E^{\times} \mapsto x^{-1}$ at $x$ is $-\mathrm P(x^{-1})$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.667215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3d0f4a43e1234f642677f9825b3630dc54cd55f6fb84c3189154d5d54f82428","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn eq:Ae-def of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Let $e=\{u,v\}$ be a bridge, where $u$ has label $1$ and $v$ has label $2$. 
Its original activation time and the lower bound recorded at activation are
\begin{align*}
 \gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \max\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u),\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\},\\
 L_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
The corresponding residual in the cumulative-hazard scale is
\begin{align*}
 R_e
 := H(\go_e)-H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) 
 = \go_e^\theta-(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta.
\end{align*}

For $q\geqslant\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the collision threshold
\begin{align*}
 L_e(q)
 :=
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
In particular, $L_e(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}})=L_e^{\mathrm{act}}$.

For $s\geqslant\mathfrak{a}_\ell\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the rescaled bridge age by
\begin{align}
 A_e(s)
 :=
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align}
Then $ L_e(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell)=\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}$.

The cumulative bridge hazard at rescaled time $s$ is
\begin{align}
 \gL_s
 &:= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}
 \left[ H\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}\right) - H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) \right]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}\left[\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell }\right)^\theta
 -(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta\right]
 \notag\\
 &=\int_0^s \frac{2\theta}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell ^\theta}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_q} A_e(q)^{\theta-1}\,\mathrm d q.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149599+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_f3f681977eb9ae940809b4e58a616eac3c6360d8024519e4cff1f440e2681399","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: an interior ball touching the boundary at the point x0 in question (and, for the strong maximum principle, the fact that such a ball can always be produced inside the open set where the solution is strictly below its maximum). Without it the conclusion 'the inward derivative at a boundary minimum is strictly positive' is false. Counterexample at a convex corner: in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with 0 < beta < pi and u(r, theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta). Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous on the closure, u > 0 inside and u = 0 on both straight edges, so 0 is a strict boundary minimum of u; but pi/beta > 1, so for every direction e pointing into Omega the difference quotient (u(te) - u(0))/t = O(t^{pi/beta - 1}) tends to 0: there is no Hopf gain at the vertex. No interior ball touches the vertex, exactly as the hypothesis requires. How far the hypothesis can be relaxed: the interior sphere condition may be replaced by an interior C^{1,Dini} (or interior paraboloid/cone-with-Dini) condition, but not by mere C^1 regularity of the boundary; there are C^1 domains where a positive harmonic function vanishing on the boundary has vanishing gradient at a boundary point - for instance the image of the upper half-plane near 0 under the conformal map z -> z log(1/z), whose boundary is C^1 but not Dini smooth at 0, and for which the inverse map has derivative tending to 0. Practical rule for an auditor: a proof that invokes Hopf's lemma (to get strict inequality, strict monotonicity, a sign of the normal derivative, simplicity of the first eigenvalue, or the strong maximum principle at the boundary) must say why the domain has the interior ball property at the relevant point; convex corners and cusps of the domain are where this silently breaks.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.706252+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4177cd22fe68cf91c4fe2f17a2753cff7d031ce3e67b55d54b5041efda274b9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop shape of arXiv:2609.00672, 'Deciding superellipticity and computing the Weierstrass normal form'] Let $g\ge2$, let $C:y_2^2=f(x_2)$ with $f\in K[x_2]$ separable of degree $2g+1$ or $2g+2$, let $n\in\{2g+1,2g+2\}$, and put $m=n-1$. Let $T_n$ be the set of $t\in\mathbb P^1(K)$ for which

\[
f_t=a\,(x-\beta)^n+b,\qquad a,b\in K^\times,\ \beta\in K .
\]

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There are $u,v\in K(C)$ with $K(u,v)=K(C)$ and $v^n=(u^2-b)/a$ for some $a,b\in K^\times$ if and only if $T_n\ne\emptyset$.
\item $T_n$ is finite. It contains $\infty$ only if $\deg f=n$, and a finite $t\in T_n$ is a root of $f$ if $n=2g+1$ and satisfies $f(t)\ne0$ if $n=2g+2$.
\item Let $n=2g+2$ and let $t\in K$. Then $t\in T_n$ if and only if $p_t=f_t'$ satisfies

\begin{equation}
m\,p_t\,p_t''=(m-1)\,(p_t')^2 .
\end{equation}

The coefficients of $m\,p_t\,p_t''-(m-1)(p_t')^2$ as a polynomial in $x$ are polynomials in $t$ over $K$, not all zero, and $T_n\cap K$ is the set of their common roots in $K$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d., or otherwise well-structured, entries of the non-Hermitian matrix M with matching moment and normalization conditions, e.g. mean 0, variance 1/n","convergence, for almost every z or in an appropriately averaged sense, of the empirical singular-value distribution of M-zI, established via Hermitian random matrix methods","a uniform bound preventing the smallest singular values of M-zI from concentrating excess mass near 0, i.e. a least-singular-value or anti-concentration estimate","sufficient regularity to justify exchanging limits with the singular logarithm in the potential-theoretic identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997859+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4189aeabe1f62c5a51a59e2d74be239517995bf2c0f01ad54eb33b87fa93fe6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To study the empirical spectral distribution of a non-Hermitian random matrix M, such as an i.i.d.-entry matrix in the circular law problem, Girko's Hermitization method associates to each z in C the 2n x 2n Hermitian matrix H_z with off-diagonal blocks M-zI and (M-zI)^*, whose eigenvalues are plus and minus the singular values of M-zI. The identity log|det(M-zI)| = (1/2) sum_i log(s_i(M-zI)^2) relates the real part of the logarithmic potential of M's empirical spectral distribution at z to the empirical distribution of singular values of M-zI, a Hermitian and hence more tractable object accessible via Stieltjes transform and local law techniques from Hermitian random matrix theory. Establishing, first, convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI for almost every z, and second, a uniform bound preventing accumulation of small singular values near 0, needed because log is singular there, together imply, via potential-theoretic uniqueness, convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of M itself, for example to the circular law for i.i.d. entries. It does not work without the delicate small-singular-value control, typically the hardest and most technical part of the proof, requiring separate anti-concentration or least-singular-value estimates, and the method inherently gives information about the logarithmic potential, from which the actual distribution is recovered only via a separate potential-theoretic uniqueness argument. Typical failure: Establishing convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI and concluding convergence of the eigenvalue distribution of M without separately proving the required small-singular-value control; without a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value, which can be genuinely delicate for matrices with dependent or heavy-tailed entries, the logarithmic potential argument can fail even though the easier half of Girko's method has been verified, historically the main obstruction in proving circular-law universality under weak entry assumptions. Canonical reference: Girko, 1984, Theory of Probability and its Applications; Bai, 1997, Annals of Probability; Tao and Vu, 2010, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.495670+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4450b784da6e0938f0a47fa2c1b4558192e92c1177f2731452ea5e06519a583","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 36 (Weight) of arXiv:2605.09459, 'Multipoint connectivity in the branching interlacement process'] Given a tree $T$ equiped with functions $\varphi : V(T) \to \mathbb{Z}^d$, and $\alpha : E(T) \to \mathbb{R}$, we define the \textit{weight} of $T$, as

# C019 v1: the averaged central peak is absent from each realized-label curve
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a local-window obstruction, not a global no-double-descent theorem.

## 1. Exact claim and dependencies
Use exactly C018's four stratified inputs, unit-norm single-index ReLU
teacher, fixed nu,kappa>0 (nu<=1), independent Gaussian hidden weights,
iid signed heads, both-layer GD step1/2 and sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(rho_e),
rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e). Unlike C018 retain the individual label realization:
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
All sixteen networks share initialization. For any fixed bounded interval
I=[A,B] with A<B, let J_e(I) be the integers k with
 b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e) in I.
Then
 lim_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P(each of the sixteen sequences (R_(e,m,xi)(k))_(k in J_e(I))
   is strictly monotone in one direction) = 1.             (1)
The direction may depend on xi and initialization. For small e, J has
many consecutive integers. In particular none of the sixteen individual
curves has decrease/rise/decrease witnesses entirely inside this window,
with probability tending to one in this iterated-limit sense.
C018's sixteen-trajectory average may nevertheless have such witnesses.
No single-realized-label theorem follows from that average. This claim
concerns only a bounded s window around (3/2)log(1/e)/b_s, not other times.

## 2. Exact unaveraged risk derivative
Write c_h=(1/4)sum_i h(i)xi_i for h=0,s,t,st, N_h=2sqrt(rho_e)c_h,
and U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e in the Gaussian width limit.
The frozen residual in mode h divided by alpha_e is
 q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h, q_h=exp(-b_h t).
Thus, with eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s, the derivative normalized by
2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st) is exactly
 D_(e,xi)(s)=sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
       {q_h N_h(N_h-U_(e,h))-q_h^2(U_(e,h)-N_h)^2},       (2)
at t=t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s.
C016/C017 give a joint Gaussian coupling, locally uniformly in s,
 e U_(e,s)->L_s=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1,
 b_t/(b_t+b_st), b_st/(b_t+b_st)->1/2, eta_e~e.
Let a=L_s^2 and B0=(L_t^2+1)/2; B0 is C017's B.
The constant-mode term is negligible faster than any power of e, even
with N_0=O(e^(-1/4)), because b_0 is bounded away from zero and
Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

## 3. Exhausting the sixteen sign patterns
The four-dimensional Walsh transform of a sign vector has just two types.
If xi has an odd number of + signs (eight patterns), all four c_h are
+/-1/2. If xi has an even number, xi is one of the eight signed Walsh
characters, so exactly one c_h equals +/-1 and the others vanish.
Consequently there are ten patterns with c_s!=0, four with c_s=0 and
one of c_t,c_st nonzero, and two with only c_0 nonzero.
This finite classification is verified exactly in the accompanying script;
it also follows by direct enumeration of the sixteen vectors.

For c_s!=0, (2) gives the locally uniform limit
 e^(3/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> -2sqrt(kappa)c_s L_s exp(-s).      (3)
Indeed q_s=e^(3/2)exp(-s), N_s=2sqrt(kappa)e^(-1/4)c_s,
U_s=e^(-1)(L_s+o(1)), and eta_e~e. The cross term
-q_s N_s U_s/eta_e has size e^(-3/4) and gives (3).
The terms q_s N_s^2/eta_e and q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e are O(1);
all remaining fast terms are smaller. Slow-mode terms are O(e^(-1/4))
and disappear after multiplication by e^(3/4). These estimates are
uniform on each fixed compact s interval.

If c_s=0 and either c_t or c_st is nonzero, the corresponding limit is
 e^(1/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> sqrt(kappa)(c_t L_t-c_st).         (4)
To check the slow terms without losing cancellations, rewrite their braces
in (2) as
 N_h U_h q_h(2q_h-1)-U_h^2 q_h^2+N_h^2 q_h(1-q_h).
Here q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)). After multiplication by e^(1/4), the
first term converges to 2sqrt(kappa)c_h times its U_h limit;
the second vanishes, and the third is O(e^(3/4)log(1/e)).
The weights tend to1/2. The fast contribution is only O(1) because N_s=0.
For these four patterns, exactly one of c_t,c_st is +/-1, so (4) is
nonzero unless L_t=0 in a t-pattern; that Gaussian event has probability0.

For the two constant patterns all nonconstant N_h vanish. Directly (2)
then gives, locally uniformly,
 D_(e,xi)(s) -> -a exp(-2s)-B0 <0.                       (5)
The constant-label term is again exponentially negligible.

Outside the null events L_s=0 and L_t=0, each of (3)-(5) has a strictly
nonzero, constant sign throughout any fixed compact interval. Uniform
convergence makes each frozen derivative have that sign for all sufficiently
small e. There are finitely many patterns, so this holds for all sixteen
simultaneously. Their integer-time frozen risks are therefore strictly
monotone throughout J_e(I). The Gaussian probability of this event tends
to one, by the coupling and bounded convergence.

## 4. Transfer of the LOCAL obstruction to actual nonlinear GD
For fixed e and finite integer horizon T, C018 Section3 proves joint weak
convergence of all actual risk values to their frozen Gaussian-width-limit
values. The proof works for each label pattern before averaging: prediction
transfer is uniform over the sixteen patterns, and squaring finitely many
prediction vectors is continuous. Choose T to include J_e(I).
The event that each of sixteen finite risk sequences is strictly monotone
in some direction is a finite union (over choices of direction) of finite
intersections of strict adjacent-value inequalities. It is therefore open
in this finite joint risk array. The open-set Portmanteau inequality gives
 liminf_m P(actual monotonicity event)>=P(frozen monotonicity event).
The right side tends to one as e decreases by Section3, proving (1).
Strict adjacent gaps need not have a uniform size in e: width is sent to
infinity at each fixed e first. No derivative of actual nonlinear GD is
introduced, and no uniform-width assertion is being made.

## 5. Consequence and exact scope
The dominant signed cross term in (3) disappears under noise averaging;
its sign is not controlled for a realized dataset. Slow signed cross terms
similarly survive in (4). C017/C018 obtain an averaged quadratic profile
only after these cancellations. Thus a high-probability peak in the mean
of sixteen trajectories is compatible with local monotonicity of every
constituent trajectory. Equation (1) is the exact obstruction to reusing
that proof as a single-dataset result. It does not rule out single-dataset
double descent in a DIFFERENT window or under another noise/initialization
scaling, nor for other input laws or feature-learning regimes.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018 are unaudited. Independent mathematical
and novelty review remain pending. The finite check certifies only the
sign-pattern classification and exponent bookkeeping, not the CLT, limits,
nonlinear transfer or this full proof. No training experiment was performed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.028487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4745d43e847bcbc7d0b5c612364593b7ae3449033d4447a268039029fb5e158","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ising-rpc of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Consider a tree with $L$ levels, rooted at $\varnothing$, in which every vertex before the last level has
		countably many children. We label the children of each vertex by $\mathbb{N}$, so a vertex at level $\ell$ is a sequence

		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:14.783041+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4a1e4398feecf96a9615ec8a660d4e03988e1e4f889a1d62f98dbfb392c0d9f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2607.11283, 'Markov Properties of $k$-Record Processes via Order Statistics'] The process $(U_n)_{n\ge k}$ is a time-homogeneous Markov chain

\begin{equation}

Q_k(x,A)
=

computation is realized by one fully connected scalar-output ReLU architecture,
and every slot of that architecture is affine in the same code vector.

\[
 \calA^{\mathrm{pad}}
 \in\aff(M,P_{\Psi^{\mathrm{pad}}})
\]
such that

=\Psi_{\calA(\bmxi)}$ for every $\bmxi\in\R^M$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.252020+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4c45b51436779753bbe4a859e0402e7ddddd845b13b88c472fd6145bdc2c2e7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 1 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (sharpened Malliavin-Stein bounds for Poisson functionals)
    Let $(\X,\nu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space and $(\MM,\QQ)$ a space of marks with probability measure $\QQ$. Let $\hat{\mathcal{P}}$ be a Poisson measure on $\X \times \MM$ of intensity $\nu \otimes \QQ$. Let $F$ be a measurable function of $\hat{\mathcal{P}}$ such that $\E F^2 < \infty$ and $\E F = 0$ and
    \[
    \int_{\X \times \MM} \E \left[\left( D_{(x,m_x)} F \right)^2\right] (\nu \otimes \QQ)(dx,dm_x) < \infty.
    \]
    For any point $x\in \X$, define a random variable $M_x$ independent of everything else, distributed according to $\QQ$.
    Then it holds that
    \[
    \mathbf{d}_W(F,N) \leq \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_0+ \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\hat{\gamma}_2 + \hat{\gamma}_3
    \]
    and
    \[
    \mathbf{d}_K(F,N) \leq \hat{\gamma}_0 + \hat{\gamma}_1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \hat{\gamma}_2 + \hat{\gamma}_4 + \hat{\gamma}_5 + \hat{\gamma}_6,
    \]
    where
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\gamma}_0 &:= \E \left| 1- \Var(F) \right|\\
        \hat{\gamma}_1 &:= 2 \bigg(\int_\X \bigg(\int_\X \E \big[ |D_{(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/4} \cdot \E \big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/4} \nu(dy) \bigg)^2 \nu(dx) \bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_2 &:= 2  \bigg(\int_\X \bigg(\int_\X \E \big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \nu(dy) \bigg)^2 \nu(dx) \bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_3 &:= 2 \int_\X \E|D_{(y,M_y)}F|^3 \nu(dy)
    \end{align*}
    and
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\gamma}_4 &:= \bigg(4\int_\X \E|D_{(y,M_y)}F|^4 \nu(dy)\bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_5 &:= \bigg(8\int_\X\int_\X \E|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4 \nu(dy)\nu(dx)\bigg)^{1/2}\\
        \hat{\gamma}_6 &:= \bigg(32\int_\X\int_\X \E\big[|\DD_{(x,M_x),(y,M_y)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \cdot \E\big[|D_{(x,M_x)}F|^4\big]^{1/2} \nu(dy)\nu(dx)\bigg)^{1/2}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^1 (Lipschitz flux suffices for the theory)","u ∈ L^∞; the test functions must be NONNEGATIVE, otherwise the inequality would force equality and lose all selection power","sgn is the usual signum, so the pair (|u-k|, sgn(u-k)(f(u)-f(k))) is the Kruzhkov entropy/entropy-flux pair"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417466+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_f4c7439626209bb4214a64c82f43190d941c048df2939c0d04fb206064491661","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^1(R;R^n) and u0 ∈ L^∞(R^n). A function u ∈ L^∞(R^n × (0,∞)) is a Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + div f(u) = 0, u(·,0) = u0, if for every k ∈ R and every φ ∈ C_c^∞(R^n × [0,∞)) with φ ≥ 0: ∫_0^∞ ∫_{R^n} ( |u - k| φ_t + sgn(u-k) ( f(u) - f(k) )·∇_x φ ) dx dt + ∫_{R^n} |u0(x) - k| φ(x,0) dx ≥ 0. Equivalently (for C^1 flux), η(u)_t + div q(u) ≤ 0 in the sense of distributions, with the initial datum taken in L^1_loc, for every convex entropy η ∈ C^1(R) with entropy flux q determined by q' = η' f'; the Kruzhkov family η_k(u) = |u-k| generates all convex entropies. Every entropy solution is a weak solution (take k larger than ||u||_∞ and k smaller than -||u||_∞ and combine the two resulting inequalities). The inequality has a sign: it expresses dissipation, and it is exactly the condition selected by the vanishing-viscosity limit u^ε_t + div f(u^ε) = ε Δ u^ε.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:32:29.005751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f50839e8583a8e7be60e84e95c5e077756857cecaefe6bfab498c202567bfe02","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem DL comp of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] {Duquesne_LeGall_06_Hausdorff}}]
  
  Let $(\mathcal{X}, d)$ be a boundedly-compact metric space.
  Fix $c > 1$ and fix a non-decreasing continuous function $g\colon [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$
  with $g(0) = 0$ and $g(2r) \leq c g(r)$ for all $r \geq 0$.
  Let $\mathcal{H}_g$ be the Hausdorff measure with gauge $g$.
  Then there exist constants $c', c'' \in (0,\infty)$, which depend only on $c$, 
  such that the following holds.
  Let $\nu$ be a Radon measure on $\mathcal{X}$ and let $A$ be a Borel subset of $\mathcal{X}$.
  Write $B(x,r) \coloneqq \{y \mid d(x,y) < r\}$ for each $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $r > 0$.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = \textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item 
    If $\displaystyle \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\nu(B(x, 2^{-n}))}{g(2^{-n})} \leq 1$ for every $x \in A$,
    then $\mathcal{H}_g(A) \geq c' \nu(A)$.

    \item 
    If $\displaystyle \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\nu(B(x, 2^{-n}))}{g(2^{-n})} \geq 1$ for every $x \in A$,
    then $\mathcal{H}_g(A) \leq c'' \nu(A)$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752684+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f508dc594a18c6b66feda84d09ec4e36e63f895880826437a51899385d203a1c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to X and let Y_n converge in probability to a CONSTANT c. Then (X_n, Y_n) converges in distribution to (X, c) jointly, and consequently X_n + Y_n converges in distribution to X + c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and if c is not 0 then X_n / Y_n converges in distribution to X / c. The constancy of the limit of Y_n is essential and is not a technical convenience: convergence in distribution alone gives no information about joint behaviour. Take X symmetric with X_n = X for all n and Y_n = -X for all n; then X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in distribution to X by symmetry, yet X_n + Y_n = 0 does not converge in distribution to X + X = 2X unless X is degenerate. Likewise convergence in probability of Y_n cannot be weakened to convergence in distribution even when the limit is constant, because for a constant limit those two modes coincide, which is precisely why the theorem can be stated with either for a constant target. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.343756+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f51a25c8b5bea8f13a97f628e6945c2109e612fd3b9a243166b3400362fbe2bf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Let $\mathcal{T}_k^{(j)}$ be the $j$-th principal block of $\mathcal{T}_n(a)$. Then, for a.e. $z \in \C$ and any $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\prob \left( \bigl| \log |\det(\mathcal{T}_k^{(j)} - zI)| - k \gamma(jk/n,z) \bigr|  \geq k \varepsilon \right) = o(1).
\]

\begin{proof}
As in the previous proof, it is enough to show that
\begin{multline*}
\varepsilon_k=\max_{1\le r \le k} \bigg(
\left| d\left( x_{(j-1)k+r,n} \right) - d\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
+\left| b\left( x_{(j-1)k+r,n} \right) - b\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right| \\
+\left| c\left( x_{(j-1)k+r,n} \right) - c\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
\bigg) \longrightarrow 0
\end{multline*}
in probability. Since the functions $b$, $c$, and $d$ are uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$, it is enough to prove that
\[
\Delta_k := \max_{1 \leq r \leq k} \left| x_{(j-1)k+r,n}  - \frac{jk}{n} \right| \longrightarrow 0
\]
in probability. In fact, we prove almost sure convergence.

Let
\[
F_n(t):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^n \mathbbm{1}_{\{U_r^{(n)}\le t\}}
\]
be the empirical distribution function. Since the $U_r^{(n)}$ are continuously distributed, ties occur with probability $0$. Hence, almost surely, $x_{(j-1)k+r,n}$ is the $((j-1)k+r)$-th order statistic and
\[
F_n(x_{(j-1)k+r,n})=\frac{(j-1)k+r}{n}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\left|x_{(j-1)k+r,n}-\frac{jk}{n}\right|
\le \left|x_{(j-1)k+r,n}-F_n(x_{(j-1)k+r,n})\right|+\frac{k - r}{n}
\le \sup_{t\in[0,1]}|F_n(t)-t|+\frac{k}{n}.
\]
Taking the maximum over $r$ yields
\[
\Delta_k \le \sup_{t\in[0,1]}|F_n(t)-t|+\frac{k}{n}.
\]

Now the Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz inequality tells us that for any $\epsilon>0$
\[ \prob \left( \sup_{t \in [0,1]} \vert F_n(t)- F(t) \vert > \epsilon \right) \leq 2 e^{-2n \epsilon^2}, \]
where $F(t)$ is the cumulative distribution function. Since our random variables are uniformly distributed, we have $F(t)=t$. It follows that, for every $\epsilon>0$ and all large $k$ and $n$,
\[
\prob(\Delta_k>\epsilon)
\le \prob\!\left(\sup_{t\in[0,1]}|F_n(t)-t|>\epsilon-\frac{k}{n}\right)
\le 2\exp\!\left(-2n\Bigl(\epsilon-\frac{k}{n}\Bigr)^2\right).
\]

The right-hand side is summable in $n$, so by the Borel--Cantelli lemma we obtain
\[
\Delta_{k(n)}\to0
\qquad\text{almost surely.}
\]
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.261671+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f51a7725a8b05d7ece0486d7d9257ea8b00386cf50d9d2af8aa98de58a6227f5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition CLEDef of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Let $\\Sigma \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z}$ and $\\Lambda \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A {\\em $\\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, \\mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\\left(C (\\Sigma \\times \\Lambda), \\mathcal{C}_{\\Sigma}\\right)$. Intuitively, $\\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of random continuous curves (sometimes referred to as {\\em lines}), indexed by $\\Sigma$,  each of which maps $\\Lambda$ in $\\mathbb{R}$. We will often slightly abuse notation and write $\\mathcal{L}: \\Sigma \\times \\Lambda \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, even though it is not $\\mathcal{L}$ which is such a function, but $\\mathcal{L}(\\omega)$ for every $\\omega \\in \\Omega$. For $i \\in \\Sigma$ we write $\\mathcal{L}_i(\\omega) = (\\mathcal{L}(\\omega))(i, \\cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\\mathcal{L}_i: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Lambda)$, which is $(\\mathcal{C}, \\mathcal{F})-$measurable. If $a,b \\in \\Lambda$ satisfy $a \\leq b$ we let $\\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]$ denote the restriction of $\\mathcal{L}_i$ to $[a,b]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215430+00:00","domain":"discrete geometry","id":"claim_f528a90663c3e15b8fac1b81c773ee78b7ca979ccfb7ac5f9bc09809c835ec77","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The phrase 'general position' carries two conventions in the theory of hyperplane arrangements, and they are incompatible. For a CENTRAL arrangement, where every hyperplane contains the origin, the useful condition is on the NORMAL vectors: every $d$ or fewer of them are linearly independent. This is the condition under which the central orthant count is exact. For an AFFINE arrangement, a widespread convention instead requires that any $p$ of the hyperplanes with $p$ greater than the ambient dimension have empty intersection. No central arrangement can ever satisfy the affine condition, because all of its hyperplanes share the origin. A central arrangement is therefore never in 'general position' in the affine sense, however generic its normals. Sources using the affine convention will appear to exclude exactly the case a central count is about, and citing one for the other is a live error.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.294524+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f52b7d5683614e53246433cb6a8171e35984fa17897dcd78ec0cf139427063bf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Lipschitz maps and Lipschitz model classes of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho_X)$ and $(Y,\rho_Y)$ be metric spaces, and let $L\ge0$.  A map
$f:X\to Y$ is called $L$-Lipschitz if
\[
    \rho_Y(f(x),f(y))
    \le
    L\,\rho_X(x,y)
\]
for every $x,y\in X$.  Its Lipschitz constant is
$
    \operatorname{Lip}(f)
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\neq y}
    \,
        \tfrac{\rho_Y(f(x),f(y))}{\rho_X(x,y)}
$.
When $h:X\to\mathbb R$ is real-valued, we also write $
    |\nabla h|(x)
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \limsup_{y\to x}
        \tfrac{|h(x)-h(y)|}{\rho(x,y)}
$ for its pointwise upper slope, with the convention that the value is $+\infty$ if the corresponding $\operatorname{limsup}$ is infinite.
\hfill\\
\noindent
For a metric space $(X,\rho)$, we define the unit Lipschitz model class
\[
    \mathcal F_1
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
    =
    \left\{
        f:X\to[-1,1]
        :
        |f(x)-f(y)|
        \le
        \rho(x,y)
        \text{ for all }x,y\in X
    \right\}.
\]
If $(X,\rho)$ has doubling dimension $0<d<\infty$, we abbreviate
$
    \mathcal F_{1:d}
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
$.
All such classes are equipped with the uniform norm
$
    \|f\|_\infty
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|
$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.396024+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f55c04608704ad20ac6944cc1b971270d7fd3596a2086e826d2859c2cd99bd49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Electrical networks}]
  Let $(V, E)$ be a connected, simple, undirected graph with finite or countably many vertices,
  where $V$ denotes the vertex set and $E$ denotes the edge set.
  (NB.\ A graph being simple means that it has no loops and no multiple edges.)
  For $x, y \in V$,
  we write $x \sim y$ if and only if $\{ x, y \} \in E$.
  Let $\{\mu(x, y)\}_{x, y \in V}$ be a family of non-negative real numbers such that 
  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y, x)$ for all $x, y \in V$,
  $\mu(x, y) > 0$ if and only if $x \sim y$,
  and
  \begin{equation}
    \mu(x) 
    \coloneqq 
    \sum_{y \in V} \mu(x, y) < \infty,
    \quad 
    \forall x \in V.
  \end{equation}
  We call $\mu(x,y)$ the \textit{conductance} on the edge $\{x,y\}$
  and $(V, E, \mu)$ an \textit{electrical network}.
  Note that the edge set $E$ is uniquely determined by conductances.
  We equip $V$ with the discrete topology 
  and define a Radon measure $\mu^{\#}$ as the \textit{counting measure} on $V$, 
  which is a Radon measure on $V$ given by 
  \begin{equation}
    \mu^{\#}(A) 
    \coloneqq 
    \# A
    = 
    \sum_{x \in V} \delta_{x}(A)
    \quad 
    A \subseteq V,
  \end{equation}
  where $\delta_{x}$ is the Dirac measure putting mass $1$ at $x$.
  Given an electrical network $G$,
  we write $V_{G}$, $E_{G}$, $\{\mu_{G}(x,y)\}_{x, y \in V_{G}}$, and $\mu^{\#}_{G}$
  for the vertex set, the edge set, the conductances, and the counting measure, respectively.
  When we say that $G$ is a \textit{rooted electrical network},
  there exists a distinguished vertex,
  which we denote by $\rho_{G} \in V_{G}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.063036+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f561cc7d8ee062ff9eafbe2733a3246f7233b0e3a022f01b2ca3ccfd7b99ee81","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] Consider a sequence $\{f_n\}= \{f_n\}_{0 \leq n < T+1}$ of non-anticipative functions $f_n:\mathcal{S} \rightarrow [- \infty, \infty]$, $n\ge0$.

\vspace{.1in}\noindent $\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{supermartingale} sequence if
\begin{equation}  \nonumber 
\overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1} \leq f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{submartingale} if
\begin{equation} \nonumber 
f_j \leq \underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}~~a.e.\;\;0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{martingale} if
\begin{equation}\nonumber 
\underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= \overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["This is a reduction of candidates, not a classification or a numerical proof for every stable index."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f56a0e147e9085ca7af811dce58bae38fe443cd2f2e9f0fb5cdcc82ab3fb1945","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the remaining-problem reduction in the partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. A law lambda is freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal nu. The source's Theorem 1.4 shows that no nondelta law of finite variance (equivalently, in the free domain of attraction of the semicircle) is freely strongly unimodal. The record's proved Cauchy obstruction excludes every nondelta lambda in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law. The same closure argument shows, more generally, that a nondelta lambda is not freely strongly unimodal whenever it lies in the free domain of attraction of a free stable law that is itself not freely strongly unimodal. Problem 3.11 therefore reduces to two questions. (1) Is some free stable law of index alpha in (0,2), alpha != 1, freely strongly unimodal? (The index-1 case is settled by the Cauchy identity, and index 2 by the source's Lemma 3.1.) (2) Is some measure lying in no free domain of attraction freely strongly unimodal? Numerically, for the free stable laws lambda_alpha with K(w)=1/w - i(iw)^{alpha-1}, the unimodal witness nu = (1/10)U[0,0.05] + (9/10)U[0,16] gives lambda_alpha boxplus nu two interior maxima at alpha = 1.95, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7. This was computed by Belinschi-Bercovici subordination and calibrated against the exact Cauchy case at alpha=1. So those laws, and the laws attracted to them, are excluded numerically; only alpha=1 is a theorem. For alpha = 0.6 down to 0.3 the same nu, and three other one-sided uniform mixtures tried at alpha=0.5, give a single maximum. This is not evidence that those laws are freely strongly unimodal. The case alpha below about 0.65 remains open. This does not answer the existence question. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational in (0,1) with continued fraction [0; a_1, a_2, ...], a_i >= 1","p_n/q_n are the convergents given by the standard three-term recursions","eta_n = ||q_n alpha|| = |q_n alpha - p_n|, and ||t|| is the distance to the nearest integer","the rotation is R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle R/Z, and 'closest return' refers to the two-sided quantity ||q alpha||"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732376+00:00","domain":"continued fractions, circle rotations, renormalization","id":"claim_f57732cc5b24796cda6e07d98d78f7bf187cb2277e435a9b21d5d4dfa548e4b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let alpha in (0,1) be irrational with continued fraction alpha = [0; a_1, a_2, ...], all a_i >= 1, and let p_n / q_n be its convergents, defined by p_n = a_n p_{n-1} + p_{n-2}, q_n = a_n q_{n-1} + q_{n-2} with q_{-1} = 0, q_0 = 1, p_{-1} = 1, p_0 = 0. Put eta_n = |q_n alpha - p_n| and note the signs alternate: q_n alpha - p_n = (-1)^n eta_n. For n >= 1 one has eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} <= 1/2, so eta_n = ||q_n alpha||; at n = 0 this can fail (if a_1 = 1, i.e. alpha > 1/2, then eta_0 = alpha > 1/2 while ||alpha|| = 1 - alpha), so ALL statements below are for n >= 1. Write R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on T = R/Z. Then:

(a) BEST APPROXIMATION / CLOSEST RETURNS. For n >= 1 and every integer q with 1 <= q < q_{n+1} and q not equal to q_n one has ||q alpha|| > ||q_n alpha|| = eta_n. Consequently the denominators q_n are exactly the closest-return times of the orbit of 0 under R_alpha: q_{n+1} is the smallest integer q > q_n with ||q alpha|| < ||q_n alpha||, and the sequence of record-setting return times is precisely q_1 < q_2 < ....

(b) RECURSION AND SIZE. eta_{n-1} = a_{n+1} eta_n + eta_{n+1}; the eta_n strictly decrease to 0; 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n) < eta_n < 1/q_{n+1}; and the exact identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 holds for every n >= 1 (and also at n = 0 with the convention eta_{-1} = |q_{-1} alpha - p_{-1}| = 1).

(c) RENORMALIZATION INTO TWO ROKHLIN TOWERS. Let J_n be the arc of T whose endpoints are the two points q_{n-1} alpha - p_{n-1} and q_n alpha - p_n (of opposite signs), so J_n contains 0 and has length eta_{n-1} + eta_n; it is split by 0 into a piece of length eta_{n-1} and a piece of length eta_n. Then the first-return map of R_alpha to J_n is the exchange of these two subintervals: the return time is q_n on the piece of length eta_{n-1} and q_{n-1} on the piece of length eta_n. Equivalently the q_{n-1} + q_n sets R_alpha^i(base) -- i < q_n over the long piece and i < q_{n-1} over the short piece -- are pairwise disjoint and tile T, which is exactly the content of the identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 in (b). This is the standard renormalization scheme behind Ostrowski expansions and the three-distance theorem.

SHARP EDGES. (a) is a statement about the TWO-SIDED quantity ||q alpha||. The intermediate (mediant) denominators b q_n + q_{n-1} with 1 <= b < a_{n+1} are best ONE-SIDED approximations but in general do not minimize ||q alpha||, so they are NOT closest-return times -- confusing the two is the classic error here. The hypothesis that alpha is irrational is essential: for rational alpha the algorithm terminates, the orbit is finite and periodic, and the tower picture degenerates. Also note eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} is an inequality, not an asymptotic equality: eta_n and 1/q_{n+1} agree only up to a factor between 1/2 and 1, and a proof that needs the exact value must use eta_n = 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n * [0; a_{n+2}, a_{n+3}, ...]).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:37.356107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f5776ba3ea724dd88faa8c59c2533d7d03716dd12c62dec72b5b678f2ad0e3fd","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 (A sufficient Lyapunov condition for discounted integrability) of arXiv:2606.17517, 'Killed resolvents and measure-valued stopping gains for reflected optimal stopping with ma'] Suppose there exists a function $\Psi\in C^2(\R^2_+)$, $\Psi\ge1$, satisfying

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:01:56.346838+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f581c59cfadc59565da344104a1612cb4697c13802b8ff8f5c61da3d20962ca0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:UDS_ of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] \textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{P}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{P}_x$. Let $x>a$, and let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a).$ 
If $\tau \in (0,x-a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-a,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau+a-x$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(a) \&~(b).)

\textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{T}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{T}_x$. To do so, we will split into two cases: (i) if $(a+b)/2<
x< (3a-b)/2$, and (ii) $x \ge (3a-b)/2$. 
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=3em]
    \item[{\textbf{(i)}}] Assume that $(a+b)/2
< x< (3a-b)/2$, in which case we can only deposit on the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. Hence, let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,x-(a+b)/2)$, and deposit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(e).)
\item[{\textbf{(ii)}}] Let $x\ge (3a-b)/2$, and $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a)$. If $\tau \in (0,x-(3a-b)/2)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-(3a-b)/2,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau-(x-(3a-b)/2)$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(c) \&~(d).)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Algorithm:} When a trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ has been deposited on either $\mathcal{P}_x$ or $\mathcal{T}_x$, there will be two leftover strips. Conditional on the first deposition, the parking procedures on these two strips are defined to be independent copies of the $\mathcal{UDA}$, with the corresponding strip types and sizes. 
This procedure is continued recursively until there are no strips remaining which can fit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["weights nonnegative, not all zero","for the variance interpretation: i.i.d. observations with finite variance"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:17:06.630627+00:00","domain":"survey statistics / weighted estimation","id":"claim_f582d2971f91e2d79df8475b7b3a84e28609376a3e46cd4588963e2174f253ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For case weights $s_1, \\dots, s_n \\ge 0$ not all zero, the effective sample size is $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = (\\sum_i s_i)^2 / \\sum_i s_i^2$. It satisfies $1 \\le n_{\\mathrm{eff}} \\le n$, with $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = n$ if and only if all nonzero weights are equal and $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ if and only if a single weight is nonzero. Its meaning: if $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ are i.i.d. with variance $\\sigma^2$, the weighted mean $\\bar X_s = \\sum_i s_i X_i / \\sum_i s_i$ has variance $\\sigma^2 / n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ - the weighted mean is as noisy as an unweighted mean of $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ observations. The same factor governs every entry of a weighted sample covariance $\\sum_i s_i (x_i - \\bar x_s)(x_i - \\bar x_s)^T / \\sum_i s_i$ to leading order, so entrywise concentration bounds for the sample covariance transfer to the weighted one with $n$ replaced by $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$. For the per-sample relative metric of ensemble stacking, $s_i = 1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, a few small-norm cases can make $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ far smaller than $n$ (measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT pool: 150 of 932 rows on one component, 8.7 of 60 in the $n = 60$ arm). (Why: $\\operatorname{Var}(\\bar X_s) = \\sum_i s_i^2 \\sigma^2 / (\\sum_i s_i)^2 = \\sigma^2 / n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ by independence. The bounds: Cauchy-Schwarz gives $(\\sum_i s_i)^2 \\le n \\sum_i s_i^2$ with equality iff the nonzero weights are equal (restricting to the nonzero ones), and $(\\sum_i s_i)^2 \\ge \\sum_i s_i^2$ since the cross terms are nonnegative, with equality iff at most one weight is nonzero. For the covariance, each entry is a weighted mean of the products $(x_{ik} - \\bar x_{s,k})(x_{il} - \\bar x_{s,l})$ with the same weights, and the centring changes the variance only at second order in $1/n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:36.183309+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f5be7d68a02046f965686fb75e917eaf27357500baaeed761098b619fbebbfe2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let rows $w_1,\\dots,w_{m-1}$ be i.i.d. isotropic in $\\mathbb{R}^m$ ($m=\\dim\\mathrm{Sym}_d^0$ or $\\dim\\mathrm{Sym}_d$), let $c$ be the unit null vector of the design they span, and let $A$ be the unit-Frobenius symmetric matrix it encodes. By isotropy $\\sqrt d\\,A$ converges in moments to the semicircle law, so $d^{k-1}\\,\\mathbb{E}\\,\\mathrm{Tr}(A^{2k}) = C_k + b_k/d + O(1/d^2)$ with $C_k$ the Catalan numbers. The correction constant $b_k$ is NOT a function of the row's fourth moment alone. Evidence at $d=14$ over $\\sim10^5$ designs per row law: (i) rows with i.i.d. coordinates of kurtosis $\\kappa$ give $b_k$ a function of $\\kappa$ only, a three-point law and a Gaussian at $\\kappa=3$ agreeing to $0.2$--$0.5$ standard errors on $k=2,3,4,5$ while $\\kappa\\in[1,9]$ moves the excess by a factor $2.3$; (ii) but two constructions with the SAME typical-direction kurtosis and different dependence disagree by an order of magnitude --- a rank-one Veronese row (kurtosis $3+24/d$) and an i.i.d. row matched to that kurtosis give $k=2$ excess $0.462$ versus $0.041$, a factor $11$; (iii) interpolating with $z=(XX^\\top-rI)/\\sqrt{2r}$, a sum of $r$ independent rank-one forms, the excess falls roughly as $1/r$ ($0.46,0.23,0.13,0.085$ at $r=1,2,4,8$) while the kurtosis $3+12\\,\\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)/r \\to 3$. So within one dependence class the fourth moment tunes $b_k$, but across classes at fixed fourth moment $b_k$ varies by a factor of order ten; a derivation of $b_k$ for the Veronese row ($b_2\\approx7.7$, $b_3\\approx49$, $b_4\\approx248$, $b_5\\approx1148$) must use the rank-one dependence of $xx^\\top$, not a kurtosis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f integrable on R^d","the inversion integral is a Lebesgue integral unless a summation method is specified"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264170+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_f5d963f67f53d5239315124b90077e023c2d3e14dc7fd67a61fb357f5541d086","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: $\\hat f\\in L^1$.
