{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:59:53.160538+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fdafdc6845ce4f5b20d1c730af2ada58b496c5e19f2e811ff6e9dea9ab4d33c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2607.02434, 'A Topological Formula for \\ Potts Lattice Gauge Theory Correlations'] The $i$-dimensional \textbf{plaquette random cluster model (PRCM)} with free boundary conditions on a finite cell complex $X$ with parameters $p\in\brac{0,1}$ and $q\in\N_{\geq 2}$ is the random $i$-complex $P$ with the following distribution:
$$\mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{X}\paren{P} = \mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{X,p,q}\paren{P} \propto p^{\abs{P}}\paren{1-p}^{\abs{X^{i}} - \abs{P}}\abs{H^{i-1}\paren{P;\Z_q}}$$
where $\abs{X^{\paren{i}}}$ and $\abs{P}$ denote the number of $i$-faces $X$ and $P.$

Moreover, if $\Lambda=\brac{-N,N}^d\subset \Z^d$ is a box, the PRCM with wired boundary conditions on $\Lambda$ is the measure
$$\mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Lambda}\paren{P} = \mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Lambda,p,q}\paren{P} \propto p^{\abs{P}}\paren{1-p}^{\abs{\Lambda^{\paren{i}}} - \abs{P}}\abs{H^{i-1}\paren{P\cup \partial \Lambda;\Z_q}}\,.$$
The weak limits of these measures as $\Lambda\nearrow \Z^d$ exist by standard stochastic monotonicity arguments and are denoted by $\mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{\Z^d,p,q}$ and $\mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Z^d,p,q}.$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.419501+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fdf17a2196d1cd144b6bea42b0864612ee5dc28726429d62afb8ae8373930a0d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: functor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Functor}] 
  We call $\tau$ a \textit{functor} on $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$ if it satisfies the following.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      For every $ (S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$,
      one has a metric space $(\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}), d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}})$
      where $\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$ is a set and $d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}}$ is a metric on it.
      We simply write $\tau(S) \coloneqq \tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$.
    \item 
      For every $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}),\, i=1,2$ 
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      one has a distance-preserving map $\tau_{f}: \tau(S_{1}) \to \tau(S_{2})$.
    \item 
      For any two root-and-distance-preserving maps $f :S_{1} \to S_{2},\, g : S_{2} \to S_{3}$,
      it holds that $\tau_{g \circ f} = \tau_{g} \circ \tau_{f}$.
    \item 
      For any $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$, 
      it holds that $\tau_{\id_{S}} = \id_{\tau(S)}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.345352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fdf3e37cc181e25abba9c3276ea83bdf3e5e9e673e9b450ed34e039af86fc26d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:singularity of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}\cap C^{3}$ have a regularly varying right
		tail in the smooth sense:
		$f^{(j)}(x) = (-1)^{j}(p)_{j}\,c_{0}\,x^{-p-j}(1+o(1))$ for
		$j = 0, 1, 2$, with $p > 1$. If $p \neq 2$, then
		\begin{equation}
			R \;\sim\; \frac{p(2-p)}{2c_{0}^{2}}\,x^{2p-2}:
			
		\end{equation}
		the curvature at the boundary of the support diverges to $+\infty$
		for $1<p<2$ and to $-\infty$ for $p>2$; for exponential or faster
		tails, again in the smooth sense, $R \to -\infty$. At $p = 2$ the
		leading divergence cancels and regularity is decided at second
		order: if
		\begin{equation}
			f(x) = c_{0}x^{-2}\big(1 + b\,x^{-\alpha} + o(x^{-\alpha})\big),
			\qquad 0 < \alpha < 2,\ \alpha \neq 1,\ b \neq 0,
			
		\end{equation}

		\begin{equation}
			R \;\sim\; \frac{\alpha b(\alpha - 1)}{c_{0}^{2}}\,x^{2-\alpha},
			
		\end{equation}
		which still diverges. Hence a quadratic leading tail is necessary
		for the curvature to remain bounded at the boundary of rank, but
		not sufficient: every second-order correction of order $x^{-\alpha}$
		with $0 < \alpha < 2$, $\alpha \neq 1$, forces divergence, while
		corrections of order two and faster, again in the smooth sense,
		leave the curvature bounded. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.663948+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe0b9ab34fde7789a1a7422e4253c7d0a94bd101e41899bde76272935b3a9354","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\ge 2k$, let
\[
q:=\frac{p}{p-2k+1},
\]
let $\varkappa\in(0,q)$, and let $a,b>0$. For $r\in\mathbb{N}$, set
\[
\beta_r:=
\frac{p\varkappa}{p(r+\varkappa)+\varkappa r(2k-1)}.
\]
Then, for every pair of mappings $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$ with
$f_j,g_j\in W^{2,p}(\gamma)$,
\[
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j\|_{\dot W^{2,p}(\gamma)}\le b,
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|g_j\|_{\dot W^{2,p}(\gamma)}\le b,
\]
and
\[
\gamma(\Delta_f\le \varepsilon)\le a\varepsilon^\varkappa,
\quad
\gamma(\Delta_g\le \varepsilon)\le a\varepsilon^\varkappa
\quad \forall\, \varepsilon>0,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
2^{14}k^{7/2}(q-\varkappa)^{-1}(a+b^p+1)\,
d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)^{\beta_1}.
\]
More generally, for every $r\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C(r,k)(q-\varkappa)^{-1}(a+b^p+1)\,
d_r(f,g)^{\beta_r},
\]
where
$C(r,k)>0$ depends only on $r$ and $k$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.846925+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe1c10e6a2d337214951b6efe897be373e6635ae64603bdae0fc5d41175318bb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2609.01996, 'Baumslag--Solitar Subgroups Obstruct Model Companions for Fields with Group Actions'] Let \(H\leq G\), let \(K\) be a \(G\)-field, and let \(\chi:H\to K^\times\) satisfy the \(1\)-cocycle condition
  \[
    \chi(h_1h_2)=\chi(h_1)\,h_1\bigl(\chi(h_2)\bigr)\quad(h_1,h_2\in H).
  \]
  Choose a section
  \[
    \rho:G/H\longrightarrow G,\quad \rho(H)=1,
  \]
  and put
  \[
    \alpha(\gamma,\lambda):=\rho(\gamma\lambda)^{-1}\gamma\rho(\lambda)\quad(\gamma\in G,\ \lambda\in G/H).
  \]
  If the elements \(z_\lambda\), \(\lambda\in G/H\), are algebraically independent over \(K\), then the formulas
  \begin{equation}
    \gamma(z_\lambda):=\rho(\gamma\lambda)\bigl(\chi(\alpha(\gamma,\lambda))\bigr)z_{\gamma\lambda}
  \end{equation}
  extend the given action on \(K\) to a \(G\)-field structure on the purely transcendental extension
  \[
    E:=K\bigl(z_\lambda:\lambda\in G/H\bigr).
  \]
  In particular,
  \[
    h(z_H)=\chi(h)z_H\quad(h\in H).
  \]

  Moreover, let \(D\trianglelefteq G\) satisfy \(D\subseteq H\) and \(\chi|_D=1\).
  If \(D\) acts trivially on \(K\), then it acts trivially on \(E\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:44:17.444565+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe2df4e80be75c800cb6f391a22ca0bc96c73ed5b797d15faf063416f6d9d57a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition cor:minibatch-variable-range-eb of arXiv:2608.25551, 'Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules'] Fix deterministic integers $t_0 \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$, and let $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge t_0-1}$ be a filtration. Let $\{c_t\}_{t \ge t_0}$ be an almost surely finite,\footnote{As in Theorem~(thm:variable-range-eb of the paper), no uniform upper bound on the process $\{c_t\}_{t \ge t_0}$ is assumed.} nonnegative predictable process such that $\left|H_t^{(i)}\right| \le c_t$ almost surely for every $t \ge t_0$ and $i = 1, \ldots, b$. \[
    \overline H_{t_0-1}^{\mathrm{MB}}

\begin{equation}
\qquad\qquad\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\varphi(G_k)\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe447b18dfa7282dbfab6cf2ff317c394d4162a056ee29db06a85660230bbec2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 60 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The set $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, is a singleton set consisting of the standard gaussian measure:
$\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)=\{\cN(0,1)\}$.
\begin{proof}
    Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$. By the definition \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, this means that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L>0$ and a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \begin{align*}
        &\WERR(\cA_{N_j}, \mu)
        =\max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big( \mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu \Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\}) \Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,, \\
        &q_0(j) \equiv \chi_{\cA_{N_j}}(0) 
        = \frac{\|\bbE \bsig_j\|_2^2}{N_j} 
        \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1
        \,,
    \end{align*}
where we abbreviate $\bsig_j\equiv \cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
    Define the perturbed (deterministic) algorithm $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ by setting 
    \[
        \tilde{\bsig}_j
        \equiv \tilde\cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
        = \frac{\bbE\bsig_j}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} \,.
    \]
This clearly satisfies $\bbE[\|\tilde{\bsig}_j\|_2^2]  = N_j$, so $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ is a $0$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.
Since $\tilde{\bsig}_j$ is a deterministic vector in $N_j$ dimensions of norm $(N_j)^{1/2}$, we have $\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1)$.
    Note that
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\bbE[
            \|\bsig_j - \tilde{\bsig}_j\|^2]}{N_j} 
        &= \frac{1}{N_j} \bbE\bigg[ \bigg\|
            \bigg(\frac{1}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} - 1 \bigg) 
            	(\bbE\bsig_j)
            - (\bsig_j - \bbE\bsig_j)
        \bigg\|^2 \bigg] \\
        &= \Big(1 - q_0(j)^{1/2}\Big)^2 + \Big(1 - q_0(j)\Big)
        \le 2\Big(1-q_0(j)\Big)\,,
    \end{align*}  
again using that inequality $|x^{1/2}-y^{1/2}| \le |x-y|^{1/2}$ for $x,y\ge0$.
    Then, by Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx}, with constants $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$, $C_2(\alpha,L)$ as defined therein, we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j}),
        	\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1) 
	\Big)
        \le \bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) 2(1-q_0(j)) + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j} \bigg\}^{1/2}\,.
    \]
Combined with the assumption that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu) \le \epsilon$ for all $j$, we find $\bbW_2(\mu,\cN(0,1)) \le \epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\epsilon > 0$, we conclude $\mu = \cN(0,1)$.
    We have thus shown $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1) \subseteq \{\cN(0,1)\}$.
    The reverse inclusion $\cN(0,1) \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$ is witnessed by the (sequence of) deterministic algorithms
    \[
        \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) = (1,\ldots,1) \in \bbR^N\,, 
    \]
    which are $0$-Lipschitz with $\mu(\cA_N) = \cN(0,1)$, $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N) = \delta_1 \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$, and $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 1$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:32:11.153586+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe51a9327c6cadc62fbac36ab460b8c694dbe5fa78c4697f354135b9b3d896ca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:RBGshell of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] Fix an initial (integer) radius $R_0$ and
an initial particle configuration $\eta_0$ with support on 
 $\partial B_{ R_0}$.
Let $N_0 := \sum_{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \eta_0(x)$ be the total number of particles at time zero. 
At each step $t \in \mathbb{Z}_+$,
given the step $t-1$, 
we set
$
R_t := R_{t-1} +   H_t,$
where 
\begin{equation}
H_{t}   : = \Big   \lceil  \,     \Big(  \kappa \,  N_{t-1}  \,   \big( \log (N_{t-1} + 1) \big)^{\beta}  \Big )^{ \frac{1}{d}}  \, \Big \rceil
\end{equation}
with $\beta= 1$ if $d=3$ and $\beta=0$ if $d > 3$. Here $\kappa>0$  is a large enough constant depending only on the dimension.
We start a RBG with radii $R_{t-1}$ and $R_t$ from the  particle configuration 
$\eta_{t-1}$ 
(which has support in $\partial B_{R_{t-1}})$
and let $\eta_t$ be the escaping particle configuration of such process 
(which has  support
in $\partial B_{R_t}$,  recall Definition (def:RBG of the paper)).
We then move to the next step $t+1$ and repeat the procedure. 
Define for any $\alpha >0$ the  stopping time (with the convention that $\inf \emptyset = + \infty$)
\begin{align}

T^{(\alpha)} & : = \inf \{ t  \geq 0  \, : \, N_t  > \alpha  N_0  \} . 
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:44:12.640568+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe6e96c0d78ae6e54024596538afe576691bb94a897f43b59fbcbfdf30ef13c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Agnostic learning of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in (0,1)$. 
Let $\ell:\RR\times\RR\to \RR^+$ be a loss function.
Suppose that $\mu$ is a distribution over $\RR^d \times \RR$ and $\cH$ is a hypothesis class where each element $h\in \cH$ is a function from $\RR^d$ to $\RR$.  
And let $\cD = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i\in [n]}$ be a dataset with i.i.d. samples drawn from $\mu$. 
We say that an algorithm $\cA$ that takes $\cD$ as input and outputs a hypothesis $f:\RR^d\to \RR$ learns $\cH$ agnostically, if with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the draw of $\cD$, it holds that
\begin{align}
    \EE_{\mu}\big[\ell(y,h(x))\big] &\le \mathrm{opt}_{\cH} + \varepsilon, \text{ where } \mathrm{opt}_{\cH} = \inf_{f\in \cH} \EE_{\mu}\big[\ell(y,f(x))\big].  
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:50:44.876226+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe70488bbc8c0d1a0a73c277c1b694502ef05593ed6c7766bfad3789e4a51c17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 57 (Sharp quadratic phase diagram on polynomial-growth groups) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $\Gamma$ be an infinite finitely generated group of polynomial growth
degree $D$.  Fix $1\le r<\infty$, $a,b\ge0$,
$0<\sigma\le D/2$, and $c_x=\langle x\rangle^{-\sigma}$.
Then $(T_{2,N}^{a,b}(c))_N$ is Cauchy in
$L^2(\Omega;\Sch_r)$ if and only if
\begin{equation}

 \frac D4<\sigma\le\frac D2
\end{equation}
and, with $\beta=D-2\sigma$,
\begin{equation}

 a>\beta,\qquad b>\beta,\qquad
 a+b>\beta+\frac Dr.
\end{equation}
Whenever these conditions hold, all the $L^p$-convergence, deviation,
almost-sure convergence, and quantitative cutoff-rate conclusions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:second-order-singular-transfer} hold.  At the logarithmic
endpoint $\sigma=D/2$, the three conditions become
\[
 a>0,\qquad b>0,\qquad a+b>\frac Dr.
\]
If $\sigma\le D/4$, no choice of $a,b\ge0$ yields
$L^2(\Omega;\Sch_r)$ convergence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:30:36.772031+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feab0c801eca517d085eb5e6d8fd868f74e9eabf9886956e0981386eb877a1a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.10102, 'Dynamical mean-field limit and replica-symmetric free energy for the orthogonally-invarian'] Suppose Assumptions \ref{assump:X} and \ref{assump:dynamics} hold with $f=-U'$,
the lower bound $\alpha>0$ in \eqref{eq:Uconvexity} satisfies
$\alpha>\Lambda_{\max}$, and Assumption \ref{assump:convergence} holds. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item The Gibbs measure $\mu_\Gibbs$ is well-defined, and there exist deterministic almost sure limits
\begin{equation}
v_*=\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle \|\btheta\|_2^2 \rangle,
\qquad q_*=\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle \btheta^\top \btheta' \rangle.
\end{equation}
\item For each fixed $\tau \in \R$, there exists a limit
$c_\theta(\tau)=\lim_{s \to \infty} C_\theta(s+\tau,s)$. This defines a
symmetric positive-semidefinite function
$c_\theta:\R \to \R$ satisfying, for some $C,c>0$ and
all $s,t \geq 0$ and $\tau \in \R$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
c_\theta(0)=v_*, \qquad \lim_{\tau \to \infty} c_\theta(\tau)=q_*,\\
|C_\theta(t,s)-c_\theta(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-c\min(s,t)},
\qquad |c_\theta(\tau)-q_*| \leq Ce^{-c|\tau|}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\item For each fixed $\tau \geq 0$, there exists a limit
$r_\theta(\tau)=\lim_{s \to \infty} R_\theta(s+\tau,s)$. This defines a
function $r_\theta:[0,\infty) \to \R$ satisfying, for some $C,c>0$
and all $t \geq s \geq 0$ and $\tau \geq 0$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
|R_\theta(t,s)| \leq Ce^{-c(t-s)}, \qquad
|r_\theta(\tau)| \leq Ce^{-c\tau},\\
|R_\theta(t,s)-r_\theta(t-s)| \leq Ce^{-cs}, \qquad
\int_0^t |R_\theta(t,s)-r_\theta(t-s)| \d s \leq Ce^{-ct}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\item $c_\theta$ is continuous on $\R$, smooth on $(0,\infty)$,
and has a right derivative $c_\theta'(0^+)=\lim_{\tau \to 0^+} c_\theta'(\tau)$
at $\tau=0$. We have the fluctuation-dissipation relation
\begin{equation}
r_\theta(\tau)={-}c_\theta'(\tau) \text{ for } \tau>0,
\qquad r_\theta(0)={-}c_\theta'(0^+)=1.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, for all $\tau>0$, we have
\[c_\theta(\tau) \geq 0,
\qquad r_\theta(\tau) \geq 0, \qquad r_\theta'(\tau) \leq 0.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.712563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feaba3cd7651eeae98cfef872e7da6be688c330e8fd8c20a8243d425094ea1e9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition t.randomfieldCLT-new of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $M=\{M(x)\}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}$ be a random field in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with values in a Polish space
$\mathbb {M} $ and $\zeta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \to \mathbb{R}$ a  measurable function. 
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a simple point process on $\mathbb{R}^d $,
independent of the random field $M$. 
Consider empirical random measures $(\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as in (equation linearstatBsigma of the paper).
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
Assume that $\mathcal{P}$ has fast mixing correlations 
as in Definition~(d.omegamixing of the paper)(i.mixing-ground-fast of the paper). Assume that either (a) the random field $M$ satisfies the fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.B-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper) or (b) 
$M$  satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL}-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.BL-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper)
and $\zeta(x,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz. If $\zeta$ satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for all $p>1$ then the central limit theorem holds for
    $(\hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, i.e., as $n \to \infty$

\[   ({\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) )^{-1/2}\Big( \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) - \mathbb {E}  \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) \Big) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,
  \]
for $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$,  provided
${\rm Var} \, {\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$.

\item  
Suppose the random field~$M$ and the point process~$\mathcal{P}$ are stationary 
(necessarily jointly so, due to their independence) with~$\mathcal{P}$ having intensity~$\rho$, 
and suppose that~$\zeta$ is translation invariant, 
i.e., $\zeta(x,\cdot) = \zeta(\cdot)$. Also assume $\zeta$ satisfies the $(1+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.
Then the mean empirical field satisfies for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}
n^{-1} \, \mathbb{E}  \, \hat\sigma_n^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta(\0,M(\0)) \int_{W_1} f(x)\, \mathrm{d} x, \quad n\in\mathbb{N},
\end{equation}
which holds  without assuming mixing conditions on~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$M$ nor  Lipschitz conditions on $\zeta$. Moreover, under either of the mixing assumptions (a) or (b) of part~(i.CLT-infinite-zeta-field-mixing of the paper) we obtain for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \sigma^2(\zeta) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d} x,
\]
where
\begin{align}  
\sigma^2(\zeta) 
&:= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta^2(\0,M(\0)) \\
&\quad + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 
\Big( 
\mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))\, \zeta(x,M(x))]\, \rho^{(2)}(\0,x)
- \rho^2\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))]\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(x,M(x))]  
\Big)\, \mathrm{d} x \in [0, \infty) \nonumber
\end{align}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357430+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feb7ff89f7ecb021ab1aa195f46a8f119ae55386714824dd65634a1101bfea88","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 241 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,\iota > 0$ and $\fq\in [1,2)$ there exists $\epsilon = \epsilon(\alpha,\iota,\fq) > 0$ such that 
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) 
	: \mu\in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
	\bigg\}
	\le \iota\,.
	\]
The same statement holds with
$\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ and
$\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ in place of $\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)$
and $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$. (The sets mentioned above specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs}, \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}, and \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L.SYM}.)

\begin{proof} Let
$\cA_N$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm. 
If $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ satisfies $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \le \epsilon$, then Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} gives, for $N$ large enough,
	\[
	\|\mu\|_{L^2} 
	\le 
	\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2} 
	+ \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}}{\le} 
	C(\alpha)^{1/2} + \epsilon
	\le (2C(\alpha))^{1/2}\,,
	\]
where the last bound holds for $\epsilon$ small enough. For such $\epsilon$, it follows by recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L} and \eqref{e:cM.Lip} that 
	\[\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon) 
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}}{=}
	\bigcup_{L>0}
		\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))\,.
	\]
For $\iota > 0$, define the set
	\[
		S_\iota = \Big\{\mu \in \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha)) : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \ge \iota\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Now suppose for contradiction that $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ intersects $S_\iota$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.
	Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq} that the $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$
	endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric
	 is compact.
	The set $S_\iota$ is closed with respect to this metric. Thus, for any sufficiently small $\epsilon > 0$, the set
	\[
		S_\iota \cap \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
	\]
	(where the overline now denotes closure with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric) is a nonempty closed subset of $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$ indexed by $\epsilon$, hence also compact.
	These sets form a nested family of nonempty compact sets, so their intersection is also nonempty.
	However, their intersection is
	\beq
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
		\subseteq  
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;2\epsilon)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip}}{=} 
		S_\iota \cap \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha)
		\stackrel{\textup{Thm.~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}}}{=} S_\iota \cap \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)
		= \emptyset\,,
	\eeq
which yields a contradiction.
This proves that there exists $\epsilon$ such that $\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le \iota$ for all $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$.
	The analogous claim for $\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ and $\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ is proved similarly, using Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.sym} in place of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main} in \eqref{e:confinement.cM.lip.to.nbd.of.ideal}.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:39:18.529941+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feb831217536e0fd64600a05ad757e6dcc26041a029ceefead162e5cae36aa83","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 57 (Failure of Euclidean rigidity without the

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.088598+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ff35855d742db6826ee06b4998e5c7ffeffa567fb2cf09cd0a51e06ee90ecf29","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 (Ewens fragmentation process $\Pp^{(n,\theta)}$) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $\theta>0$ and an integer $n\ge 1$.
We construct a random finite rooted tree $(\mathcal T_n , K)\in \Omega$ as follows.
Each vertex $u$ carries an integer mass $K(u)\in\{1,2,\dots\}$.
The root is denoted by $\varnothing$ and has mass
\[
K(\varnothing)=n.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Splitting rule.}
Let $u$ be a vertex.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $K(u)=1$, then $u$ is declared a leaf and produces no children.
\item If $K(u)=k\ge 2$, set $m:=k-1$ and sample an $\mathrm{Ewens}(m,\theta)$ partition with count vector
$(C^{(u)}_1,\dots,C^{(u)}_m)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:ewens}.
Let $(A^{(u)}_1 \ge A^{(u)}_2 \ge \cdots \ge A^{(u)}_{\delta(u)})$ be the corresponding partition of block sizes, i.e.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\delta(u)} A^{(u)}_i = m,\qquad
\#\{i: A^{(u)}_i=j\}=C^{(u)}_j.
\]
Then $u$ produces $\delta(u)$ children, denoted $(ui)_{1\le i\le \delta(u)}$, with masses
\[
K(ui):=A^{(u)}_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,\delta(u).
\]
\end{itemize}
All splitting variables at different vertices are sampled independently. We
denote $\Pp^{(n,\theta)}$ the probability measure on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$
corresponding to this procedure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627086+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_ff59d2398b1d8908abce8ec01c01a24a737fa38a46423f1defdc0f7bb6f05a02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space. The Borel sigma-algebra B(X) is the smallest sigma-algebra of subsets of X containing every open set (equivalently, every closed set); its members are the Borel sets. It is the intersection of all sigma-algebras containing the topology, so it exists and is unique. On the real line, B(R) is generated equally by the open intervals, by the closed intervals, by the half-lines (-infinity, a] with a rational, or by any base of the topology; every open, closed, F_sigma (countable union of closed sets) and G_delta (countable intersection of open sets) set is Borel, and the Borel sets are stratified by the Borel hierarchy of countable length omega_1. B(R^n) equals the product sigma-algebra of n copies of B(R). Every continuous map between topological spaces is Borel measurable (preimages of Borel sets are Borel), as is every pointwise limit of a sequence of Borel measurable real functions; but the image of a Borel set under a continuous map need not be Borel - such images are the analytic sets (Suslin, 1917). B(R) has the cardinality of the continuum, 2^{aleph_0}, while the Lebesgue measurable sets number 2^{2^{aleph_0}} (every subset of the null Cantor set is measurable), so there exist Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel: Lebesgue measure on B(R) is completed by adjoining all subsets of Borel null sets. Every finite Borel measure on a Polish space is regular (inner regular by compact sets: a Radon measure), which is why Borel sets are the natural domain of measures on metric spaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198610+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_ff61ff48cce572f4f7d51c7a320ea48eadc31611bdd1fdfe4cc31d52318be257","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For A a subset of a topological space (X, tau), the subspace (relative) topology on A is tau_A = { A intersect U : U in tau }: its open sets are the intersections with A of open sets of X, and likewise its closed sets are the intersections with A of closed sets of X. This is a topology - it contains A and empty, and the identities (A intersect U1) intersect (A intersect U2) = A intersect (U1 intersect U2) and union of (A intersect U_i) = A intersect (union U_i) give closure under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. It is the coarsest topology making the inclusion i: A -> X continuous, since i is continuous for a topology sigma on A iff A intersect U is sigma-open for every U in tau, i.e. iff tau_A is contained in sigma. Universal property: for any space Z, a map f: Z -> A is continuous iff the composite Z -> A -> X is continuous - the property that characterizes the subspace topology.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:46:00.323880+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ff635e43a4f7183ed9fb0206c430cd5e4a3e6443e49c6893a5579d9ac52c8682","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:sec5-boundary-fan of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Fix $0\leq\lambda\leq1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(i) One-sided boundary probe.}
Fix $\xi\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_r\in\mathbb{D}$, where $r\geq1$.
There is a random connected compact set
$C=C^\lambda_{\xi;z_1,\ldots,z_r}\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ such that
$C\cap\partial\mathbb{D}=\{\xi\}$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_r\in C$, and, for every
compact $E\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with $\xi\notin E$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_C\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{\{C\cap E=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(C,E)}
 \right]
 =\prod_{j=1}^r
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi,z_j)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi,z_j)}.
 \end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(ii) Two-sided boundary probe.}
Fix distinct $\xi_+,\xi_-\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and
$z_1,\ldots,z_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s\in\mathbb{D}$, where $r,s\geq1$.
There is a random compact set $C\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with at most two
connected components such that $C\cap\partial\mathbb{D}=\{\xi_+,\xi_-\}$, one
component contains $\xi_+,z_1,\ldots,z_r$, and one, possibly the same,
contains $\xi_-,w_1,\ldots,w_s$. Moreover, for every compact
$E\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with $E\cap\{\xi_+,\xi_-\}=\varnothing$,
\[
 \mathbb E_C\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{\{C\cap E=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(C,E)}
 \right]
 =\prod_{j=1}^r
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi_+,z_j)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi_+,z_j)}
 \prod_{k=1}^s
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi_-,w_k)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi_-,w_k)}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:54:15.635168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ff8fa2a8bed173d7379bab4bfdb4f16506e169c9ee531dec09763549ad4379a3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 97 (Typed Hoffman interface and collision kernel) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let $E$ be finite dimensional and fix a stochastic weight $N\ge2$.  =\frac12Y_{s,t}^{\otimes2}+\operatorname{Alt}_2\mathbb Y^I_{s,t}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:10:05.795845+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ff91bb7a170547899a3b17eaa7ad9a11ddc947f90939d7baa4b872b5ddd0d1a0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(\Lambda:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be finite, \(C^1\), and strictly convex,

\[
        J(x):=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb R}\{\theta x-\Lambda(\theta)\},

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on R^n","M is the centered or uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553467+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, maximal functions","id":"claim_ffa8aee1191447b8b8fa930b110a55716c66233d776634ca4058ba7238a266e6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality is WEAK type (1,1), never strong type (1,1), and Marcinkiewicz interpolation gives nothing at p = 1 (its constant contains p/(p - p_0) and blows up as p -> 1+). Precisely: if f is in L^1(R^n) and f is not a.e. 0, then Mf is NOT in L^1(R^n). Global counterexample: pick R with c = int_{B(0,R)} |f| > 0; for |x| >= R the ball B(x, 2|x|) contains B(0,R), so Mf(x) >= c / (v_n (2|x|)^n), which is not integrable at infinity. Local counterexample showing the failure is not only at infinity: f(x) = |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-2} 1_{{|x| < 1/2}} is in L^1, but averaging over B(x, 2|x|) gives Mf(x) >= c' |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-1} near 0, which is not locally integrable. The correct endpoint substitutes are: (i) the weak (1,1) bound |{Mf > t}| <= 3^n ||f||_1 / t; (ii) Stein's L log L theorem: for f supported in a ball B, Mf is integrable over B if and only if int_B |f| log^+ |f| < infinity. So a proof that applies 'M is bounded on L^p' at p = 1, or that interpolates strong (1,1) with strong (infinity, infinity), is wrong; the same warning applies to any operator known only to be weak (1,1), such as the Calderon-Zygmund singular integrals and the Hilbert transform.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is locally integrable on R^n","balls are Euclidean and |.| is Lebesgue measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552000+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, real-variable methods","id":"claim_ffa9201fa7a9c6fdbdafe36863b70b61b6ad169b72c4ec8441e19549baf37472","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For f in L^1_loc(R^n) (Lebesgue measure |.|), the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is Mf(x) = sup_{r>0} (1/|B(x,r)|) int_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, with values in [0, infinity]. The uncentered version is M'f(x) = sup over all open balls B containing x of (1/|B|) int_B |f|; one has Mf <= M'f <= 2^n Mf. The set {Mf > t} is open for every t (so Mf is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel measurable), M is sublinear, M(f) = M(|f|), and ||Mf||_infinity <= ||f||_infinity. Cubes in place of balls give a pointwise comparable operator (constants depending only on n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.451352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ffb62c7a1f08a5115d281b8f53372db505a32bb2534fc39b7b35447823a85c6b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 15 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] Let $\Tr^1(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ be the space of trace polynomials in $d$ variables, $k \in \N_0$, $R > 0$, and $Q \in \Tr^1(X_1,\dots,X_d)$. Write
\[
\norm{Q}_{j,R} \coloneqq \sup_{(\cA,\tau) \in \mathbb{W}}\ \sup_{n\geq 0}\ \sup_{j_0+\dots+j_n=j} \norm{\Big(\widetilde{\partial}^{(j_n)}\circ\cdots\circ \widetilde{\partial}^{(j_1)}\circ \partial^{(j_0)}Q\Big)^{\cA}}_{\cA,R},
\]
where
$$ \norm{f}_{\cA,R} = \sup \left\{ \norm{f(x_1,\dots,x_{j+1})}_{\cA^{j,j+1}} \colon x_a\in\cA, \norm{x_a}\leq R, \forall a,b, x_a\sim x_b \right\}, $$
where one says that $x\sim y$ if $x$ and $y$ have the same noncommutative law, and given $P_1,\dots,P_{j+1}$ trace polynomials, we set

and we define $\cC^k(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ to be the Fr\'echet-space completion of $\Tr^1(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ with respect to the family $\big\{\norm{\cdot}_{\cC^k,R} : R > 0\big\}$ of seminorms and $\cC^{\infty}(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ to be the completion with respect to the family $\big\{\norm{\cdot}_{\cC^k,R} : R > 0, \, k \in \N\big\}$ of seminorms.","status":"unverified"}

\[
